Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.

#3279. US charges three men over $129m scheme that faked CEOs’ voices with AI

Prosecutors in New York say the men posed as executives and lawyers on calls, then laundered the money through crypto.

The men are Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42. Spanish police arrested Soall and Hazan in June and August, and UK police arrested Sheetrit in September. The US has asked for all three to be extradited.

The scheme ran from 2024 to 2026, according to the indictment. The men would call an employee while posing as the company’s chief executive, using AI to mimic the boss’s voice or image. They would ask for help with a secret deal.

The fake CEO then told the employee to contact a lawyer at a large international law firm. Another member of the group posed as that lawyer and gave the bank details for a large transfer.

The victims included a Missouri hospital system, which lost about $4.8m, and a UK fintech company, which lost about $11.6m. A Rhode Island bank, a California hospital system, a Massachusetts mutual fund, and a Florida pet food company were also hit.

The money went to accounts in countries including Spain, Greece, the UAE, Singapore, and China. It was then turned into cryptocurrency to hide where it came from, prosecutors said.

Soall mainly posed as UK lawyers and kept a handwritten script called Lawyer Call, according to the indictment. Hazan and Sheetrit are accused of laundering the money. Hazan was convicted of bank fraud conspiracy in the same court in 2008.

The three face charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and aggravated identity theft. The most serious counts carry up to 20 years in prison. The charges are allegations, and the men are presumed innocent.

The case is a larger version of a 2019 voice-cloning fraud, in which criminals faked a CEO’s voice to steal $243,000. Since then, AI impersonation scams have grown fast.

#3278. Apple’s DOJ antitrust battle sparks disputes with Epic, Samsung, Oura, Roblox, more

Several tech companies are pushing back against subpoenas issued by Apple and the DOJ in their ongoing antitrust battle. Here are the details.

In March 2024, the Department of Justice and 15 states, plus the District of Columbia, filed a lawsuit accusing Apple of restricting competition, limiting interoperability with rival products, and making it harder for consumers to switch to competing devices. Apple denies these allegations.

Since then, despite recent reports of settlement talks happening behind the scenes, the two sides have clashed repeatedly over discovery, which is the pretrial process through which both sides exchange evidence relevant to the case.

As part of its effort to refute the DOJ’s arguments, Apple has subpoenaed several third-party companies and organizations, seeking documents and information relevant to its defense. That includes Epic Games, Samsung Electronics America, Meta, Oura, Garmin, Playco, Ultrahuman, PayPal, Match Group, and the Connectivity Standards Alliance, among others.

The DOJ and plaintiff states, in turn, have issued their own subpoenas, including to Roblox, Epic Games, Snap, and the Connectivity Standards Alliance, seeking evidence to support their allegations against Apple.

Google, Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, and Capital One are also named in legal documents.

In essence, both sides are trying to use data from Apple’s competitors and companies with which it has commercial relationships to establish how its policies affect competition, and whether those policies are justified or constitute anticompetitive behavior.

Over the past couple of days, multiple letters submitted to the court reveal disagreements over the scope of the subpoenas, the information being requested, and whether the companies should be required to produce certain documents.

Epic Games, for instance, argues that Apple’s requests for documents from three previous lawsuits (Epic v. Apple in the US, Epic v. Apple in Australia, and Epic v. Google in the US), along with extensive searches of internal files belonging to three senior executives, including its CEO, would be disproportionately burdensome.

Still, the company has offered to produce several categories of information, including Fortnite user and revenue data, contracts with Google and Samsung, and records relating to Apple’s Core Technology Fee.

Samsung, in turn, has agreed to search documents belonging to two executives, which the company says have yielded nearly 900,000 documents matching the agreed-upon search terms.

However, Apple wants to expand the searches to six additional executives, including Samsung Electronics America’s current and former CEOs, and obtain deposition transcripts from Samsung executives who testified in the DOJ’s antitrust lawsuit against Google.

The companies also disagree over whether Samsung Electronics America should be required to produce documents held by its South Korean parent company, which is a dispute we covered here before.

As for Oura, the company is pushing back on several fronts, including whether Apple should reimburse it for reviewing more than 32,000 additional documents, and whether it may withhold or redact certain information it considers trade secrets.

Garmin has raised similar objections to Apple’s requests for confidential financial and strategic information.

Roblox, which is the only company among these recent filings subpoenaed by the DOJ and plaintiff states rather than Apple or other plaintiffs, is disputing requests for information about its relationship with Apple and how Apple’s App Store policies are applied. The government, meanwhile, argues that the documents could help establish whether Apple consistently applies its App Store Guidelines to developers.

Another interesting dispute involves Japan-based instant gaming company Playco, which is resisting Apple’s requests for documents concerning its efforts to influence App Store policies, including lobbying activities.

Playco argues that producing these materials would violate its First Amendment rights, citing a 2021 court decision involving similar requests Apple made to Match Group.

Several of the companies have also requested until November 11 to continue negotiations before their disputes are formally declared at an impasse, potentially avoiding further court intervention.

All of this is happening against the backdrop of another dispute between Apple and the DOJ involving the company’s efforts to obtain documents from 14 federal agencies.

Although a special master has twice sided with Apple, the order remains on hold while the court considers the government’s appeal.

#3274. When Electric Cars Were for Women

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3273. HH Princess Sophia Wolkonsky brings royalty, global business leaders and esports figures together in Vienna for Castillia 2026

The Castillia founder and CEO hosted an exclusive three-day Heritage Gala and marked the launch of AVOR, with HRH Prince Omar bin Faisal of Jordan, HRH Prince Gabriel of Nassau of Luxembourg, Johann Strobl, Vlad Marinescu and TNW CEO Alexandru Stan among the attendees.

From left: HH Princess Dr. Michaela Wolkonsky, ⁠HIRH Archduchess Herta Margarete Habsburg-Lothringen, HRH Princess Fenosoa Ralandison Ratsimamanga of Madagascar, HH Princess Sophia Wolkonsky.

VIENNA, Austria, HH Princess Sophia Wolkonsky, founder and CEO of Castillia, brought together members of royal families, international business leaders, technology executives and esports figures in Vienna from October 30 to November 1 for Castillia’s Heritage Gala 2026, an invitation-only celebration of cultural heritage, innovation and international connections.

Under her leadership, the three-day gathering connected guests from royalty, finance, entrepreneurship, technology, sports and culture across several of Vienna’s historic venues.

Among the attendees were HRH Prince Omar bin Faisal of Jordan, President of the Jordan Esports Federation; HRH Prince Gabriel of Nassau, a member of Luxembourg’s Grand Ducal family; Johann Strobl, former CEO of Raiffeisen Bank International; Vlad Marinescu, President of the International Esports Federation; and Alexandru Stan, CEO of The Next Web (TNW).

Founded and led by Princess Sophia Wolkonsky, Castillia focuses on historic properties, cultural heritage and curated experiences that connect tradition with contemporary international communities. The Vienna Heritage Gala reflected that vision, pairing formal celebrations with conversations about the future of cultural preservation.

The programme, themed The Enchanted Forest, included an opening reception, a Heritage Salon with panel discussions, a formal gala dinner and a farewell brunch. Its central milestone was the launch of AVOR, a new nonprofit cultural initiative.

Esports was among the emerging industries attracting interest from participants at the Vienna gathering, although it was not the official focus of the gala.

HRH Prince Omar bin Faisal has played an influential role in esports through his leadership in Jordan and involvement with international esports organizations. Vlad Marinescu, President of the International Esports Federation, also attended, bringing an international perspective on competitive gaming and its institutional development.

Filip Šoć, President of the Alliance of Electronic Sports of Montenegro and founder of Montenegro Future Festival, was also present. HRH Prince Gabriel of Nassau also expressed interest in the sector.

The gathering also included Johann Strobl, former CEO of Raiffeisen Bank International, alongside entrepreneurs and leaders from other sectors. Their presence illustrated the event’s breadth beyond traditional cultural and royal circles.

The inauguration of AVOR was a central moment of Castillia 2026. According to the official invitation, the international nonprofit initiative is developing a Global Cultural Atlas, with young people documenting the stories and places that shape cultural heritage.

The launch took place on October 30 at Vienna Private Members, Wiener Rennverein, at Palais Esterházy. On October 31, the Heritage Salon was held at Park Hyatt Vienna, followed by the formal Heritage Gala at Palais Pallavicini. The programme concluded on November 1.

The event was held under the patronage of figures including HRH Prince Omar bin Faisal of Jordan, Princess Ratsimamanga Ralandison Fenosoa, Maharani Sahiba Nivritti Kumari Mewar of Udaipur, Duke Michael zu Mecklenburg and Prince Constantin Sturdza.

By bringing historic families, cultural leaders, business executives and figures from emerging industries into the same setting, Princess Sophia Wolkonsky’s Castillia offered a meeting point between the preservation of the past and the opportunities of the future.

Disclosure: TNW CEO Alexandru Stan attended Castillia 2026 as a guest. TNW received no payment for this article, and Castillia did not cover travel or accommodation for our attendance.

#3272. watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love

watchOS 27.3 arrived this week in beta alongside iOS 27.3, with a major new feature for the latest Apple Watch models: Siri Recap, which I’m already really loving.

If you bought an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 this fall, there are two exclusive new features coming in watchOS 27.3: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Both ‘Audio Intelligence’ features were announced at Apple’s September keynote, but just debuted in beta this week.

Siri Recap in particular has stirred some controversy. Here’s what the feature does, per Apple:

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Siri Recaps can be set to automatically delete after a period of up to 7 days unless you choose to explicitly save them.

It’s understandable why users would be concerned. Once enabled, Siri Recap can turn your Apple Watch into a device that’s always listening and often takes notes on what it hears.

Speaking strictly of the functionality of Siri Recap itself, however, I’ve been very impressed.

I enabled Siri Recap after installing the iOS and watchOS 27.3 betas on Tuesday. When I checked the first recaps on Wednesday inside the Siri app, I was blown away.

Siri had created a record of the things I’d done Tuesday afternoon and evening with remarkable accuracy and detail, as seen above.

One example that especially shocked me: after shopping for Christmas decorations with my family, Siri documented the size of a table runner we looked at. The thing is, I had no memory of anyone even mentioning its size. My wife must have, but despite me missing it, Siri wrote it down.

Another fun one: Thursday morning during breakfast, my son wanted to listen some music on our HomePod. Later that day, I found that the songs we’d listened to were saved at the bottom of my latest recap.

It’s still very early days with Siri Recap, which is only in beta right now, but what I’ve seen this week has been really exciting. And so far at least, I’ve seen zero information in a recap that I’d consider too sensitive to be included.

What’s your take on Siri Recap? Have you given it a try? Let us know in the comments.

#3271. I ran 35 miles in the Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX, and it’s a great waterproof shoe for mixed terrain running

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX is a waterproof running shoe designed primarily for gravel, but it’s also very capable on roads and other light trails. It will suit some runners’ needs perfectly, but the waterproof upper can run hot.

Comfortable midsole with good energy return

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

For those of us in the Northern Hemisphere, the cold, wet days of winter are approaching fast, and if you plan on running through the season, there are some benefits to buying a specialist set of running shoes for it.

The two features I look for in the best running shoes for the winter are an outsole that grips well in wet conditions and a water-repellent or waterproof upper.

Both boxes are ticked by the Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX, which has a Gore-Tex membrane in the upper, is fully waterproof, and has a gravel-ready outsole that works well on a wide variety of terrain.

I’ve used the shoe for a mix of runs on roads, light trails and grassy hills and it’s impressed me as a winter-ready daily trainer. If you don’t need its waterproof upper or versatile outsole, though, you’ll get a better ride from some lighter, bouncier road options like the Asics Novablast 6.

The Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX launched in fall 2026 and costs $160 in the U.S. and £145 in the U.K., which is $20/£20 more expensive than the standard model of the shoe without the Gore-Tex upper.

Salomon also released the Aero Glide 4 GRVL in its line-up, which is a slightly softer and more cushioned option than the Blaze, which some runners might prefer for easy long runs in particular.

The Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX is currently available in four colors, including Vanilla Ice, the model I tested for those who want to show off the dirt they run through, and an all-black design for those who don’t.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

My US men’s size 10 weighs exactly 10oz, which is light for a shoe with a thick outsole, waterproof upper, and tall stack of foam in the midsole.

The stack height is 37mm at the heel and 29mm at the forefoot for an 8mm drop, which is a little lower than the stack on the Aero Glide 4 GRVL.

I found the shoe fit me well in my normal running shoe size, and the Gore-Tex upper wasn’t stiff or uncomfortable during my testing.

The Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX uses a mesh upper with Gore-Tex lining and padding on the tongue and around the collar.

During my testing, I was able to run in heavy rain and splash through puddles without my feet getting wet, and I also like that it’s quick and easy to clean the waterproof upper after muddy runs.

However, the drawback is that it’s not the most breathable material, and when running in warm conditions or using the shoe for walks, my feet got sweatier than normal.

Rather than traditional laces, it has Salomon’s QuickLace Neo system so you can loosen and tighten the fit quickly with the pull toggle, which you can then tuck under an elastic band so it doesn’t bounce around on the run.

The Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX uses a supercritical TPU foam called OptiFoam Squared in its midsole, with a mild rocker shape helping to roll you from heel to toe with each stride.

I’m a fan of this foam, which is also used on the Aero Glide 4 GRVL. It’s soft enough to be comfortable without being overly squishy, and it gives a good amount of energy return when you hit faster paces.

The rubber outsole on the shoe has 2.5mm deep, chevron-shaped lugs that are built to grip on gravel tracks but also work well on roads and other light trails.

This outsole is a star feature on the shoe because it allows you to tackle such a wide variety of terrain with confidence, even in wet conditions.

The Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX proved to be an enjoyably versatile shoe in my testing. I used it as my main daily trainer, tackling easy, steady-paced runs mainly on the road and forest trails.

I also used it for one run on slightly more technical trails with rocky and grassy sections, and throughout all my testing, the grip was impressively reliable, even in very wet conditions. It’s not a good option for deep mud, but can handle most other trails well.

That versatility extends to the paces the Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX can handle. The midsole has a responsive feel at faster paces while soft enough for long, easy runs — it felt good at all the paces I’d run at outside dedicated interval workouts.

The waterproof upper does its job on rainy days well, and also helps keep your feet warm on easy runs in cold conditions.

However, this upper did limit me because it can be a bit too hot at times. My feet got very sweaty on longer runs on dry days, and if you’re a runner who uses one shoe for everything, a fully waterproof sneaker like this probably isn't the best buy.

The Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX does a great job in the role it’s built for. The waterproof upper is great on wet, cold days; the outsole grips well in wet and dry conditions on both the road and light trails, and the midsole is enjoyably energetic.

If that all sounds good but you want something a little softer and more cushioned, the Salomon Aero Glide 4 GRVL also comes in a Gore-Tex model, and Salomon also has non-GTX models of both shoes, and road versions with less substantial outsoles.

There are a lot of choices in the line-up, and I’d say all are good shoes thanks to the OptiFoam Squared midsole at the heart of them, so you can tailor your Blaze or Glide to suit your needs and preferences.

If you’re sticking to the roads during your winter runs, I’d also consider the Adidas Adizero Evo SL ATR, which has a water-repellent upper and small lugs on its outsole. It’s a good option if the full waterproof upper and thick outsole on the Aero Blaze 4 GRVL GTX is overkill for your needs.

Nick Harris-Fry is an experienced health and fitness journalist, writing professionally since 2012. He spent nine years working on the Coach magazine and website before moving to the fitness team at Tom’s Guide in 2024. Nick is a keen runner and also the founder of YouTube channel The Run Testers, which specialises in reviewing running shoes, watches, headphones and other gear.

Nick ran his first marathon in 2016 and became obsessed with the sport. He now has PBs of 2hr 25min for the marathon and 15min 30sec for 5K. Nick is also a qualified Run Leader in the UK.

#3270. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

If you look at the ARPU numbers over the last several quarters, the declines have been getting lower and lower and lower, and we kind of got back to the point this quarter where it was kind of flat year-over-year.

That was driven off strong success in -- across pretty much all of our segments, as I said, mix shift towards plans in value -- higher value plans in the T-brand side, migrations within our brands kind of up the value stack. On the B2B side, we saw strong sequential growth across both SMB and enterprise. And to answer your other question, no, there wasn't anything done funny with the numbers. Those were kind of legitimate numbers on our side. And I think you can see it in our service revenue growth at 1% year-over-year.

I think the final point I'll just say around kind of discipline is we also took a very disciplined approach to subsidy throughout the quarter in Q3 and made sure as we will do through Black Friday, that if we were participating in a subsidy promotion, it was only on ones where we were backed up and supported by our device partners, device OEM partners. So that would be it. Victor, do you want to make any comments on that?

Victor Dodig: I might make a few comments on the PureFibre. I'll hand it off to Gopi then briefly as well. I mean, in the end, when you listen to Dave speak and hopefully from all of our remarks, you get this sense that there's an intentional strategic pivot to profitable growth with a good return on capital. I mean that's the way we're thinking about our business and serving our customers with their needs in mind and making sure that they're happy being served by TELUS. When it comes to fiber-to-the-home, Vince, it's worthwhile reemphasizing control is important to us. That is table stakes, foundational.

When it comes to valuation, we do think that the current shares don't even reflect the value of that fiber. It is very valuable. We know that from investors that have already knocked on our door to say, look, we can unlock some value here for you, you can redeploy it. And that's exactly how we're thinking about it. So Gopi, maybe just shed a little light on perhaps some of the directional numbers of how we think about things.

Gopi Chande: So Victor, I'm going to stay away from anchoring on any valuation. And specifically, that's because we're still defining our perimeter. We have a lot of options in terms of what we can include in that. And so that is good flexibility for us. That will influence the valuation. So we don't want to anchor on that. But again, very excited about the potential on our own balance sheet that echoing Victor's comments, we don't feel are reflected in our share price.

Victor Dodig: Excellent. I think you actually had something in your research report long ago, Vince, you can kind of do the numbers and tell us what you think it's worth one day.

Operator: The next question is from Tim Casey from BMO Capital Markets.

Tim Casey: A few for me. One, just on the PureFibre. I mean, is the structure of this deal akin to kind of a structured equity arrangement similar to what one of your peers have done that essentially becomes long-term money. Is that what you're proposing here?

Gopi Chande: Yes. So Tim, I'll jump in. We're still working through the structure. But in general, no, that isn't what we're looking at. So this is more about structuring this in a way that there's a partnership in terms of the returns between whoever we partner with or groups that we partner with and ourselves and then contemplating whether at which point we put build of future fiber into the structure. So we'll continue to iterate on this and come back, but not similar to what one of our peers do.

Victor Dodig: All about driving organic growth, Tim. Good organic growth with a good return on capital.

Tim Casey: On that, you talked about -- you put one number around your AI strategy that was $500 million in revenues over the next few years. How do we square that with the projections from the previous management team that had a $2 billion number. Could you help us reconcile those? And then second, on the $450 million in OpEx, Dave, can you talk a little bit about what's different? Because monetizing automation on telecom platforms is kind of table stakes. Everyone is doing that. If you're not doing that, you're falling behind.

So can you give us an idea of things that you're not going to do that were being done under previous management to help us understand how you're going to surface that $450 million?

Victor Dodig: All right. Tim, that's a good question. So why don't we answer the first one, which talks about what the previous target was, what the current target is. And I will say that there's been a refinement to our strategic narrative so it's much more focused on our core domestic market and revenues that we have line of sight to in businesses that we're good at and understand. The previous target was maybe a little more ambitious and a little more global in perspective when you actually think about our overall strategy of going back to our core, that fits tightly within that.

So maybe, Navin, you can shed a little bit of light on that, and I'll hand it off to Dave for the other part of the question.

Navin Arora: Yes. I think, Victor, you hit it at a high level, and it is the refined strategy that we're moving ahead with, which is very much focused on 3 key pillars in our AI digital infrastructure play. So the first -- just to kind of summarize them again. The first is our PureFibre network connectivity to the data centers that are being built across Canada and mostly in our incumbent zones. The second is the expansion of our existing data center facilities and bringing in the sovereign AI compute as well as turnkey wholesale capabilities. And then the third part of our infrastructure strategy is to look at powered shell data structure or data center infrastructure.

And so on the powered shell piece, that's not in the number that Victor shared, the $500 million. We are looking at it and we'll consider that as part of our AI number going forward. And I would say the original number that we shared included a lot of the TELUS digital elements. And we've now removed the TELUS Digital elements, and we'll be focused on these 3 pillars, specifically within Canada and specifically on our infrastructure play.

David Fuller: Yes. So I would focus first on -- I mean, the $450 million, it's actually slightly more than that. It's closer to 55% of the $900 million by the time we get to the run rate savings at the end of '28 are coming on EBITDA-enhancing initiatives, primarily through OpEx reductions. It's kind of driven across 4 areas, right? So it's not just simply AI automation. And I'm sorry if I confused things by using that automation word. It starts on the care side of the business, right? So we have, we believe, significant opportunity to basically reduce the friction points and the reason customers call us today. So I think that's across everything from rate plan simplification.

Like a big part of this focus is around simplification of our rate plans of our products, trying to reduce the number of unprofitable products that we're taking into the marketplace, our service offerings and bill simplification, right? A huge percentage of calls we get today are questions around bill. You've seen across the board, we've moved to Shock-Free plans on both mobility and on our wireline side. So again, there's less reasons to call. So a large part of it is reducing pain points and reasons to call.

Then in the calls that still have to happen, that's where AI comes in, in terms of enabling self-serve options more easily for our customers to be able to answer their questions or answer or make whatever change they want to make with our service offerings themselves through our web portals and our apps. And then eventually, if you do need to speak to an agent, Agentic AI can help in that regard as well. And by no means are we going to be in a world where there's never a chance to talk to someone at TELUS.

That will happen at kind of the tail end of that journey if we've not been able to answer your questions and help you out prior to that. The second area is channel optimization, right? I think there's a big opportunity, and we've really focused the team in on focusing on profitable loading, right, and profitable gross adds. And that's across not just the profitability of the product, which we're also looking at enhancing, but it's also around cost of acquisition, right, and streamlining our cost of acquisition, and we think there's a substantial opportunity in that regard. Third is reliability.

So using AI to be proactive about reliability across our networks, across our products, across our services, across our systems and again, streamlining repair calls, reducing repair calls, reducing reasons to roll trucks. And then the last area is around field force efficiency where we think there's another significant opportunity for us there. So it's not just simply AI-based automation and table stakes as you termed it, but it's kind of across transforming how we support service our customers today.

Operator: The next question is from Jerome Dubreuil from Desjardins.

Jerome Dubreuil: I'd like to dive into your efficiency program. It's good to see the $900 million in savings that you expect. But can you share if there's a benchmark against what this objective is set maybe in terms of a certain absolute level of OpEx or CapEx so we can track the process and start to think of a pro forma TELUS, for example, is the half of the $900 million CapEx savings, including or excluding the Ontario and Quebec opportunity, just because we've had a few synergy numbers in the past in the industry and was something that was difficult to reconcile those.

Victor Dodig: Yes. So Gopi is going to answer that question. I'll just remind you that the $900 million number of deals with our core business footprint as it currently stands. As we -- and you have to think about our growth also very, very much connected to the resources that we free up not only from that program, but from the monetization of assets as well as from the equitization of PureFibre. All of that will create a different growth profile that we'll continue to update you on as those numbers become clear. But your number -- your question is specifically on the $900 million. Gopi, do you want to address that?

Gopi Chande: Sure. Yes. And I want to pick up, Jerome, on Victor's transparency comment. You will get from us next year how to track this through exactly for the year. We will continue to report on the $900 million. And because there is an active asset monetization strategy, that is why we have carved out how much is telecom, how much -- versus how much is in the other businesses. I want to reinforce as well what Victor said around what we're using this for, it is going to be for a balance of delevering as well as investment in growth across what we'll do in fiber as well as AI and monetization of our fiber while maintaining control complements this.

So it will be the combination of both of these. And as Victor mentioned earlier in the call, it is always going to be a balance between delevering and getting us flexibility on our balance sheet, but also stoking the growth that we see for the future of TELUS.

David Fuller: Yes. My only top-up would be, Gopi, this was not the result of a top-down, let's just do a benchmarking exercise. This was the result of 2 months of detailed involvement from many team members across TELUS to do a bottoms-up review around how we can change our processes, where we need to invest in our systems and our digital capabilities to make sure that we can drive these cost savings out of our business. And that's what gives us confidence in the number as we move forward, right?

So there are detailed initiatives across each of these levers that we strongly believe in and are starting to work on already to make sure that we drive these efficiencies in our business.

Operator: The next question is from Matthew Griffiths from Bank of America.

Matthew Griffiths: Maybe the first one is just on the wireless business. I think in the MD&A, you guys referenced or there is a reference to kind of lower equipment margins. And so I just wanted to hear your thoughts on whether, I guess, the better net add performance, how that might be linked to the lower equipment margins that you're reporting? And then secondly, on the AI kind of opportunity, just trying to break out here the -- you've laid out these 3 buckets. One of them being expanding your current DC and the other is the powered shell opportunity.

So I wanted to understand perhaps that like the 38 megawatts that you referenced kind of links to your expanding of your current DCs. And then if there's an additional ability to secure power, that would link to the powered shell opportunity. And so linked with that, do you have any secured power that could support the powered shell infrastructure opportunity?

Victor Dodig: So why don't we work backwards on that? We get Navin to again answer I think more granularity on the data center side, the 3-pillar strategy. The first 2 pillars are activated. The 3 pillars kind of under development. We'll come back to you with it. Anything you want to add there, Navin? And then Dave will answer the next question on wireless.

Navin Arora: Yes. Maybe I'll just top up that on the expansion to 38 megawatts, we're not only seeing healthy IRRs, but what we are seeing on the GPUs themselves is a payback period of less than 2 years. So we feel very confident around that investment. And in terms of the powered shell, your comment or your question around confirmed power, we're working through that. And when we're ready to announce any projects that we're going to move ahead with, we'll let you all know.

Victor Dodig: Good. And just to add on Navin's point, that second bucket, where we're actually expanding our own data centers, there has been a refinement in our strategic go-to-market approach to not finance all of the GPUs but some of the GPUs and some clients are going to want us to do that. Others will want to do that on their own, and that will be a much -- and both of them are very, very attractive from a return standpoint. We're also mindful of capital intensity when it comes to growing our data center business. And that's going to be very, very much linked to our monetization, equitization and transformation strategies, right?

So Dave, maybe you can answer the question on wireless.

David Fuller: Yes, sure. First thing to remember is equipment margins and equipment revenues are largely hinged actually off renewals, not acquisitions, right? So we have a much bigger base than we have gross adds in any given quarter. And so renewal activity is the predominant driver of that. I would say our equipment revenues were down on lower volumes year-over-year. Our gross adds were down, as I already mentioned, some 32,000 or so year-over-year. And we also focused on being quite disciplined throughout the quarter in terms of subsidy promotions and rate plan promotions. So all of that meant lower volumes across the board, including in renewals. And on the margin front, they were marginally different year-over-year, but not significantly so.

Sequentially, they were up -- but that's a function of the fact that back-to-school is always a heavier loading and renewal period than earlier in the year.

Ian McMillan: Carl, let's take the last question from the queue, please.

Operator: The final question is from David McFadgen from Cormark.

David McFadgen: Just a couple of questions. So given you took the write-down on TELUS Health, I was wondering if you can give us sort of a ballpark as to what you think that business is worth now? And then second question is, what would it take for you to eliminate the DRIP entirely? And is that something that you want to do?

Victor Dodig: Sure. Well, Gopi, maybe you can highlight some of the comments around both of those questions, starting off with the impairment.

Gopi Chande: For sure. So thanks for the question, David. A reminder, the impairment is noncash, driven by the 3 items I mentioned. So some updated growth expectations, market conditions and current valuation perspectives. I'm not going to comment on the specific valuation of TELUS Health. I wouldn't read in too much to this impairment in terms of what that means for each of the assets within it. What you can read into it is how far along we are on parts of the monetization.

So one of the items to think about is, as we go through this monetization process, we're going to have to look at each sale, whether it's the service line or within a business or the business itself. We look at it independently. We assess the likely sales proceeds against the allocated accounting value, and then that's going to give us an impairment or a gain. So you're going to hear us talk about this for a while as we execute our strategy and there's puts and takes. And while we continue to have these businesses, we are going to invest in them, look after our customers and look after our team.

So we'll continue to keep you posted as that progresses. And then with the discount remaining on the DRIP, we're -- it's not something that's on our radar right now. It's a low uptake that we have of people remaining without the discount. So it's something we'll continue to monitor. We're very committed to returning value to our shareholders. So it's an item we'll watch, but not something of major concern right now.

Ian McMillan: Thanks, David. Thank you, everyone. Before we close out the call, let me pass it back to Victor for some brief closing remarks.

Victor Dodig: Well, thank you. Thanks, Ian, and thank you, everyone, for your great questions today. We have -- what we've set out to do here today is to share a transparent update on our transformation strategy and the path forward to achieve TELUS' full potential. And we're in the early innings of what we believe will be full potential. TELUS is building from a foundation of strength. We're an exceptionally well-positioned company backed by industry-leading customer service, our expansive PureFibre and 5G networks, our growing infrastructure capabilities, which we tried to outline to you today and an increasingly collaborative and energized culture. We have the right leaders in the right roles.

We have an executive leadership team that possesses a deep institutional understanding of our business and seasoned experience necessary to navigate change and very, very focused on our strategic pivot to profitable growth and a good accretive return on capital. Our approach is grounded in disciplined execution and clear accountability. We've already demonstrated this through some decisive actions that we've already taken across all 3 strategic priorities. Again, those are to strengthen our financial foundation, hone our operational discipline to free up resources and deploy that capital to areas of sustainable growth in Canadian telecom and digital infrastructure.

We're aggressively pursuing monetization of noncore assets to support further deleveraging and balance sheet strength, and we're exploring the equitization of our PureFibre assets to support strategic investments in our core telecom and Canadian AI infrastructure businesses. It's all underpinned by our $900 million cash savings program. We're building a leaner, we're building a more focused TELUS to better position ourselves to compete, innovate and create long-term value for Canadian consumers and businesses at a time where this sector and TELUS is very much needed. We're moving with clarity, we're moving with urgency, we're moving with purpose. And we're confident that our transformation strategy will position us for stronger performance as we head into 2027 and beyond.

When we report our fourth quarter results in February, we'll provide our full year 2027 outlook and an update on our transformation strategy progress, and I'm sure we'll see many of you between now and then. Thank you for your time today and continued interest in TELUS. And I think that's it, Ian.

Operator: Thank you, Victor. This concludes our Q3 earnings call today. Please reach out to the IR team for any additional follow-ups.

#3268. Report: Apple faces congressional scrutiny over ICE tracking apps and Trump donations

Reuters and The Washington Post report that Apple is among the tech giants potentially facing congressional investigations as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers in January. Here are the details.

Earlier today, The Washington Post reported that “Democrats are laying the groundwork to investigate some of the country’s largest companies, setting off a scramble among executives who courted the president.”

The report notes that Washington law firms are advising companies and executives on how to prepare for potential congressional investigations, with some also pitching their services to Elon Musk:

Multiple firms have crafted pitches for why they should serve as Musk’s personal counsel, aware that the world’s richest man is likely to receive a barrage of subpoenas and that any casework stemming from those investigations will be both lucrative and the highest-profile investigative work available in the coming year, according to two of the people.

When it comes to Apple, the report noted that lawmakers are gearing up to investigate the company “over its hosting of tracking apps used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.”

While the report refers to Apple’s hosting of tracking apps used by ICE, the company has previously faced scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers over its decision to remove apps used to track ICE agents from the App Store.

Last year, Apple removed ICEBlock and several similar apps from the App Store following pressure from the DOJ, citing concerns over the safety of federal agents.

The move came shortly after a gunman opened fire on an ICE facility in Dallas, ultimately killing two detainees in an attack that federal authorities described as targeted violence against ICE.

Since then, Apple has faced questions from Democratic lawmakers over the extent of the Trump administration’s involvement in the decision and whether the removals infringed on constitutionally protected speech.

“over its hosting of tracking apps used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.”

The word “by” seems important here. That quote is clearly not about the apps used to track ICE, it’s about apps that ICE uses itself.

That makes me wonder if the original article is confused, though. Is ICE really “hosting” its own internal apps on the App Store rather than deploying through some enterprise/MDM distribution method? I guess Apple is involved in that process, too? And if the incoming Congress takes the posture that ICE has been operating an illegal human trafficking ring, then assisting them is a crime.

Apple was pathetic and ridiculous for removing ICEBlock and similar apps. It was also blatantly unconstitutional for the DOJ to threaten them into doing it.

Reuters, meanwhile, reported that Senator Richard Blumenthal, “who is set to take over as chair of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations,” called on Apple “and others who donated to [President Trump’s new White House] ballroom project to turn over records” or “face possible subpoenas in January.”

As The Washington Post reported last month, Apple and Nvidia each pledged $25 million toward the ballroom, making them two of the project’s largest donors.

Apple did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters or The Washington Post.

You can read the full Reuters report here, and The Washington Post’s here.

#3267. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and the secretary of the IEEE Computer Society Central Indiana Chapter. He is also the chair of the IEEE Central Indiana Student Activities Committee.

#3266. iOS 27.3: New features, release date, more

This week, Apple released the first iOS 27.3 beta. The update includes multiple new features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 …

As my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone users sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo. That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.

Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:

So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.

The redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final update.

The redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 users, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.

For Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a new Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.

As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.

For iPhone Duo users, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support. This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left to make it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.

Reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.

iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.

When it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with new clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.

This includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The update also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.

iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the update expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains:

We started rolling out these new capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

There are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

With iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test new ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple says it will start shipping to customers in a few months.

iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to new languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:

iOS 27.3 is a major update to Safari. First, the update adds support for a new vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.

iOS 27.3 also adds a new Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

For Apple Music users, iOS 27.3 adds a new “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.

The update also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

#3265. Raycast combines voice dictation and screen awareness in new AI feature

Following the recent release of Screen Awareness, Raycast got an interesting update this week that lets users talk to AI about whatever is on their screen without having to explain the context. Here are the details.

Last August, Raycast announced Screen Awareness, which lets users bring context from their active app or window directly into AI Chat, “so you don’t have to copy text, attach screenshots, or explain what you’re looking at,” said Raycast.

This week, Raycast took that functionality a step further with Dictate to AI, a new command that lets users speak their requests while automatically providing AI with context from the active app.

Here is Raycast’s Pedro Duarte showing how Dictate to AI works:

here's how the new Dictate to AI command works https://t.co/vApN7nHAPV pic.twitter.com/Dmmexor8q1

Raycast also noted other recent updates and additions, including that Raycast Notes now supports images and unlimited notes for free users, while the Mac app received several performance improvements, including faster search and lower memory usage.

#3264. Apple TV renews ‘Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars’ for season three

Award-winning culinary show ‘Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars’ is getting a third season, in an announcement that came hours after its second season came to a close. Here are the details.

Just as ‘Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook’ premiered with a two-episode combo, and ‘Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars’ aired its second season finale, the company confirmed that the latter will return for an eight-episode third season.

‘Knife Edge: Chasing Michelin Stars’ is hosted by Topjaw’s Jesse Burgess and executive produced by Gordon Ramsay. Each season tells the story of several restaurants around the world as they compete to earn, retain, or increase their Michelin Star ratings.

The show premiered on Apple TV in 2025 to a perfect 100% Tomatometer score and has since been nominated for a BAFTA Television Award in the Factual Entertainment category, and won Best Popular Factual Programme at the 2026 Broadcast Digital Awards.

With eight episodes in each season, the show has taken viewers inside some of the world’s most acclaimed restaurants, including Brazil’s Evvai, the first in Latin America to earn three Michelin Stars, and Ynyshir, a two-star restaurant in rural Wales.

“What I love most about making ‘Knife Edge’ is that, however much time I spend in restaurants around the world, I’m constantly surprised by the extraordinary people and stories we discover. Behind every restaurant is a very personal journey, and for the chefs we follow, a Michelin Star can represent years of sacrifice, obsession and an enormous amount of hard work. It’s a privilege to be able to tell these stories, and I’m absolutely thrilled that we get to do it all again for a third season”
