#3263. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

#3262. PSQ Holdings (PSQH) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Payments now drive nearly half of revenue as headcount shrinks sharply.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

PSQ Holdings, Inc. (PSQH +18.18%) has completed its transition from a diversified marketplace and consumer brands entity to a focused financial infrastructure company. Management reported that the company has reduced its headcount by 50% while growing payments and credit revenue, resulting in its second consecutive quarter of positive non-GAAP operating income. The company stated it has remediated a material weakness in internal control over financial reporting that had been reported since the third quarter of 2023. Management reaffirmed full-year 2026 revenue guidance and noted a path toward achieving positive monthly operating cash flow in 2027.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for joining us, and welcome to PSQ Holdings Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to William Kent, Head of Corporate Affairs. Please go ahead.

William Kent: Welcome to the PSQ Holdings Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. Joining me today are Dusty Wunderlich, our Chairman and Chief Executive Officer; Mike Pena, our Chief Financial Officer; and Krista Wenzel, our Chief Accounting Officer. Before we begin, please note that the information we discuss today, including our outlook, is current as of today and includes forward-looking statements that involve risks and uncertainties. We are not required to update these statements if new information arises. For details on factors that could cause actual results to differ, please see today's earnings press release and our SEC filings, including our 2025 Form 10-K and our subsequent quarterly reports on Form 10-Q.

We will also discuss non-GAAP measures alongside financial measures calculated according to GAAP. Reconciliations of those non-GAAP measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures are included in today's earnings press release, which is available on our Investor Relations website. If you'd like to submit a question for management to answer during the Q&A portion of today's call, please e-mail [email protected]. With that, I'll hand the call over to Dusty.

Dustin Wunderlich: Thank you, Will, and good morning, everyone. I want to use my time this morning a little differently. Krista and Mike will walk you through the quarter. I want to take you through the last 3 quarters because the third quarter only makes sense as part of that story. Where we started. Go back to the plan this company went public on, a value-based shopping marketplace and later a family of consumer brands. In 2024, that plan used $34 million of cash in operations and lost $58 million. In 2025, it used another $20 million. The marketplace, the company was named for never covered its costs. Neither did the brands.

The one business with a real reason to exist was Credova, the smallest of the 3 when the company bought it. It was carrying the overhead of a company built for something else. A year ago, we had 72 employees, and we're using about $6 million a quarter in operations. In January, the team that built Credova took over running the whole company. Mike, Jim and I built Credova as a private company that paved its own way. We never had a capital market to cover a loss, so every product had to earn its keep. And that is how we have run this company since.

We told you we would do 4 things: get out of consumer brands; cut the cost structure down to the business we actually have; grow payments and credit without growing headcount; and get this company to the point where it funds itself. We put numbers on each of those and ask you to hold us to them. Doing those 4 things meant ending the strategy this company went public on. What we have done? Three quarters later, here's where that stands. In that time, we shut down the marketplace, sold the brands business, cut the workforce in half, completed a reverse split, took our payment stack in the consumer lending with 3 new integrations to more than double revenue.

We did all of it at once while running the business day-to-day. Any one of those is a year's work in most companies. The marketplace is gone. It was fully wound down by the end of June. EveryLife was sold this week to Freehold Brands for $5.5 million before fees and customary adjustments. The exit from consumer brands is complete. Those were hard calls and the numbers show they were the right ones. In the first 9 months of last year, the Marketplace and Brands business lost $7.2 million between them. In the first 9 months of this year, they lost $0.5 million.

That is a $6.7 million improvement from 2 decisions, brought their operating costs down from $10.5 million to $3.7 million. We didn't sell EveryLife as the broken business. We cut its operating costs by 43%, while its revenue grew 8% and was close to breakeven in the third quarter when we sold it. For the first time since the company went public, every dollar of revenue report comes from moving money. The cost structure has been reset. We committed to roughly $8 million of annualized savings and delivered closer to $10 million. We have 35 people today, half the team of a year ago.

And the bar for adding $1 of cost back is that has already earned its way in. The business grew through it all. Third quarter revenue was $7.3 million, up 67% from a year ago. For 9 months, revenue has more than doubled. Payments volume was $197.3 million in the quarter, up 121% year-over-year. Credova grew originations 23%. In the firearms market, it grew about 2.5% in the quarter. That growth came from a team half the size. That is the whole turnaround in one sentence, revenue up 2/3, headcount down half and nothing broke. The consumer side is changing and explains the shape of our credit growth.

This year, applications from consumers with credit scores below 640 are down about 7%. Applications from 640 and up are higher and the 720-plus band grew the most. We didn't decline more of the lower score customers. They stopped applying. That's the K-shaped economy people talk about. Higher income households are still spending and a lot of them pay with a card. Lower income households are pulling back on the purchases they used to finance. Against that, we converted better. The share of approved customers who went on to complete a finance purchase rose in every credit band. Our primary installment product more than doubled and drove nearly 3/4 of our contract growth, while higher APR volumes shrank.

So this year's credit growth came from closing more of the customers already in front of us. There's a limit to how that far that grows, and that's why the next leg of growth is putting the monthly payment in front of customers before they decide how to pay. And the losses are closing. Operating loss went from $9.7 million a year ago to $3.3 million. But the number I care about most is cash, and I want to be plain about why. A business that burns cash runs on other people's money and sooner or later, that market sets the terms. A business that pays for itself sets its own.

For its first 2 years as a public company, this one burned cash. This year, we've cut it every quarter. In the first quarter, operations used $4.1 million; in the second quarter, $2.3 million, down 44%. In the third quarter, $1.7 million, down another 26%, and that included about $600,000 of onetime costs Mike will walk you through. In 2024, this company burned more than $8 million a quarter. We are now at 1/5 of that. Next year, the business pays for itself. Our target is positive monthly operating cash flow in 2027. On a non-GAAP basis, we've already earned an operating profit 2 quarters in a row. I'll give you one more number, and then I'll stop reciting them.

In the third quarter of last year, each employee at this company supported about $61,000 of quarterly revenue. This quarter it was $210,000, 3.5x in 12 months. AI is a large part of how we did that in underwriting and engineering and finance and risk monitoring. And it is why we report revenue per employee every quarter and expect it to keep improving. From here, that metric only moves if revenue moves, which is exactly how we want to be measured. Why this is all worth doing? None of this would matter if the business we kept was not worth keeping. So let me spend a minute on why it is.

Credova serves markets the banks and large processors walked away from: firearms and outdoor retailers, consumer lenders, campaigns and nonprofits. These are lawful businesses that get declined or priced as high risk on a basis of the category code rather than on how they actually perform. We underwrite the category ourselves and we price to the defaults and chargebacks we actually measure. Years of that performance data in categories most lenders will not touch is the asset. Every merchant we add makes the pricing more accurate. And because most of our merchants run both payments and credit through us, each one adds data on both sides of the transaction. That position is hard to copy. We hold state lending licenses.

We've run machine learning underwriting on our own data since 2021, and we're the exclusive payments and credit provider inside Rayon AI's firearm software. A competitor would need all 3 and years to build them. That is why our demand does not depend on outspending anyone. Merchants come to us because the alternative is being shut off, and we continue to see businesses outside our core outdoor category seek us out for the same reason. We get asked what if a friendlier regulatory climate brings the banks back?

Consumer lenders face the same exclusion our firearms merchants do, the difference is scale and frequency, and a lender processes a repayment every month on every loan for the life of loan. In August, we announced LendSuite, Dealer Cash and Roja. Those integrations take our payment stack into loan repayment processing. And together, they put us in front of roughly 150 lenders on 3 loan platforms and more than 100 auto dealers in Texas. We expect these relationships to be contributing in the fourth quarter of 2026 and first quarter of 2027 and to build through 2027. Credit quality remains strong and losses and delinquencies are inside our expectations. So what comes next?

Our priorities for the rest of the year have not changed. We are reaffirming our 2026 outlook, $32 million of revenue and positive non-GAAP operating income for the full year. Mike will walk through what the fourth quarter has to deliver and why we believe it will. Beyond that, the target is positive for monthly operating cash flow in 2027. We said that in July, and we are saying it again today. I want to be clear about the standard we hold ourselves to. We are not declaring victory on 3 quarters and turnaround is not finished until the business funds itself.

What 3 quarters have shown is that this team does what it says it will do, and that business underneath it is a real one with a real reason to exist. Krista will show you that the financial statements now tell the same story I just did. Mike will take you through cash and the outlook. Krista, handing it to you.

Krista Wenzel: Thank you, Dusty, and good morning. I'm going to keep the 3 things in the financial statements that I think matter most and leave the line-by-line detail to the release. First, the shape of revenue. Payments is now almost half of our revenue, up from about 1/3 a year ago, and that shift changes our margin profile. Payments carries transaction fees and cost of revenue. So as the mix moves towards payments, cost of revenue rises with it. Cost of revenue was $3.5 million this quarter, up from $1.5 million a year ago. That means after transaction costs, we kept about $0.52 of every revenue dollar compared to $0.67 in the prior year quarter. Those fees are variable.

They move with the volume that generates the revenue. And once the merchant is live, each additional dollar processed requires very little incremental operating cost. So while the percentage declined, revenue less cost of revenue grew about 30% in dollars. At the same time, the cost actions that began in late 2025 and that we significantly deepened this year cut operating expenses in half. Together, those 2 drivers closed our operating loss by 2/3. A lower margin, higher volume revenue stream on a much leaner cost base is how this business reaches profitability, and the third quarter shows that model working. Within credit, revenue continues to shift towards selling originations rather than holding them.

Lease merchandise revenue is running off by design since we stopped adding new consumer leases on the balance sheet a year ago, while revenue from loan and lease contracts sold nearly tripled. Less of our capital sits in lease merchandise and the revenue line reflects that. Second, the cost reduction. Operating expenses, which we define as G&A, sales and marketing, and R&D were $5.5 million, down 50% from a year ago. About $4 million of that decline reflects lower share-based compensation, which largely came from the headcount reductions under the plan. Because it's noncash, I would rather you hear that from me than from a model.

Excluding share-based compensation, operating expenses still fell by roughly 1/5 on a revenue base that is 2/3 larger. The cash flow statement confirms it. Cash used in operations fell 72%, and Mike will walk through that in a moment. Third, the bottom line. Net loss for the quarter was $4.9 million compared to $12 million a year ago. On our first quarter call, I spent time on noncash movements in our warrant and earn-out liabilities that distorted the comparison. This quarter, there is nothing like that to explain. Those items were small in both periods. The $7.9 million improvement comes from the business, more revenue, lower costs and a much smaller loss from discontinued operations.

Net loss per share adjusted for the reverse split in July improved to $1 from $3.90, and that improvement came even as our weighted-average share count grew by about 1/3. On discontinued operations, EveryLife was still classified as discontinued operations on September 30 since the sale closed after quarter end. Loss from discontinued operations was about $100,000 for the quarter, down from $1.9 million a year ago, reflecting the marketplace wind down and the cost actions taken at EveryLife ahead of the sale. The final accounting for this transaction will come through in the fourth quarter. Before I turn it over to Mike, one more item.

Beginning in the third quarter of 2023, our filings have reported a material weakness in internal control over financial reporting related to the presentation of our statement of cash flows. Over the past several quarters, we strengthened our review process for complex transactions and added experienced accounting professionals to the team. After testing the design and operating effectiveness of those controls, management concluded that the material weakness was remediated as of September 30, 2026. I want to thank our finance and accounting team for their disciplined work behind this result. I'll now turn it over to Mike.

Michael Pena: Thank you, Krista. So cash first. Dusty walked through the trend. Let me explain what's inside this quarter's $1.7 million of operating cash burn. Roughly $600,000 of that was onetime, mostly severance and deal costs and another $650,000 of annual payments that land in the third quarter. The structural burn is lower than the headline and the headline has fallen every quarter regardless. On the balance sheet, we ended the quarter with $6.8 million of cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash, of which $3.8 million was unrestricted cash from continuing operations. On the revolver that funds Credova originations, $6.8 million was drawn against the $10 million facility. That line turns over as receivables are collected or sold.

So think of it as working capital for the credit book rather than corporate debt. EveryLife closed after quarter end. Of the $5.5 million purchase price, we received $1 million in cash at closing and the balance payable monthly over the following 12 months. As for the 2026 outlook. We are reaffirming our $32 million of revenue and positive non-GAAP operating income for 2026. And I want to be direct about the arithmetic. Through 9 months, we have $22.6 million of revenue. So the fourth quarter needs to deliver roughly $9.4 million. That would be the largest quarter in the company's history.

Above the $8.2 million we reported in the first quarter, we are reaffirming because the fourth quarter has 2 things going for it that no other quarter does. First is seasonality. Hunting season and the holidays make the fourth quarter the strongest period of the year for credit originations and for payments volume across our outdoor merchants. And secondly, new payment merchants going online. This includes the LendSuite, Dealer Cash and Roja relationships, which begin contributing in the fourth quarter of 2026 and into the first quarter of 2027, and we expect them to continue building throughout 2027. On non-GAAP operating income, we are at a loss of $100,000 through 9 months after 2 consecutive positive quarters.

The fourth quarter at the revenue level I just described takes the full year positive. Our capital priorities have not changed, keep reducing burn, hold the operating discipline and convert that into positive monthly operating cash flow in 2027. That target includes the interest we pay on our convertible notes and the revolver, which is why the operating improvement has to keep coming and why we are not adding cost back ahead of revenue. With that, back to Dusty.

Dustin Wunderlich: Thank you, Mike. 12 months ago, this was a company without a cogent story and a cash problem. Today, it is one business with half the people, 2/3 of our revenue, a fraction of the burn and 2 straight quarters of non-GAAP operating profit. That was done in 3 quarters by the team that ran Credova as a private company that generated cash. We intend to get back there. Every eligible director bought stock in our August private placement at a premium to market and with no warrants. In July, I said I was not asking you to believe me. I was asking you to watch what we do against what we said we would do.

That is still the standard. Operator, we will take questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] your first question comes from the line of Thomas Forte with Maxim Group.

Thomas Forte: Congratulations on the successful divestiture of EveryLife. I have 2 questions initially and then Dusty, depending on your answers, I might have more. I'll go one at a time. So for starters, it's best exemplified by the initial success of Meta platforms' Muse when you go by app data -- or sorry, app download data. Dusty, I'd appreciate your thoughts on agentic commerce and the opportunities it creates for your company.

Dustin Wunderlich: Yes. Tom, good to hear from you. I always appreciate you being on this call. And we've -- you and I've kind of gone over this question after the last couple of quarters. And I've been pretty -- I mean, I think the whole world is starting to use AI, is starting to see how rapidly the adoption is. It's unlike anything I've seen in the last 20 years in my career. And in fact, I just made my first payment with an agent myself personally this week. So the time of a agentic commerce is upon us. And I would really position it, Tom, similar to our overall company thesis.

What we do best is we go into industries into merchants that have what I would call a lot of complexity. And what I define as complexity is regulatory complexity, operational complexity and political complexity as well. A lot of financial institutions want to streamline underwriting and pricing, and they don't like to deal with complexity. So I believe from an agentic commerce perspective, that's going to be the same, and that will run true. So for example, a Link or a Shopify with their integrated agentic wallets are likely not to put in the time or effort to go and do something around the firearm industry that has serialized products that have to go through background checks.

So we think the thesis runs true even with agentic commerce. It's something we're thinking about in our road map, and we'll continue to serve the industry that we think will get rejected because of that complexity risk with other traditional financial companies.

Thomas Forte: All right. So before I get to my second question, I have a follow-up. So one of the things that I'm trying to determine is, will agentic commerce result in a greater portion of total transactions through existing marketplaces? Or will there be an element that it's an equalizer and then will result in incremental transactions for smaller players within different categories?

Dustin Wunderlich: Yes. It's a great question, Tom, and one I've been thinking a lot about as well as I'm playing around with it myself as a consumer. And I think we're in a very interesting time in the sense of who is adopting agentic commerce and who is not. And for example, right now, Amazon has blocked all agents from their site. So you have some very powerful players that are going the route of not adopting. If you look at someone like Stripe that has built a wallet around agentic commerce.

So I think you're going to initially see a lot of probably smaller to medium-sized players in e-commerce, in particular, adopt agentic commerce, whereas the bigger players are probably going to resist it as they figure out where they position because essentially, what agentic commerce is going to do is it's going to make e-commerce effectively a commodity. As agents more and more just start to interact with e-commerce and personalize it in our own experience, that UI/UX that you have in e-commerce is just not going to be important anymore. These are just going to be API calls that are being passed there.

And an example I'll give, one of the agents that I've been using a company called Instinct when you go to the landing page, it is literally 3 or 4 lines. It's a stick figure. And it effectively says sign up with your phone number and there's no UI/UX. Everything I do is personalized and through my text message. So the days of us having these robust e-commerce sites and UI/UX experiences are going away. So that battle is happening. I think it's going to drastically change the environment, and it's probably going to come from the bottom up. I think it's inevitable.

I think that the majority of transactions will be done with agentics -- with agents in the next 5 years. But I think we're going to see a massive mix up in e-commerce over the next 5 -- 3 to 5 years.

Thomas Forte: Excellent. All right. So then switching to my second question. So judging from the market's reaction to your stock following the midterms, it seems to me there's a misunderstanding regarding what the results of the midterms mean for your business. So in my opinion, I could see how a Democratic controlled Congress could be a catalyst for your sales to the extent it inspires more second amendment focused companies to sign up for your payment services on a greater concern of potential disruption. And Dusty, I'd appreciate your thoughts.

Dustin Wunderlich: Yes. No, I greatly appreciate that and the nuance in which you look at our company, Tom, because I do believe the market has a misunderstanding of that is we -- this industry, particularly, firearm industry, which is a big portion of our sales, is very counterintuitive to what a lot of Wall Street and just the general public realizes. One, geopolitical events move the industry in a pretty significant way. Elections in particular do that. And when there is a change to a more democratic controlled governance structure, that tends to be a windfall for the firearm industry.

And the reason why is consumers start to get worried that they're going to be restricted from buying products that they want to buy. So it basically brings demand upfront. There is a reason for demand to move upfront in the households if they think that, that product they want will no longer be available. So -- although we have a tougher regulatory environment, it tends to be a better revenue and sales environment for the company. The same is true with the economic environment as well as this is -- the industry tends to do better during economic hard times.

So it is -- you could call it in a way that the firearm industry is recession-proof in the sense that it's countercyclical to the macroeconomic environment. A lot of that, too, is just driven by consumers in tough times that moves demand upfront for them to have their firearms, protection is more of a thing and that might -- it might even be subsistence hunting, things like that tend to drive the consumer behavior. So I'm glad you brought that up because I do believe there is a fundamental misunderstanding. It's something we're going to continue to message to the market in the coming days.

Thomas Forte: Excellent. Last question, unless you answer this and inspire me for one more. So I've been incredibly impressed by your ramp in revenue per employee. Can you talk about an endpoint, meaning that you think that you can operate the business at this level of total operating expenses on your path toward cash flow generation?

Dustin Wunderlich: Yes, Tom. Thank you, Tom. That's something we are very proud of as a team and something we think about all the time. Like I said, even in my first earnings call, I believe that revenue per employee in and the age of AI is going to be a very important KPI. I think adoption of AI is wildly different from company to company and industry to industry. And I think this is going to be the metric that really shows you which industries and which companies are using AI. So we're proud of being early adopters there. I continue to have the figure in mind that we can do $2 million per employee of revenue.

And that would effectively mean we can, with about where we're at from a headcount right now, double the company without adding any additional headcount. And I'd caveat that with AI is moving so rapidly that, that figure may change from quarter-to-quarter. But I continue to think that's a good North Star for us in this company. I might have an entirely different answer for you in 6 months, Tom. But as of right now, that is our North Star. And I think it's very reachable based on what we're seeing in general.

Thomas Forte: Okay. Great. So then I'll step aside and depending on the additional question you get, I may star 1 for a follow-up.

Operator: We will now move to our pre-submitted questions. I will hand the call back to William Kent.

William Kent: Thank you. We did receive a number of pre-submitted questions ahead of the call. We'll cover a couple of them here to the best of our ability. The first question is in regards to the EveryLife sale. The EveryLife sale was originally announced as a $5.5 million all-cash transaction, but the final structure consisted of $1 million in cash and a $4.5 million secured promissory note. Can management explain what drove this change in terms?

Dustin Wunderlich: Thank you, Will, and thank you for the pre-submitted question. It's an important question. And I'd like to zoom out a little bit to talk about the EveryLife sale process. I believe there's really 2 things happening here as we went through this process. The first was really operational. I mean the Board and the company made the decision to divest of the Brands division and the marketplace. Those were decisions that were made at a point in time about a year ago, but there was still the operational component of the business and getting that business ready for sale.

Prior to that and prior to kind of how former management was running companies, this was -- company was running at a deep loss. And what you heard in the earnings today is once this team took over, we were able to still grow the company while reducing operating OpEx at about 40%. So part of the process was getting the company ready for sale. The second component that I would say is because of the pro-life mission of EveryLife, it is -- there is, without a doubt, just like our firearms market in the payments and credit side, there is an untapped market there.

It is what has built that company, and it's what Freehold is going to, I think, be able to grow in a really good fashion. But that narrows buyers. That narrows bank financing because of that. I mean, whether we like it or not, we live in a politicized market. And you can see that in even the recent rulings and executive orders out of the admin around debanking and the concept of banks using reputational risk. That is the reality of the market we live in, whether you like it or not, that's where we're at. So the buyer had struggles with finding the correct bank partner to finalize this transaction.

So we made the decision that it's best to finish this transaction. We'll take seller financing and find the right bank. This is something that we have become experts in on the Credova side. So we've been working hand-in-hand with the buyer to find them the right bank to refinance us. Those are active conversations happening. And it was very important to us to stick to our word and make sure the company was divested, which we did. And we will be back to you very soon, I think, with good news on helping the buyer find the right bank for the right mission and get this seller-financed note refinanced.

William Kent: Thank you, Dusty. Our next question is in regards to the NYSE listing risk. With PSQ facing pressure on its 30-day average market cap and the NYSE's $15 million minimum threshold, which represents a significant near-term risk, what concrete steps is management taking to address this risk? Is the company actively considering an additional PIPE, strategic investment or other measures to protect its NYSE listing? What is the contingency plan if the threshold is breached?

Dustin Wunderlich: No, it's an important question. Thank you for submitting that, very thoughtfully worded as well. Look, the shareholder value is deeply important to me. Outside of sell to cover, all of -- I've never sold a share. We did all equity in our deal. I am tied to the shareholders and always thinking how do we maximize shareholder value. I believe this team, since it's taken over, has executed flawlessly to drive shareholder value with doubling our revenue, reducing OpEx, reducing cash burn. We've done everything within our control to drive shareholder value. I feel very confident with that. I have no regrets in how we've executed in doing that.

Now I opened the earnings call today with what the company did in the past. And there was a tremendous amount of cash and capital that was squandered away without return. And we are paying the price for that. We're also in a very tough market right now. I mean P/E ratios are at historical highs. Gas prices, everyone is aware of, the consumer is strapped. The markets are very tough. So timing has just been very difficult. And it's very frustrating as a shareholder and from the management team to see us produce the results that we're producing and continue to see the stock doing what it's doing.

In a lot of ways, it's unfair, but that's what we have, the cards we've been dealt. So the answer of what are we doing about it? First of all, we are doing what we can to control and drive great results operationally, which I think we've done. Second, we continue to look at all options, and we went through the same issue back in August, and the Board stepped up with a PIPE into the company to show the market that they believed in management, they believe in the story. We put out a number of releases on new partnerships to prove that we are driving shareholder value to drive up market cap.

We continue to be in conversations with NYSE on almost a daily basis right now regarding this issue. And look, we think this is an extraordinary situation that we have been working with NYSE on, and there is, we believe, room for special exemptions through the exchange. And we are exploring all of those options as part of other options in the capital markets to make sure that the company stays listed and we continue to drive shareholder value. We think we have a very good story in which to justify that and what we'll continue to fight for with the exchange.

William Kent: Thank you, Dustin. And for our last submitted question, given the strong growth in PSQ payments, how much additional runway do you see? And as payments and credit become increasingly more bundled, could that momentum help accelerate Credova's growth as well?

Dustin Wunderlich: Yes. Payments has been phenomenal growth. And the great part of that is it's primarily been from merchants that we already had into our credit product and building that bundle. One, it has created a more sticky merchant because of the bundling, the pricing we can give. There's also benefits we're finding in the data of having both of these products combined that is making it even more powerful than we originally thought. So the bundle is something we are really leaning into that we think is going to be a real driver for both products.

Now in regards to continued payments growth, we have entered a new market, which we've been talking about with our partnerships with Roja, LendSuite and going into the consumer lending space, which we believe has a lot of the same components of the firearm industry in the sense that risk is mispriced because of the complexity of that. There's high levels of debanking occurring in that industry. It's one, we know because we are a consumer lender, but two, we have a deep bench with the Board and our management team that understand that space from a payments perspective.

So we continue to see really strong growth in our opinion, with the emergence of a new merchant and new industry that we're going to serve. So I expect to continue to see good growth in payments and in credit in the coming quarters.

Operator: We have reached the end of the Q&A session. I will now hand the call back to Dusty Wunderlich for closing remarks.

Dustin Wunderlich: Yes. Thank you all who participated in the questions. Thank you all who have been following the journey. We've had a number of discussions with different people over the last quarter that have been following our story, have been watching what this management team is doing. And we appreciate the support. We're going to continue to execute the best we can in what we say we're going to do. And hopefully, we've continued to earn the trust of that over the last 3 quarters as we've proven out what this management team is capable of. Thank you all for the time, and we look forward to the next earnings call in 2027.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

#3261. Anthropic reportedly must face claims its Claude Max ads misled users

A federal judge in California found the “5x or 20x more usage” promise plausibly misleading, Courthouse News reported.

A US judge has ruled that Anthropic must face key claims that it misled customers about how much use they get from its Claude Max plans. Magistrate Judge Alex Tse dismissed several other claims on Friday, Courthouse News reported.

The proposed class action, Kahn v. Anthropic, is in the federal court for northern California. TNW has not read the ruling.

Anthropic told buyers that its $100 and $200 Max plans give five or 20 times more usage than its Pro plan. However, the lawsuit, filed in June, says the plans give far less over a full week.

The plaintiffs, Karl Kahn and Solomon Smith, calculated that for one Claude model, the $200 plan gives six times Pro’s weekly usage. The $100 plan gives 3.5 times, they said.

The gap comes from how limits work. Max users get five or 20 times more use in each five-hour session, but their weekly limits are not five or 20 times higher.

Anthropic argued that customers should understand the extra usage as applying per session, and pointed to a help page. Tse was not persuaded, according to Courthouse News.

“Anthropic’s per session disclosure is located two hyperlinks away from the primary sales pages on claude.com,” Tse wrote.

Because customers pay monthly, they could reasonably read the promise as applying each month, the judge found. The plaintiffs can go ahead with claims of negligent misrepresentation and breach of contract.

Meanwhile, Tse dismissed claims under two California laws on unfair business practices and false advertising. He also dismissed Kahn’s claim under a state consumer law, but gave him the chance to add detail. Smith’s claim under that law survived.

Tse also rejected a claim that Anthropic acted unfairly by tightening usage limits during billing periods. Anthropic and the plaintiffs did not immediately respond to Courthouse News. Separately, Anthropic renamed the Max plans last week.

#3259. Apple Music Classical gets new black-and-white icon in latest update

Following the redesign of the Apple Music app icon, which replaced the familiar white music note on a red background with a black-and-white look, Apple today updated Apple Music Classical to match the new design.

Today, Apple updated the Apple Music Classical app icon and interface to bring them in line with Apple Music’s new visual identity.

The new icon retains the familiar G-clef musical symbol, but now features a black symbol against a white background.

Interestingly, unlike the regular flat Apple Music icon, the Apple Music Classical icon kept its three-dimensional look, with subtle lighting, shading, and transparency that give it a sense of depth.

Inside the app, the red accents for buttons have also been replaced with a shade of blue that’s closer to the default color Apple uses across its other apps.

Today’s update came just weeks after Apple unveiled a much more colorful branding campaign for Apple Music, in addition to its new monochrome app icon, with visuals created by using sound waves to move water.

While many assumed Apple would eventually adopt the more colorful design as Apple Music’s new app icon, today’s Apple Music Classical update suggests that the company is sticking with the black-and-white look for its apps.

Apple Music Classical requires an active Apple Music subscription. You can sign up for $11.99 per month, with 1 month free, or as part of the Apple One bundle.

#3258. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

#3256. IEEE Program Schools Preuniversity Educators On Tech Topics

The TryEngineering workshops help teachers deliver engaging STEM lessons

An educator constructs a microchip model during the IEEE Making a Microchip lesson plan demonstration.

Now in their third year, the IEEE TryEngineering educator sessions continue to empower preuniversity teachers with specialized professional development programs on engineering topics and classroom-tested lessons.

This year’s sessions, held across the United States, have focused on educating teachers about artificial intelligence and semiconductor technology. One session was held in Egypt.

In all, 54 educators learned about the engineering design process this year. They received an overview of TryEngineering resources including the Making of a Microchip and Train Your Tree lesson plans.

Workshops are scheduled this year in Greece and Guatemala.

The TryEngineering program is administered by IEEE Educational Activities.

These teachers and guest speakers attended the two-day session held at the Florida Semiconductor Institute and SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.IEEE Educational Activities

Central to the educator session program’s success is its university network. Host campuses welcome teachers into their facilities, where faculty provide background information about some of the technologies being taught, as well as possible engineering career paths and job opportunities for students.

This year’s sessions involved the educators in hands-on projects. Facilitators at each location were selected based on their experience in engineering education, and they worked with the TryEngineering staff on their presentations.

Sixteen teachers from nine schools participated in the session, held in Cairo. It was facilitated by Marwa Soudi, an IEEE member, and Senior Member Stamatis Dragoumanos. Both are past chairs of the IEEE preuniversity coordinating committee. GEMS provided outstanding STEM facilities for teachers, Saudi and Dragoumanos said. Participants received an overview of the Working With Wind Energy and Tall Tower Challenge lesson plans.

Another educator session is scheduled for later this year.

Educators from across the state gathered at the university’s Florida Semiconductor Institute, headquartered in Gainesville, and FSI’s NeoCity high-tech manufacturing campus near Orlando. The session was hosted by Roseanne Perez, an FSI workforce development program specialist, and Sophia Watson, FSI’s assistant director of workforce development. The two-day experience featured an inside look at microelectronics through a guided tour of a SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.

Engineering instructor Mary Acken facilitated hands-on lesson demonstrations for the 15 attending teachers.

Reflecting on the workshop’s impact, one participant said the SkyWater tour was excellent, the instructors were great, and the teachers enjoyed learning from like-minded educators.

Michael Kozicki, an IEEE member, and Stefan Myhajlenko from the university’s engineering school welcomed 11 Arizona teachers to the Tempe campus.

The session was facilitated by Janet Hartkopf, an Arizona school leader and a former TryEngineering educator session participant. Hartkopf highlighted collaborative learning, the need for diverse perspectives in engineering education, and career paths.

The teachers received instruction on how to implement the hands-on lessons in their classrooms, and they toured the university’s NanoFab facility to observe microelectronics research.

“This training was amazing!” said a participant who leads an elementary after-school STEM club. “I loved the hands-on lessons and e-books, which I will definitely be using with my students. I am excited to explore all the resources on the TryEngineering website. The experts from ASU were great.”

Sixteen STEM educators attended this session, held at the university’s International Institute for Biosensing in Minneapolis. Its director, Patricia Khashayar, an IEEE member, introduced participants to the capabilities of the university’s Supercomputing Institute and Nano Center.

Under the guidance of Claire Dietz, an education and outreach coordinator, and Pam Schumacher, an instructor at St. Paul College, the teachers completed classroom-ready lessons including a photonics experiment using the Nano Center’s equipment. Schumacher attended last year’s TryEngineering educator session.

Nano Center Director Sarah Swisher, an IEEE senior member, provided an overview of semiconductor operations and highlighted growing job opportunities for the state’s young people.

The experience inspired all 16 teachers to plan student field trips to the Nano Center during the upcoming academic year, they said.

“Great class!” one participant said. “I’m excited to bring some of the TryEngineering materials back to our school.”

This year’s sessions built on the momentum from last year when, with financial support from Onsemi’s Giving Now program, nearly 80 teachers attended sessions across five U.S. states and Mexico.

Driven by that success and the demand for more, the IEEE Educational Activities Board continued its support. Upcoming global sessions are expected to expand the program’s international footprint.

“I appreciated the time to collaborate with peers on how to implement hands-on lessons,” one participating teacher this year said. Some participants said they planned follow-up visits with the experts and campus tours.

You can learn more about the sessions by emailing TryEngineering.

Debra Gulick is director of IEEE student and academic educational programs.

#3255. Micron and Sandisk Lead the Memory Market. 1 Stock Has Far Greater Upside.

SK Hynix is a clear leader in the memory market, and its latest quarterly results indicate a bright future.

Shares of Micron Technology and Sandisk have soared 280% and 457%, respectively, over the past year as demand for memory processors in data centers jumped.

Spending for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure isn't slowing down right now -- as Alphabet's (GOOGL +0.78%) (GOOG +0.78%) recent quarterly results show -- and that's great news for Micron and Sandisk as they continue to benefit from a booming memory market.

But as impressive as the rise of Micron and Sandisk has been, the lesser-known SK Hynix (SKHY +2.78%) could have more upside potential. That's because the company holds a leading position in the most in-demand types of memory processors, and its customers are already buying up all available memory.

Here's why putting some money toward SK Hynix stock now could be a smart move.

SK Hynix recently released its third-quarter results, and the company's phenomenal growth showed just how much the company is benefiting from the artificial intelligence boom.

Revenue rose 328% to $78.9 billion, while the company's operating profit jumped 632% to $62.3 billion. Those increases came as SK Hynix's customers exhausted the company's memory supplies, and management noted that more than 50% of its 2027-2028 production capacity is already tied up in long-term contracts.

That's a great problem to have, and one reason SK Hynix is in such a good position is that it sells memory products across high bandwidth memory (HBM), dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), and NAND flash memory.

SK Hynix is the undisputed leader in HBM memory with a 50% market share. That's especially important right now because HBM is the most widely used memory in data centers. For reference, Micron is also a player in this space but holds just 18% of the market, and Sandisk doesn't sell any HBM.

Meanwhile, DRAM and NAND are also in high demand for certain data center needs, and SK Hynix holds 25% market share in DRAM and 19% in NAND, trailing only Samsung Electronics in both categories and ahead of both Sandisk and Micron.

These strong market positions, paired with booming AI investments, have led to unprecedented growth for SK Hynix and to an impressive 80% operating margin in the third quarter.

Wall Street analysts have an average price target of $260 for SK Hynix stock, representing 71% upside from its current price as of this writing.

And while there's no guarantee the company's share price will climb, SK Hynix is clearly tapping into significant and persistent growth trends in the memory market. Consider that the latest Bank of America estimates show that tech companies' data center investments will more than double between now and 2028, reaching $2.1 trillion.

Some of that spending will go directly to memory processors, and it's part of a larger trend among AI cloud companies as they expand their data center capacity to meet demand. Alphabet was the latest company to show that AI spending isn't slowing, with management committing up to $205 billion in capex this year. Alphabet has benefited from the spending as its Google Cloud sales more than doubled to $30.7 billion in the third quarter.

What's more, SK Hynix's leadership says soaring memory demand could last over the next several years. Its leadership said in a press release that a "virtuous cycle has taken hold" in which productivity gains from AI are boosting infrastructure spending, which in turn drives further productivity gains and more spending.

The result is that SK Hynix's management expects memory demand to outstrip supply through 2030. For tech investors looking to tap into the memory market with a clear leader and seeking a stock with significant upside as sales and earnings rise, SK Hynix looks like a good buy right now.

#3254. Apple @ Work: Mac admins are shipping AI-written code with mistakes, but fixing the problems is taking days

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

There’s no doubt that AI tools are making IT admins faster at writing code, researching issues, etc. As a Mac admin, I’ve seen slow but steady growth in how I’ve used it in my daily work across all aspects of IT. It’s not perfect, though. I’ve used it to write scripts, troubleshoot networking errors, and more. A new report from Fleet puts numbers on the problem: it’s easy to ship things, but it’s hard to undo mistakes.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

For this report, Fleet surveyed more than 250 enterprise IT folks who manage Apple, all with admin access to their device management systems. The folks responding to the survey manage an average of 2,000 devices, and nearly half have 6 to 10 years of Apple admin experience.

The debate over whether IT teams should use AI day-to-day is over. They already are, and in the past 30 days, 68% of those responding reported using AI for troubleshooting or log analysis, 62% used it to write scripts, and 61% used it to author device management profiles or configurations. The log analysis is something that I use AI for often. 86% allow AI-written output into production after some form of review, and only 14% keep it out of their production environments entirely. There simply is no world where IT can operate at the speed needed without AI tools.

69% of respondents can’t roll back a bad configuration change within an hour, and 43% need more than a day. Another 26% of those responding can recover the same day, but only by doing it by hand. This is the biggest red flag of the survey, in my opinion. AI lets you ship anything fast, but AI can ship bugs just like humans can.

Here’s a real scenario that can happen: an IT admin asks an AI assistant to write a configuration profile, takes a quick pass at it, and pushes it to a few thousand Macs in seconds. If something is wrong with it (a bad network setting, a restriction that locks people out of an app they need), unwinding it could take a while.

“Mac admins are basically engineers now, whether their job description calls them that or not.”

I agree with him, and I am somewhat not happy about it. The job of an Apple admin has moved a long way from deploying Macs and iPads and managing through a device management console. Today it’s identity, security, compliance, and app lifecycle, all on top of a macOS release that forces changes every year. IT teams keep getting more and more added to them without additional resources or taking things away.

31% said keeping up with Apple’s release cadence is their single biggest IT challenge, far ahead of everything else on the survey. On the bright side, Apple’s own management architecture is moving in the right direction. 53% already have declarative device management in production.

Apple has done a lot of work here, and it’s not even Apple that is to blame for the frustration. Apple has built the platform for IT to do everything it needs to do. It’s everything else. Security is harder. AI has made it harder. It’s the expectation that IT has to own AI while owning literally everything else.

IT is using AI to help with its work because it’s the only way to survive the onslaught of the AI era. You aren’t getting more help, but you’re expected to do more without anything being taken away from you. Even systems that don’t need as much day-to-day management as they did years ago, you still have to own and secure them. Hosted email is a good example here. Yes, 365 and Workspace have made it easier to keep email running. You aren’t managing servers as you did 20 years ago, but email is still not easy. You traded server management for AI-driven phishing scams, MFA management, and more. It’s two steps forward and one back. We need a period of three steps forward and zero back to get back to where IT needs to be.

You can read Fleet’s full Apple in the enterprise report on its website.
