Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Quantinuum third quarter earnings conference call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your first speaker today, Shub Mukherjee, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Shub Mukherjee: Good afternoon, and welcome to Quantinuum third quarter 2026 earnings call. With me today are Raj Hazra, President and Chief Executive Officer, and Nitesh Sharan, Chief Financial Officer. Before we begin, I will cover the safe harbor statement. Today's remarks contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act. These include statements about our technology roadmap, commercial expectations, and 2026 and 2027 outlook. Actual results may differ materially. Please refer to the risk factors in our earnings release issued earlier today and our most recent Form 10-Q filed with the SEC. Statements speak only as of today, and we undertake no obligation to update them.

In addition, during today's call, we will be discussing certain non-GAAP financial measures. Please refer to our earnings release for additional information regarding these non-GAAP financial measures and reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measures. With that, Raj, over to you.

Rajeeb Hazra: Thank you, Shub, and good afternoon, everyone. Quantum computing, the largest market opportunity across all quantum technologies, is moving more rapidly from promise towards practical impact than it has ever in the past. What we are moving to, that opportunity is enormous and growing. Discovering new medicines and materials, improving financial modeling, optimizing complex logistics networks, and in general, finding solutions to many other problems that remain well beyond the reach of classical computers. Governments are making quantum a strategic priority, and most interestingly, enterprises are investing now in the expertise, partnerships, and applications needed to put quantum to work. As I said last quarter, the central question is, who will lead the creation of this new era of computing?

Our view of what it takes to lead and a leader is very clear. Leadership starts with building quantum hardware that can deliver accurate results at the speed customers need. Customers need to solve business problems, which means having answers that they can trust in a timely manner. Efficient fault-tolerant quantum computing at scale is the foundation of that trust. But having the best fault-tolerant quantum hardware alone is not enough. Leadership also means integrating quantum with classical computing and AI, and giving developers the tools to build applications that solve real business problems. That is what Quantinuum is building, a full-stack platform designed to deliver useful quantum computing at scale.

Our third quarter marked significant progress across all three parts of that strategy. First, in product technologies, we achieved world record logical fidelity on Helios, our commercial system, and significantly de-risked the hardware and error correction capability that will be required to deliver universal, fully fault-tolerant quantum computing with our Apollo system in 2029. In the area of software, we announced a multi-generational Nexus roadmap designed to accelerate application development on today's systems and enable those applications to scale well into the fault-tolerant era. And perhaps most importantly, in commercialization, we added new customers, deepened customer engagements, secured the largest cloud agreement in our history, and expanded access through major cloud and enterprise ecosystems. These are not 3 separate initiatives.

Together, these efforts position Quantinuum to accelerate commercial value creation before the end of this decade, delivering universal, fully fault-tolerant quantum computing by 2029, while building the software, applications, and the ecosystem customers need to use it today and in the future. Let me take a few minutes to walk through the details of our progress this quarter. I'll first focus on product technology and supply chain. The path to fault tolerance requires two things advancing together: accurate hardware, including an architecture that can scale qubits efficiently, and scalable error correction. We significantly advanced both in the third quarter. Well, not just advance, we demonstrated results that illustrate our significant lead in fault-tolerant hardware over the rest of the industry.

More of this in a minute, but first, let me do a quick update on our systems roadmap. Sol remains well on track for delivery in the second half of 2027. And given our step-by-step de-risking approach for these systems, we have greater confidence in its timeline today than we had for Helios at the same stage of development. For Sol, following the first traps returned from fabrication that I spoke about in the second quarter, in the third quarter, we validated Sol's entire control system for moving qubits in the two-dimensional trap at full product scale. That demonstrated the control and movement of ions required to validate our QCCD architecture in Sol and machines beyond, like Apollo.

We are now in full system integration and assembly on Sol, and on track to complete that in the first quarter of 2027. Next will come system validation and verification, including running real jobs before commercial availability in the second half of 2027, as planned, as promised. Sol is expected to be the world's first commercial quantum system with 100 logical qubits, targeting a logical error rate of 10 to the power minus five. That is approximately one error in 100,000 operations. Apollo, our universal fully fault-tolerant quantum computer, is progressing to plan through its design phases and remains solidly on track for 2029.

Our teams are progressing through key subsystem designs, including validating our cryogenic cooling system, which is critical for a machine at Apollo's scale. We are also building the supply chain we will need to scale production for Apollo and future machines with deep, longstanding partnerships with GlobalFoundries, Infineon, Honeywell Aerospace, Monarch Quantum, and others. These partners bring deep expertise early into the design of critical components, helping us reduce complexity, improve reliability, and make production more repeatable. In September, we finalized our CHIPS R&D award following the previously announced letter of intent, which will help accelerate our supply chain efforts. Quantinuum was the only trapped-ion company selected for that award.

Beyond the roadmap, as I had promised, I will get back to our industry-leading results in fault tolerance, which is very, very exciting, not just for us, but for the industry at large. in Q3, we introduced a scalable end-to-end logical architecture that brings together tailored AI decoders, all-to-all qubit connectivity, high-fidelity physical operations, and hardware-level error correction. These capabilities, working together to improve computational accuracy, providing the foundation for universal fully fault-tolerant quantum computing at scale, is essential for leadership. The end-to-end logical architecture's flexibility also allows us to test, refine, and combine different error-correcting codes, balancing our accuracy, efficiency, and speed for an increasingly larger set of diverse, demanding business applications.

We have already implemented this logical architecture in Helios. in September and October, two different error correction codes running on that architecture on Helios delivered back-to-back world records for logical fidelity. October's result reached 99.9995%, equivalent to five errors in one million operations. That error rate, just to put it in perspective, was 10 times lower than our own September record and 100 times lower than Google's, which had published the previous best results amongst the various hardware modalities. Critically, these results point to significantly lower error rates with lower error correction overhead.

Each two-step increase in the error correction code distance reduced logical memory errors by a factor of approximately 12, compared with roughly two in Google's published superconducting result. This stronger error suppression means that we will need 30 times fewer physical qubits, yes, 30x fewer physical qubits to reach target logical error rates, reinforcing another significant scalability advantage of our trapped-ion modality and our QCCD architecture. Today, we are very clearly leading in scaling accurate, high-fidelity computational power, and that underpins our confidence in delivering the world's first universal, fully fault-tolerant quantum computer in 2029. Next, let me move to software. Our Nexus platform had a very significant quarter of progress as well.

Nexus is a platform as a service that brings quantum application development and deployment into one environment and converts these hardware advances into capabilities customers can use to build meaningful applications and deploy them on hybrid quantum-classical infrastructure. Today, 215 organizations are building on Nexus, up nearly 20% from the 180 I had quoted last quarter. More than just the number, total job submissions increased tenfold in the 12 months through August 2026 compared with the preceding 12-month period. Today, we announced a significant advance for Nexus, a multi-generational roadmap to develop this platform into what we believe will be the industry's first platform as a service designed for the fault-tolerant era.

It aligns software capabilities with each generation of our hardware through Apollo and beyond, giving customers predictability for application development and deployment. This is a fundamental aspect of accelerating the adoption of useful quantum computing. We are already delivering the foundations of that roadmap. Our September release of Nexus extended our Guppy programming language with tools for programming logical qubits and applying supported error correction codes, including our own optimized codes and third-party codes, thereby reducing the need to rewrite application logic for each type of error correction code. Developers can now test programs and emulation, execute supported programs on Helios, and customize their approach while benefiting from advances in error correction.

The upcoming December release will expand capability to deal with hybrid workflows, allowing applications that have both classical and quantum code to respond to quantum results as soon as they become available, thereby making the performance of those systems more efficient and more effective. It will also add supported error correction codes and execution analytics to help developers optimize further the performance they get on our leading hardware. As our hardware and software advance together, the applications, the workflows, and expertise customers build on Nexus will become invaluable. That gives them a compelling reason to build with Quantinuum today and carry that investment forward with Quantinuum into the fault-tolerant era.

Last but not the least, let me talk about our progress with commercialization. We are adding new customers, developing applications around valuable customer problems, securing commitments across hardware generations, and expanding access through established cloud ecosystems. Let me give you just a few examples of new developments this quarter. Our work with Johnson & Johnson applies quantum computing and AI to the creation of new cancer therapy materials, with the potential to accelerate drug development and enable more effective treatments sooner. With GE Vernova, we are advancing research into superconducting materials in order to build smaller, lighter, and more efficient electrical infrastructure.

A new collaboration brings together Abu Dhabi Maritime Academy, part of the AD Ports Group, AI-powered logistics company Quincus, and Quantinuum to explore quantum AI and high-performance computing for complex maritime and logistics applications. We also signed our largest-ever cloud agreement, a multi-year, multi-generational commitment from a leading global financial institution for access to our systems through Apollo using Nexus, supporting fault-tolerant application development deployment across multiple core business functions. In addition to this, we are also expanding access to our infrastructure through cloud and enterprise environments that already serve millions of developers. Building on our announced partnership with Oracle last quarter, we are advancing commercialization of the hybrid quantum plus classical capabilities in the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.

We jointly launched a beta program for select customers to explore hybrid quantum and AI applications in the areas of defense, financial services, automotive, manufacturing, and general research. We demonstrated our joint offering at Oracle AI World, and Helios deployment into the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure's AI data center remains well on track for full deployment later next year. In addition, we also signed a new agreement with a leading hyperscaler serving millions of developers and enterprises worldwide. Bringing our hardware and software into that ecosystem significantly broadens our reach and is expected to accelerate the integration of quantum into existing AI, high-performance computing, and enterprise workflows.

Alongside this enterprise and cloud momentum, we are seeing continued government investment and strategic focus in the U.S. and internationally, benefiting Quantinuum. In the U.S., we continued progress through the DARPA Quantum Benchmarking Initiative for the QBI initiative. We are actively discussing a QBI Stage C scope of work with DARPA as we continue to execute on our Stage B contract. Separately, with the FSU, we are participating in four winning university proposals in phase one of the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission. These draw on our systems and expertise across algorithms and nuclear reaction design, quantum chemistry and new material creation, and AI-driven design of next-generation quantum processors.

Beyond the U.S., internationally, our second Helios system is on site in Singapore and is being assembled with commissioning on track for next spring. Next week, we are commissioning an upgraded computer at RIKEN in Japan as part of the world's most advanced hybrid quantum supercomputing system of its kind. We are also discussing potential deployments with several other governments at this stage. Together, these developments show how our commercial strategy is successfully accelerating the industry's adoption of quantum computing, in particular, developing applications around customer needs, securing long-term commitments to our products and services, and building the distribution and deployment pathways that are needed for broader adoption and scaling.

Lastly, on the ecosystem front, supporting our technological and commercial progress, we are growing the broader ecosystem around our full-stack platform. First, we worked with Sandia National Laboratories and NVIDIA to introduce QUOPS, a new performance benchmark that gives customers a capability that they were lacking. That capability is a credible, repeatable way to assess the size of a useful computation a system can execute and how quickly it can execute it. We are building alignment amongst partners in the ecosystem and government stakeholders towards an industry standard around QUOPS that will help customers compare systems and make informed purchasing decisions expediently. We are also growing the community that develops applications and brings new capabilities to our platform.

We've now grown Q-Net, our community providing developers and researchers with resources to do more with our platform, to over 800 participants, and added eight startups, new startups, to our Quantinuum Startup Partner Program. Finally, we are working closely with our government and commercial customers to grow the quantum ecosystem. A case in point is a quantum challenge we designed and ran in Singapore, supported by Singapore's National Quantum Office. Over 200 teams submitted proposals, and the winner will be announced later this month. These initiatives help build practical expertise and applications around our technology stack. These efforts reinforce one another. Clear benchmarks help customers evaluate systems, developer programs build expertise and applications, and public-private programs create pathways to adoption.

Our third-quarter execution increased our technology lead. With deeper customer commitments and expanding routes to market, we believe we are positioned to turn that leadership into momentum, into accelerated commercial growth, and further extend our industry leadership. Our momentum across technology and commercialization has been accelerating through the year. As I look at 2027, I'm more confident of our opportunity and our ability to capitalize on it than I was when we spoke last quarter. With that, over to Nitesh to take you through our financial results and outlook.

Nitesh Sharan: Thank you, Raj, and good afternoon, everyone. Let me start by building off of Raj's thoughts. Our goals were clear this year. Through the IPO, we shared an aggressive and credible plan, grounded in reality. We are running ahead of that pace, and our momentum is accelerating. We believe we have a multi-year technological lead versus the competition, and each new deal we close makes it harder for others to catch up. We don't take that for granted. We are constantly on the offense while being measured about the risks.

Our investments are thoughtfully calibrated, designed to maintain and extend our lead through the engineering required to be the first fault-tolerant, to scale manufacturing with a diverse and proven supply chain, and to execute the go-to-market strategies that we expect will unlock the greatest value for customers. We are fueling this from a position of capital strength that sets the foundation for disruptive growth and outsized return, and that continues to translate into near-term financials that outpace even our own expectations. Let me illustrate that in the Q3 results. Revenue for the third quarter was $9.1 million, up 233% from the prior year. Growth was driven primarily by strength in our cloud platform, along with research and services.

Revenue remained well-diversified across customer types and geographies, with government representing the majority and enterprise also a significant contributor. Customer concentration also continued to improve in the quarter. Let me emphasize a point that is important to understand when contrasting our results with others in the quantum sector. Every dollar of revenue we report is directly related to quantum computing. As Raj noted, that is the grand prize we are focused on as the largest part of the quantum ecosystem, and it is what will catalyze the world-changing breakthroughs that we see on the horizon. Bookings are a forward indicator of future revenue.

In the quarter, we recorded bookings of $98 million, including the Oracle deal we announced during the last earnings call. These deals were across government and enterprise, and served several of our core industry verticals, notably financial services, chemicals, and pharma. Our 2026 year-to-date bookings now stand at approximately $104 million, and we expect to achieve more than $120 million in bookings over the full year, setting us up well entering 2027. More on that when I get to the outlook. Moving to the cost structure. Cost of sales was $3.2 million in the third quarter, including roughly $0.7 million of stock-based compensation. Non-GAAP gross margin, which excludes stock-based compensation and other non-cash charges, was 74.6%.

The year-over-year improvement in gross margin this quarter was largely driven by revenue growth. This line will move with revenue from quarter to quarter and be heavily influenced by product mix. The gross margins this quarter reflect the heavy mix of cloud business. Over time, we will increasingly emphasize design for cost and manufacturing for scale, and we have a great set of supply chain partners working closely with us on these objectives. Research and development expenses were $97.5 million, including $27 million of stock-based compensation, up from $42.4 million a year ago. We are investing at every level of the technology stack, our leading quantum hardware, the Nexus developer platform, and in end-user applications.

These capabilities amplify one another and are increasingly fueled by direct customer engagement, providing direct clarity towards unlocking end-user value. Sales and marketing expenses were $14.9 million, compared with $4 million in the prior year period, and included roughly $4 million of stock-based compensation. We are building our government, commercial, and consulting direct sales engine. Our indirect channel partners will enable us to further leverage this line item to capture more of the market, and we are enabling all of that through targeted high-ROI marketing spend across brand development, demand generation, and lead execution. General and administrative expenses were $22.1 million, compared with $5.3 million in the prior year period, and included $5.5 million of stock-based compensation.

The increase reflects the investments required to operate as a public company, including finance, legal, compliance, and operations. We continue to invest in our controls infrastructure, from the foundational IT to modern applications that improve overall process and administration. In total, stock-based compensation was $37.2 million in the quarter. Adjusted EBITDA, which excludes stock-based compensation, depreciation and amortization, and other one-time and non-cash items, was a loss of $80.5 million, compared with a loss of $45.3 million in the prior year period. As a reminder, at the GAAP net income level, we separate the economics attributable to legacy shareholders who have not yet exchanged their shares into the post-IPO public entity as non-controlling interest.

Our total GAAP net loss for the third quarter was $117.9 million. Of that, the net loss attributable to Quantinuum Inc. was $17 million, or a 46-cent net loss per share. On an adjusted basis, non-GAAP net loss was $75.2 million, and non-GAAP EPS was a loss of 29 cents per share. These measures are calculated across our full shareholder base, and they exclude stock-based compensation, depreciation and amortization, and other one-time and non-cash items. Turning to the balance sheet. We ended the quarter with over $1.9 billion in cash and equivalents with no debt.

We have a strong balance sheet, with what we believe is more than sufficient cash to fund our technology roadmap and invest in the critical capabilities that we expect to fuel the path to profitability. Maintaining a strong balance sheet is a critical priority for us and a source of strength. Before turning to guidance, let me describe the accounting related to one of our big wins in the quarter, the CHIPS award. As we noted, we were awarded $100 million from the Department of Commerce to help develop the U.S. quantum ecosystem. As part of the structure of the deal, the U.S. government received roughly two million shares and provides cash and milestones, with the majority upfront.

This deal is characterized as an equity contract and accordingly does not affect the P&L. As of Q3, the cash did not impact the cash and equivalents line on the balance sheet, and its direct effect on the balance sheet will vary quarter to quarter. Overall, just note that this is an incremental investment to fund our pathway to fault tolerance, providing incremental capital protection and diversity of funding sources that may not be fully reflected on the cash line. Turning now to our outlook. Our execution velocity and commercial momentum have picked up through the year, and this gives us higher conviction in our near-term revenue.

We are raising our full-year 2026 revenue outlook to $31 million-$34 million from $28 million-$32 million previously. It also makes us more bullish on 2027. Based on our current bookings and backlog and our assumptions around contract timing and revenue recognition, we continue to expect revenue growth of more than 100% in 2027. That growth now builds off of a higher 2026 base. Put simply, our expectations for both 2026 and 2027 are higher today than they were just last quarter. In closing, our momentum is clear. Given our early-stage nature, things will not move linearly. Each quarter will have its own unique element, but we expect the longer-term trajectory is exponentially upward.

The technology leadership Raj described is converting into commercial traction, and that traction is showing up in our financial results with accelerating momentum. We believe we are building a diversified business with an attractive long-term financial profile that we expect to deliver sustained growth, profitability, and high returns. With that, we will now open it up for Q&A.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Krish Sankar from TD Cowen. Please go ahead.

Sreekrishnan Sankarnarayanan: Hi. Thanks for taking my question, and congrats on the strong results. Raj and Nitesh, the calendar 2026 outlook improvement from three months ago, just wondering what drove it? Is it cloud, enterprise, government, R&D? Is it within U.S., overseas, any specific industries? Just extrapolating it onto the 2027 revenue growth of 100% off a higher base, what kind of specific verticals are driving the growth in 2027 too? Thank you very much.

Nitesh Sharan: Sure. Thanks for your question, Krish. on the 2026 raise, it really is broad-based. We are seeing great progress on the cloud business. We are seeing it across governments, not just in the U.S., but across the world, and in enterprises across some of the verticals we highlighted in the prepared remarks. As you go forward into 2027, certainly we were excited last time to raise that outlook as well. Talked about significant deal with Oracle that we are excited about, that has some revenue characteristics that gives us conviction. We also this time announced some other deals, another hyperscaler in the mix, some other enterprise deals. Quite frankly, our momentum is broad-based.

It is across governments, it is across national labs, it is across universities, it is across enterprises. It is in the U.S., it is in Europe, it is in Asia. I think more importantly is that the traction, which over time you will see in GAAP revenue, but it is really the engagement, the levels of both in the developer ecosystem, but end user customers, the algorithms they are working on, the advancements, obviously we talked about on the tech roadmap that is resonating with customers and our sales team and the pipeline that they are building.

We are seeing it across all of the pieces, and so that is why we had enough conviction, which still, in our view, reasonable amount of conservatism and prudence in our planning, that we would be able to raise 2026 and also give you an early view of an increase in 2027.

Operator: Our next question comes from Vivek Arya from BofA Securities.

Unknown Analyst: Hi, thank you. This is William Paul on for Vivek. I wanted to start just on the error correction side. You said the October result means you need about 30 times less physical qubits to hit your target logical error rates. Could you discuss how that changes how you design Apollo and Lumos, and particularly how we should think about Lumos in terms of size and that logical qubit count longer term? Thank you.

Rajeeb Hazra: Thanks for the question, Vivek. As you stated, there were two really big things we announced in the error correction. One was reaching that absolute five errors in 1 million operations. But the second big thing was the error correction efficiency, where we achieved an exponential reduction in error correction for a reasonably small amount of increase in the number of physical qubits that are used to create a logical qubit. That comes from the architecture that we have, our modality, and the very strong all-to-all connectivity that we support in our particular implementation of two-dimensional QCCD. As we think of that going forward, there are two things.

One is, obviously, these results, even achieved on Helios with a universal gate set, give us very high confidence that as we move to Sol and Apollo, and the physical qubits themselves get better, that we are in very good de-risk shape to achieve Apollo's targets that we put forth and achieve them at full fault tolerance across all operations of the universal gate sets.

We have not made public yet the logical specs on Lumos, but what we expect is that Lumos to continue the physical qubit improvements to some extent, but most importantly, aggressively adopt these error correction techniques that we have now proven are scalable from the scale of Helios to a million-plus qubit machine, that we will effectively continue to run that exponential and therefore deliver essentially the best error rates in the industry for the smallest amount of system size. That is very important from a reliability standpoint, cost standpoint, and simply manageability standpoint of these systems.

Unknown Analyst: Thank you. On your largest ever cloud deal, the multi-generation commitment through Apollo, what is driving customers to sign multi-year commitments before fault tolerance arrives? How is their spend trending? What kind of conversations you are having with them, and are they moving from research and exploration projects into production use cases?

Rajeeb Hazra: Great question, Vivek. There is really two drivers. One is being engaged early, actually having a use case roadmap that tells them what can be achieved at what portions, with what portions of unlock from machines like H2, Helios, Sol, and Apollo. The first thing is conviction that their business-relevant use cases can grow. The second is the predictability of our roadmap now and the confidence that if they invest in technologies or application building input in, say, the Sol timeframe, that carries forward in a timely manner to a machine called Apollo, which is not maybe at some point, but it is definitely in 2029.

The nature of our conversations very clearly, as you see these kinds of deals that we are seeing both extend in time, expand in size of dollars, and extend over multiple generations, that came from the early engagement, which was kind of more proof of concept, to now it is almost pre-building of the application that in some cases will unlock at Sol at a full production scale or Apollo. That path of getting ready so there is not a delay between when the technology is available and when the applications are deriving business value, that gap is minimized.

We are very much from the age of kind of discovery to the age of acceleration when it comes to these kinds of commercial customers and their applications.

Nitesh Sharan: And just to add one thing to the tail end of what you asked, in this particular case that you asked about, there is an expansion of what they're spending with us, and actually we're seeing that across a number of customers as well because of the value that Raj just articulated.

Operator: Our next question comes from John McPeake from Rosenblatt Securities.

John McPeake: Hey, guys. Congratulations on the progress here. My question is the same question I had last call, actually. I will ask it again since one quarter has passed. The de-risk since the last call relative to the transition from Sol to what is likely the first fault-tolerant machine, Apollo, maybe you could just give me the key points there, what you have accomplished. Because you did the crossing with Helios, and now you have the chip, I guess, running, and you are crossing ions in the trap. Anything there would be great, and then I just have one follow-up.

Rajeeb Hazra: Sure. Maybe I can answer that, and even though you asked the same question, I will give you a different answer and a better answer this time. Because we have advanced. We have advanced, and what we have done is, last time I told you that Sol is the building block for Apollo. Why? Because it is the same two-dimensional QCCD. Sol chip came back, and the big thing in Helios, we had one crossing, so you had to manage only one pair of qubits crossing each other.

Of course, in Sol, with 198 qubits, we have near 100 pairs of qubits to actually move around the chip and pipeline them, and that is a complex control system, but it is the heart of what makes a 2D trap for Sol and Apollo work. That we have proved on real silicon at the 192-qubit scale and then simulated it beyond to give us confidence that the basic heart of the Sol's qubit transport system, which is essential, essentially, to moving qubits, giving them values, gating them, and reading them, and even cooling them, is functional. So that is one of the things that, while it is proven on Sol and de-risked Sol, we carried that forward into Apollo.

The other two things that we have made advance on Apollo is actually, one is the cryogenic system, because at the scale that Apollo is, you have to ensure that system is balanced to the load and the larger chip that Apollo is. The second thing is, of course, advances in what we call the laser optic system, because Apollo carries more qubits.

Even though you can move the qubits around, as we've proven with Sol and Apollo, the ability to actually show that you can have beam formation, beam delivery, and working with our partners like Monarch Quantum prototyping those, to us then being able to say, "Yes, we can see Sol working in 2027, and by 2027, 2028, we would have de-risked our path significantly through proven subsystems into Apollo, which then we integrate." That has been our strategy.

Prove out the most critical subsystems first in emulation, then in silicon, test silicon and prototype, and then build them and integrate it and build the whole system together with far less risk than waiting for everything to come together at the end.

John McPeake: Excellent. With the recent novel error correction that you're using, triangular error correction, and the results that you're getting there, is there potentially upward pressure on the logical- error rates, because on the logical error rates in Sol, Apollo, and Lumos?

Rajeeb Hazra: Actually, with the error correction results that we got, that we have said, shown on Helios, which is five errors in a million operations, which is five times 10 to the power minus six, we have de-risked the error rate. Because with Helios and 96 qubits, we have been able to show that all elements of the magic state factory and some of the ancillary and some of what we call coding overhead is easily managed to deliver that error rate. Now, in Sol, we have two tailwinds. One is we have more physical qubits, and so more resources. Number two is Sol's qubits, physical qubits themselves are better.

That gives us a significant boost in being able to do more error correction per round than we've even been able to do on Helios, which is about six times better than the published result on any other modality. Does that make sense, John?

John McPeake: It makes sense. When I say upward pressure, I guess it is upward pressure on fidelity is really what I meant, not on error rates. The final one is, what I think some of other modalities are struggling with is the non-Clifford gates and the distillation magic states and all that, and the overhead that is required. You guys are going to give us, at some point soon, I think, some information on non-Cliffords and universal gates, I guess, right? With the new error correction codes.

Rajeeb Hazra: Absolutely. In fact, I want to be very clear. We have already, and we were the first to demonstrate a universal gate set. Our results are universal gate sets and a distribution of non-Clifford gates along with Clifford gates. We define universal full fault tolerance as what we need for the era of full fault tolerance. It is not about just doing the Clifford gates and not the non-Clifford gates. That is already in our results. If you look then, if you are trying to compare, for instance, where our magic state or some of the components of end-to-end error correction are, we have results.

In fact, we published it in 2025, where we have slightly better results than what Google published, which was their 40x reduction in magic state errors, with a significantly higher acceptance rate. What I mean by that is, the way you do magic state distillation or cultivation is you have to try over and over and over again, and sometimes they work, and sometimes they do not work. The acceptance rate is how accurately you are doing the magic states versus doing them and throwing them away and then only keeping the good magic states.

What that practically means is, if your acceptance rate is high, then you are using the physical qubit resources very efficiently, and you are also cutting down the time required to get these magic states built. All in all, we enjoy this end-to-end logical error rate advantage due to a number of factors, one of which is best-in-class magic state fidelity and magic state utilization, if you think of it as space-time utilization, which is really how well we can scale as we get to larger qubit counts.

John McPeake: Great. I am really looking forward to Sol and Apollo.

Operator: Our next question comes from David Vogt from UBS.

David Vogt: Great. Thanks, guys, for taking my question. Raj, I just wanted to follow up on John's question regarding the Apollo roadmap. Appreciate all the color on Sol, where we are going to be from a validation and a commercial availability perspective next year. Can you help us understand from a simulation, from an emulation to silicon emulation roadmap, what other sort of subsystem designs or what other roadmaps should we be paying attention to as we move forward with Apollo outside of sort of the build-out of the supply chain in terms of tracking the progress?

Obviously, I know Sol is critical next year, but just want to keep an eye on what else is being focused on from a subsystem perspective for Apollo as you go to a full tolerance solution. I have a follow-up.

Rajeeb Hazra: Yeah, absolutely. The first major subsystem, as you see Apollo being a larger version of Sol, is the transport subsystem that we have completely now validated at scale. It is important to get that right, even at scale. Why does scale matter? Because all of the pipelining and therefore the functioning, the time-based performance of the chip, the speed of the chip depends on very efficiently being able to move these qubits, not just being able to move them. That is the first subsystem, is the transport subsystem. The second subsystem, as I mentioned, was essentially the laser, the optic subsystem that then interacts with the qubits on the chip that are controlled electrically in their movement.

That, we made significant progress along with our supply chain partner, Monarch Quantum, that we have been engaged with for now over two years, in building out the exact, what we call the beam delivery and the beam concentration and the beam localization capabilities so that you can actually have those moving qubits being brought to the computational zones, which are many more in Apollo than in Sol, and being able to accurately use them to give us the kind of fidelities that we enjoy today in Helios and see moving forward in Sol and Apollo. Third is the cryogenic system. Again, we do not need cryogenics to actually manufacture qubits like superconducting folks do.

We need the cryogenics, which is, I would say, gentler cryogenics, in order to create a good vacuum. At Sol scale and then at Apollo scale, it is important that we have a very efficient cryogenic system, which is not just a technical matter, but it is also a closed loop so that it does self-recovery of the cryogenic material, which is helium, and that impacts the practical TCO of the machine. So, a percentage of gain in actual the end-to-end round trip recovery does impact the TCO and the operating cost of the machine. We made great progress there as well.

We have been kind of focused on the hardware, but the next big piece is the infrastructure software stack Nexus. In Apollo, the Nexus roadmap is one where developers are not going to have to think of error correction as something that is their responsibility. The Nexus capabilities snapped to Apollo will be able to use Apollo's hardware and offer developers who bring in just their application a choice of error correction codes that they can link in like a library.

In some cases, if they do not know which ones, the machine will actually, using some level of machine intelligence and understanding the application, suggest what may be the best error correction code to use for that application and the resources it needs. So, very sophisticated environment in software that aids developer productivity and effectiveness enabled by very high performance, fully fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

David Vogt: Great. No, that is incredibly helpful. Maybe just a quick follow-up for Nitesh I know, Nitesh, you are not in the habit of giving longer-term outlooks, but just trying to understand when I look at your outlook for next year that you expressed confidence in and the bookings number that you alluded to earlier for this year, I think $120 million bookings for the full year. How do we think about the way bookings start to filter in when Sol becomes commercially available later in the year? What is the lead time? When do you expect commercial engagements to really start to impact those metrics and then ultimately convert into revenue?

Recognizing that obviously you still have some validation and integration work to do, but just want to get a bit of an understanding on how the model works in that sense.

Nitesh Sharan: Yeah, maybe I will make two points. One is that we are seeing some of that commercialization happening now. In fact, some of the contracts that we have actually have a graduation of how people will have their journey going forward. I think to an earlier question, Raj talked about, a lot of these customers that we talk about continuing with us, upsizing their contracts, renewing, oftentimes there is a long journey of algorithmic development, how these use cases will build and build upon one another. So, it is actually in our pipeline, it goes further out beyond Sol into Apollo as well.

So, I think you are certainly going to see greater emphasis on that as we go through next year in terms of the opportunity. But I think if underpinning one of your questions, how does this model play out over several years? We are very early in this opportunity, and we do see the market growing substantially, especially when you get to fault tolerance. The opportunity in terms of the value of these systems grows step function, and so that will be catalyzed in our revenue and our bookings.

Ultimately, we are talking getting towards this billions of dollars of opportunity in the not too long horizon, capturing a meaningful part of the market because, again, our focus is quantum computing. We are leading. We think we have a multi-year lead against competition. The engagements we are having with enterprises, governments, universities, and so forth is showing that back to us that we are doing the right thing. We are trying to make our systems more readily accessible to folks, and that is happening not only through the hardware side, but also through the Nexus side, as Raj just talked about.

We do think all of this leads to ultimately we are in hypergrowth mode, and the numbers that we are laying out for the near term, the next 12 months and so forth, it will move to exponential growth as you get into the latter part of this decade and we start to move from Helios to Sol to Apollo and to Lumos.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our next question comes from Joe Moore from Morgan Stanley.

Joseph Moore: Great. Thank you. I wanted to ask about the DARPA Stage C. You talked about the progress that you are making there. I guess to the extent that some others did pass through Stage C, just wanted to give you a chance to address if that means anything, and certainly we are confident that you are in a strong position. I guess to the extent Stage C is about whether the system can be built and operated as designed, what key pieces of Lumos do you need to demonstrate to get there? Thank you.

Rajeeb Hazra: Hi, Joe. Thanks for the question. Just the facts, what DARPA has said is Stage C is a phased set of awards depending on which companies were in their Stage C commitments and delivery. We continue to work with Stage finishing up on our Stage B and are in active discussions with DARPA on our Stage C scope of work. We see the DARPA as an important kind of validation confidence builder, but we are also engaged very deeply, as Nitesh talked about and I talked about, with enterprise customers.

Our view of what these systems need to be, what error rates they need to reach, what scale they need to reach, and how we build them is built partly on the conviction of our own technology view and partly on the conviction that our customers say these are the right kinds of systems, these are the right kinds of system capabilities. We are moving down with Apollo and Lumos and our roadmap very confidently as we de-risk critical components of that fully fault-tolerant computing stack, and in parallel, continue to work to finalize our Stage C scope of work based on this particular de-risk, highly credible roadmap that we put forward for the industry.

Operator: Our next question comes from Mark Moerdler from Bernstein.

Mark Moerdler: Thank you very much for taking my question. Congratulations on all the progress you are making. It is really quite impressive. I would like to switch gears a little bit and talk about the hyperscaler partnership you have and the likely, maybe you will get more of these going forward. I would like to understand some more on the economics of this. Who is selling the usage. How is it being monetized. Are they reselling just the compute or the software platform. Is it consumption agreements, or they are paying something upfront.

Any color you can give so that we can get a better understanding as the scales of what the opportunity and monetization is, and what the use cases they are using it for.

Nitesh Sharan: Thanks, Mark. I will start, and then Raj can add on. First, yeah, we are excited to have continued growth, both direct customer activity, but also through these channel partners. Excited last time to disclose Oracle, and then excited now to talk about hyperscaler, and to your point, yeah, there is a lot of opportunity. For us, what is most important is that the arrangement is a strategic one, that we are providing customers with differentiated service. Ultimately, for us, it is a go-to-market access play. We are providing the full stack capability.

We talked last time about how Oracle were actually the first to put a quantum system in a data center, and it is going to be natively built up, integrated, and so forth. Here, it is not exactly that construct, but it is another one where we are able to have joint go-to-market. The revenue model is, openly, we are still working through some pieces, but there is ultimately that, if you have an end customer of the hyperscaler that wants access to the best breed of quantum system out there, they can access our systems, and then we will obviously accrete the revenue associated with that.

Rajeeb Hazra: Yeah. The only thing I would add, Mark, is, the hyperscaler models are different depending on how the integration happens. We provide the flexibility through our software stack and our business model to be able to do that. But in the Oracle case, as we said, Oracle bought the system and our full stack along with it, monetizing it. We may have future opportunities to build on top of that as we bring additional customers in. In other cases, we are a full stack. Think of it as a full stack capability within that, and we get paid for the value we unlock for customers that are already on that hyperscaler or come to that. The key point is twofold.

One is, we are seeing increasing number of end customers already on the public cloud wanting to integrate AI, HPC, and quantum workloads, which is what is driving these hyperscalers to look aggressively at incorporating the QPU along with the GPU and the CPU in the data center. Number two is we are monetizing our full stack. This is the hardware, our Nexus layer, our value-added libraries and applications and chemistry, and not just commoditizing the hardware in these kinds of partnerships with our hyperscalers.

Operator: Our next question comes from Vijay Rakesh from Mizuho.

Unknown Analyst: This is Rahul covering for Vijay. Congratulations on the strong results. I was wondering how many of those organizations that you have on Nexus could become on-prem clients over time, and is there something specific that would drive their conversion from cloud to on-prem? Is there some usage level or maybe a customer size?

Rajeeb Hazra: Yeah, it's a great question. The first thing is, when customers get on Nexus, it's a highly sticky environment because you're choosing the programming language, you're binding your applications to specific libraries, and it's a very sticky environment that then you want transportable on whether you want it in a private cloud or you want it on a public cloud, and the private cloud is the on-premise cloud, right? We have architected our full stack to be able to do that. The organizations, we have about 215 organizations today on Nexus, and a large majority of them are using the hardware in the Quantinuum cloud as we move forward, but some of them are already on a private cloud.

For instance, we have Singapore, for instance, as a customer, Japan as a customer, that are actually using a private cloud and Nexus on their private cloud where they have the hardware on their premise. As we move forward, what I see is how the world played out for enterprise workloads. You will see some of the workloads and some portion of the workflows happen in the public cloud, but some stay on the private cloud for data governance, data security, and simple economics of moving large amounts of data back and forth.

We have customers across all of those segments, which is why we have a good set of inputs as to how to create a flexible architecture that essentially says, "We meet you where you need the service.

Unknown Analyst: It's very helpful. Maybe one follow-up. When you think about 2027 growing over 100%, how much of it is already covered by backlog and pipeline? Maybe what portion of it is an Oracle deal or maybe other big deals that you have secured?

Nitesh Sharan: A good amount is covered. I know I won't give you too precise an answer, but I'll just say that we are feeling like we're in really good position. Obviously, there's still details that play out of when actually revenue plays through, but the line of sight we have, including the existing backlog, gives us a fair amount of confidence that we can deliver at least 100% next year. It is, Oracle's important, but there are definitely other deals. We talked about a few of them in the earnings call this time. So, it's broad-based.

Operator: Our next question comes from Quinn Bolton from Needham & Company.

Shadi Mitwalli: Hey, guys. This is Shadi Mitwalli for Quinn. Thanks for taking the question. I guess on the agreement with J&J, I know in the past you guys have talked about outcome-based IP being a potential revenue stream, so was just curious to hear if that's something that can come out of this agreement.

Rajeeb Hazra: Yeah. We see it certainly monetizing our full stack. We are working with some chemistry customers. For instance, I'll give you one example where we have IP around a workflow to deal with metal-organic frameworks, which can be used from anything from carbon sequestration to delivery, creation of drug delivery elements. That's an IP we own and that we are actually actively monetizing in a couple of the engagements we have with pharma customers. That is very much still a way these services get delivered for end users into solutions, and we see that as a value add for us going forward.

Operator: Our next question comes from Troy Jensen from Cantor Fitzgerald. Your line is open.

Troy Jensen: Hey, gentlemen. Congrats on the results. Sorry I jumped on a little late here, but I guess a question for Raj. Just with the balance sheet you have right now and just the thoughts of acquisitions, software, and I guess ultimately I would love to know if multimodality is something that Quantinuum would ever pursue, or is it always going to be just trapped ions? Thank you.

Rajeeb Hazra: Great question. It would be kind of getting into speculation at this point, and I don't want to do that. What I will simply state is, number one, we have great confidence in the modality path we've chosen and our delivery, and it just demonstrates further confidence in the way we are acting. On the software spaces, we look at a gamut of possibilities from deep partnerships to enabling folks on Nexus, collaborations on standards and benchmarks.

We have, with the balance sheet we have and our position, we are always actively looking at what's the best way to propel our business and deepen our moats, and we will continue to be good stewards of that capital and use it for those purposes to drive our business forward and accelerate where necessary.

Troy Jensen: Just maybe a follow-up. I guess, your thoughts on trapped ions. Do you think that's the time to solution and time to cost winner for all applications, or does it cover most of the applications? I'm just kind of curious. I always thought that there could be different modalities that are good for better applications, but I'd just love to get your thoughts on that.

Rajeeb Hazra: Yeah. I'm glad you used the word time to solution, because time to solution incorporates not only the speed of the computer, but the accuracy of the computer as well, because there's no point calculating the wrong answer quickly. As we look at our lead in fault tolerance, for instance, and being able to generate with fewer qubits and fewer rounds of error correction the entire chain of correction, we actually see time to solution being in favor of those modalities, including trapped ion and us, that actually have the highest fidelity, and fidelity being more important in order to deliver an effective, real, usable answer, of course, within the time to solution bounds that answer needs.

We actually look at our approach on building fidelity and building the best fidelities, and then innovating to cut that down to as fast as we can deliver that fidelity in terms of execution speed as the right way to meet our customers' workloads and use cases that they want from us.

Shub Mukherjee: Thanks, Troy. Operator, I think, sensitive to time, we will take one final question.

Operator: Okay. Thank you. Please stand by. Our last question comes from Tyler Anderson from Craig-Hallum Capital Group.

Tyler Perry Anderson: Hi, this is Tyler Anderson on for Craig-Hallum. Thank you for taking my question. I was hoping I was going to make the cut. I was reading your work on the error correction codes, and to me, this seems like something that could be used to separate out, whether it be a magic state factory or just something to create T-gates, such that area requires much less resources than what would be otherwise, and then have a separate area for, let us just say, the logical or the logic compute of the system.

I am wondering, to what degree does that free open logical qubits for you and enable you to calculate with greater depth and a faster time to solution?

Rajeeb Hazra: If I understood your question correctly, Tyler, thank you for asking it. What I will tell you is, if you want to build a universal fault-tolerant quantum computer, you are going to have to have magic state distillation or at least magic state cultivation to a certain extent. What is critical is that the magic state output is high fidelity.

But you also, because magic states are built or magic state factories depend on the number of magic states you may have to inject and how effectively you can build them, it actually, we stand with a very distinct advantage because we can build those magic states using far less physical qubit resources than anybody else can because of the improved physical qubits we have, the all-to-all connectivity, and our ability to be more efficient, therefore, in a higher acceptance rate. When we look at a full logical computation which has a universal gate set, we are already lower in the number of magic state resources that we need, and I just told you why.

Therefore, what we see is not complicating the developer's life by giving them two completely separate paths, because we are already generating the world's best leading logical error rates and have a path forward on continuing to do that without running into a wall.

Tyler Perry Anderson: Okay. That makes sense, and I agree with the trying to abstract away for end users. I think that is very important. That is all for me. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes the question and answer session. Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program, and you may now disconnect.

#3239. Roku is taking away a fan-favorite screensaver – but you have alternatives

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

One of Roku's most popular screensavers is about to make its last splash. Here’s how to switch before Dec. 1.

A fan-favorite Roku screensaver is going away, and users aren’t happy.

Over the last several days, users with the Aquatic Life aquarium screensaver set as the default have noticed a message appearing when the screensaver opens. “Starting Dec. 1, 2026,” the message reads, “the Aquatic Life screensaver will no longer be available, and your screensaver will switch to Roku City.”

Also: The free Roku City screensaver game has me hooked

The screensaver, which displays a digital aquarium with tropical fish swimming back and forth, was available as a downloadable theme pack and was a popular pick for many years.

Users on Reddit quickly lamented the loss in many posts, with dozens noting that the aquarium was part of their daily routine. Roku responded to one post, saying, “That makes sense, and we hear you. Aquatic Life has a lot of loyal fans, and we’re passing your feedback along to the team.” The post noted that when “the fish swim off,” Roku devices with Aquatic Life will switch to Roku City.

You can browse to Settings > Theme > Screensaver to find another theme.

Several online reports indicate that the removal is a licensing issue and that the creator of the screensaver posted on Reddit that he removed the license after Roku’s sale to Fox. That thread has now been deleted, so the comment is unavailable. Roku hasn’t issued any statement of its own about why, but I have reached out to ask. I’ve also reached out directly to the screensaver’s creator.

If you’re looking for the exact screensaver, it’s still available as a 2-minute clip on Roku’s YouTube channel. It takes a few extra steps, but if you want to keep the screensaver running on your TV, you can create a YouTube playlist with just that video, set it to loop, and use the YouTube app on Roku whenever you want to see it.

Even though the announcement of the screensaver’s departure happened less than 24 hours ago, the comments section of that video is packed with users begging Roku to keep Aquatic Life.

Also: I started clearing my Roku cache, and it fixed my biggest TV complaint

Alternatively, you could open one of the many YouTube videos that have aquarium displays and let one of them run for as long as you want.

There are also several dozen aquarium apps for Roku. I checked out several of them, and while they don’t look exactly like the Roku one, they do fill the void. Note that if you opt for one of these, most of them do have ads that play before the aquarium starts.

Lastly, you can download the original app for your phone or computer from SereneScreen.

#3238. What to Know About Meta’s Muse AI Before It Learns Too Much About You

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Meta’s Muse AI agent keeps a running profile of everyone who uses it. Yes, even if you deny it permission to do so. And by doing so, it’s effectively made Jolly, its “cute and cuddly” mascot, a harbinger of concerning security architecture.

Muse requests extensive access to personal data, including passwords, full disk access, email messages, calendar, contacts, Notes and WhatsApp. By default, Meta also appears to use your interactions with Muse to train its AI models, so you have to manually opt out in the settings.

If that wasn’t enough, there’s also a widely publicized case in which Muse mistakenly shared the home address of a Toronto tech reviewer, Matt Robb, with a potential buyer on Facebook Marketplace. Muse invited the stranger to Robb’s home without his explicit consent or knowledge, then later apologized for doing so, as detailed in a Threads post. Robb hadn’t realized that he had inadvertently granted Muse blanket permission to automatically reply to Marketplace inquiries using the details he provided, including his address.

Before facing a potential security nightmare, here’s what to know about Muse.

Meta’s Muse appears to blatantly ignore user permissions, according to a report by AppleInsider. In one case, the AI agent synced roughly 187,000 lines of a user’s Apple Messages without their consent, even though “Full Disk Access” was turned off.

The report shows that Muse pinged a user’s messages database thousands of times despite disk access being disabled. Muse then successfully harvested texts from the user’s Mac — not from Meta’s Messenger, but from Apple Messages.

Even people who refuse to use Muse may have their data collected by the AI if they text someone who does have it installed.

Before Meta launched the ability for its Muse to make outbound business calls on your behalf, internal Meta documents revealed that the company planned to rely on human contractors at call centers to help make reservations and appointments.

That means not only would the software have access to all your private data, but a total stranger might also be managing your personal commitments — all without your knowledge. The human concierge feature appears to have been rolled back for now, according to Reuters.

The VPN company Surfshark said it found that Meta Muse is collecting — or attempting to collect — 31 out of 35 types of data, putting it far ahead of other popular chatbots like Gemini, ChatGPT and DeepSeek. Muse also collects highly sensitive personal information like location data, sexual orientation, genetic information or biometric data.

Muse (along with Meta AI and Gemini) also reserves the right to use collected audio data for other purposes, such as analytics or product personalization. Surfshark released a full dataset for what it uncovered.

Want to share your experience with Meta’s Muse or other AI agents? Email us at editors@cnet.com.

#3237. Windows 11 can run better on PCs with 8GB now, Microsoft says – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

The latest updates to Windows 11 offer improvements in speed, performance, and memory management.

The more memory your Windows PC has, the faster it should perform, especially when juggling multiple apps, files, and other data. My laptop has 32GB of RAM, while my desktop has a hefty 64GB, and both are absolutely zippy. Does that mean computers with only 8GB of memory, or even less, are also-rans? Nope, not according to Microsoft.

Also: How much RAM does your PC really need?

In a new blog post published Tuesday, Microsoft touted the gains in speed, performance, and memory management in Windows 11 achieved by the latest updates. These especially impact PCs with just 8GB of RAM, which can now run multiple apps and files faster and more efficiently than before.

To reach this goal, the company said it had three notions in mind.

The first was to make better use of the existing memory on each Windows 11 PC. The second was to protect the tasks that need to feel instant even as more memory gets used. And the third was to ensure that key apps and Windows require less memory. Yes, a computer with 16GB, 32GB, or 64GB of RAM can better handle more intensive activities. But Microsoft wanted to make sure that systems with 8GB could also keep pace.

Based on its own lab tests of PCs with 8GB of RAM, the company claims that Windows is now 20% more responsive and that multitasking is 40% faster than before the latest updates. Here’s how.

As more memory gets allocated, Windows must move inactive apps and files from RAM to the hard drive. When you need to access those apps and files again, you have to wait for Windows to move them from disk storage back to RAM. Normally, PCs with less memory have to do a lot of this disk swapping.

One way Windows eases the pain of this process is through compression. Here, the operating system shrinks less-active data into a smaller format so it can remain in memory. Though Windows has used compression for many years, Microsoft has fine-tuned the technology to determine how much to compress, when to move data from RAM to your drive, and when to fetch it back, especially on PCs with 8GB of memory.

Also: 5 apps I always install on new Windows PCs – most are free

As such, Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory rather than moving it to storage, Microsoft said. An inactive app, file, or browser that you leave open is less likely to have to reload from your hard drive when you return to it.

Opening the Start menu, launching File Explorer, right-clicking a folder or file, and searching for an item are all tasks that need to feel instant; otherwise, Windows itself feels sluggish. To achieve this on PCs with less RAM, Windows tries to prioritize certain actions you need to accomplish while backing off background tasks like search indexing, Microsoft said.

Here’s one example. After you update your computer and reboot, Windows has some housekeeping to do. But any setup work that occurs shouldn’t affect how long it takes to open an app or file.

Also: How to upgrade your ‘incompatible’ Windows 10 PC to Windows 11 – for free

The latest version of Windows 11 speeds up these types of tasks and interactions by up to 20% compared with the January 2026 version, according to Microsoft.

However, multitasking places the greatest strain on a PC with only 8GB of RAM. To analyze this, Microsoft said it conducted two tests on the same PC with 8GB of memory. One test measured the current version of Windows 11, while the other gauged the January 2026 flavor. Here, the testers opened 20 tabs in Microsoft Edge, kicked off a 4K video, and launched large files in Word, PowerPoint, and Excel, one after another. The current version of Windows is up to 40% faster than its predecessor, the company said.

To reduce the need for RAM among Windows and certain key apps, Microsoft said that it has improved how memory is managed and when it’s used.

As one example, memory is allocated to Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook more efficiently, resulting in a 360 MB savings in RAM. This maneuver also extends to third-party apps such as WhatsApp, which has reduced its memory requirements.

Also: 11 Windows apps I replace on every new PC (and the ones I keep)

On PCs with 8GB of memory, the Widgets app loads only when you open it and frees up about 200 MB of RAM when you close it. In Microsoft Edge, inactive tabs now go to sleep after 15 minutes, down from two hours previously, reducing overall memory allocation.

Across Windows, Microsoft 365, and Edge, those improvements reduced the growth in required memory by up to 900 MB, Microsoft said.

How does Microsoft test these scenarios to see whether the latest Windows updates and fixes are helping PCs with less memory?

“We test those fixes across a broader collection of over 20,000 PCs in our labs, including current 8 GB models, using automated workloads based on activities such as browsing, working in Microsoft 365 apps, joining video calls, and downloading files in the background and even using high-speed cameras to measure the time from an action, such as opening Start or launching an app, to the moment the result appears on screen,” the company explained.

Also: Why your RAM options cost 4X more now than last year

The ability to use Windows without much RAM on your PC is critical these days in light of the “RAMageddon” crisis. With AI companies scooping up massive amounts of memory and flash storage chips, remaining supply is limited, and the prices have surged. The more memory you add to a new or existing PC, the more you’re going to pay. That’s always been true, but now more than ever.

Of course, memory is only one part of the picture. Your PC’s processor and other hardware also play an important role. Here, Microsoft found that a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8GB of RAM showed 94% faster multi-core CPU performance than a 2021 8 GB model. But the same 2026 8GB PC performed on par with a 2021 16 GB system. This shows that memory does matter for multitasking, but that the processor also impacts performance.

Whether your Windows 11 PC has 8GB of RAM, less, or more, how can you take advantage of the latest enhancements? For that, you’ll want to make sure that you’ve updated to the newest version of Windows. That would be Windows 11 26H2, build 26300.9818 or later, according to Microsoft. But that includes the latest optional preview build released in late October. If you don’t want to install that one, you’ll be fine with build 26300.9711 for now.

Also: The best laptops: Expert tested and reviewed

To check, head to Settings, select System, and then click About. The section for Windows Info shows the current version and build. If you need to update, stay in Settings and go to Windows Update. Assuming your PC qualifies, you should find the latest Windows 11 26H2 build ready to install.

Beyond updating Windows, you also want to keep your apps current. If you use Microsoft 365, open any app in the suite, click the File menu, select Account, click Update Options, then select Update Now.

With most other apps, you have to update them manually or individually. To ease the process, consider a good software updater program. These will automatically scan most of your installed applications to identify which need updating, then download and install the updates for you.

#3236. The Swift Observatory Dropped Back to Earth This Week. Here’s What to Know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

NASA believes most of the space telescope burned up in the atmosphere, but some fragments may have made their way down to Earth.

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, formerly known as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer, has reached the end of its journey. Launched into orbit in 2004, the space telescope completed an extraordinary 22-year mission when it plunged back into Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday.

“Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long,” Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA, said in a statement last month.

NASA says the telescope hit the atmosphere Wednesday at 7:39 am ET, just four hours after the space agency predicted.

The space telescope entered orbit over the North Sumatra region of Indonesia, just west of Malaysia. NASA says that most of the space telescope likely burned up upon reentry but that some components may have survived.

In preparation for Swift’s reentry, NASA shut down operations in late October after conducting its final observation on Oct. 20. It was orbiting at just 171 miles above Earth’s surface at that point, and the increased atmospheric drag prevented Swift from doing any further work.

It was a bittersweet moment for those who worked on the project.

“It is a sad time at the Penn State Mission Operations Center, as we have carefully tended Swift to control its science operations, its health and safety, and responded to anomalies day or night, every day for 22 years,” John Nousek, director of mission operations for Swift and professor of astronomy and astrophysics at Penn State, said in an email to CNET.

Swift’s initial mission helped advance science’s understanding of gamma-ray bursts and their role in phenomena such as the birth of black holes and the history of the early universe.

That initial mission ended in 2004, but the observatory was doing so well that NASA extended its operations to continue collecting data. Its name changed to the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory in 2018, in honor of pioneering NASA astrophysicist Neil Gehrels, who served as the agency’s chief of the Astroparticle Physics Laboratory from 1995 until his death in 2017.

The space telescope was designed to help solve the mystery of gamma-ray bursts by rapidly detecting them, determining their sources and then further analyzing them for study back on Earth. It also enabled unique sampling to observe newly discovered objects only minutes after their light reached Earth, Nousek said.

The volume of science research conducted using Swift’s data is difficult to match. According to NASA, Swift scanned over 2,000 gamma-ray bursts, took 1.5 million images from its ultraviolet/optical telescope and sent home 12 TB of data. That data is showcased in an estimated 7,000 research papers, which averages out to just under one study per day over its 22-year run.

“We hope Swift has set the standard for time domain astrophysics,” Nousek said.

The space telescope also helped pioneer many policies that ultimately shaped those discoveries, such as making data immediately accessible and providing over 1,000 guest investigators with the opportunity to use Swift throughout its long life.

It’s only a stroke of bad luck that kept the observatory from floating for even longer. NASA attempted a rescue of Swift over the summer of 2026. However, after a series of engineering difficulties and control issues, the attempt was abandoned, sealing Swift’s fate. NASA turned the instruments back on and kept recording data as long as possible.
