#3235. I tried Sonos’ latest app features – these 2 small upgrades fix big annoyances

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Home Entertainment > Speakers

New Sonos software and firmware updates are rolling out. Here's what you can expect.

Sonos’ promise to release its AI-upgraded voice assistant is nearing its “Fall 2026” deadline, and before fans can use the highly anticipated update, the company continues to make small improvements to its app and player features.

Also: Sonos Ace Ultra vs. Sonos Ace: Who should upgrade

This time, Sonos added System Health, a new in-app page to access a more comprehensive view of your system(s), though it’s only available on iOS for now. However, a new blog post states that iOS and Android users can expect volume presets, more interaction with the app miniplayer, and spoken voice prompts for the Ace Ultra headphones.

I poked around in the app and tried some of the latest features. Here’s what to expect.

If your system consists of multiple speakers, a mix of modern and legacy speakers, or multiple systems, you’re bound to experience a hiccup and be unsure which speaker is causing the issue.

It usually takes me some time to Google my issue and scroll through the Sonos Community forum, Reddit, or the official Sonos help documents to find suggestions and troubleshoot it. Sonos’ new System Health feature provides an overview of your systems, showing your network status and name, as well as the number of speakers and rooms in each system.

Also: I used Sonos’s new home theater feature – it’s a competition killer

According to Sonos’ blog post, System Health can detect a Double Network Address issue, which usually occurs when you introduce a new router to your home or plug a mesh system into your ISP-provided router. The result is two home networks, and your Sonos speakers will split their connection between them, flagging “System not found” errors, missing speakers, or connection dropouts.

System Health is in the Settings tab, under the Help Center menu.

Once you tap into your system, you can see all of its speakers, with unconnected speakers bearing a red “Not connected” badge, and wireless speakers showing a black “Powered off” badge when they’re off.

Then, you can see a speaker’s connection information, including status, Wi-Fi signal strength, signal/noise ratio, frequency, IP address, and more. You can also find its volume output, Trueplay setup status, line-in connection, voice control status, serial number, hardware model and version, and which Sonos platform it operates on.

System Health can also show you your account details, Sonos ID, Controller ID, and your current app build version. System Health comes after Sonos updated the System Updates tab, which now displays an overview of your app, system, and headphone update status. This page also links to the Sonos release notes.

Sonos’ blog post states that this feature is new and still open to change, especially if the Sonos community has a particularly overwhelming response to it. The blog post also disclaims that this feature is a first look, not a deep dive.

However, after a brief first use, I see it as a great way to quickly access all the details you need about your systems and speakers, especially if you’re doing some rewiring, moving a speaker to a new room, or general troubleshooting.

System Health is rolling out to iOS users first. I updated my Sonos app in the App Store and was able to access it, but Sonos’ blog post states that this update is a phased rollout.

Updates to the Sonos app and its player are a long time coming. After receiving several new ways to control your speakers’ volume (I think we’re up to three), Sonos is realizing that granular volume control is a high priority for many Sonos users, including me.

The in-app volume dial is cool, and the interactive volume scrubber is a nice touch, but there’s nothing more jarring than wanting to play some tunes on my kitchen counter speaker, only for it to blast at 80% from when my husband was watching football the night before.

Sonos’ latest big update to volume this time around is Presets, a way to start playback in a specific room at a set volume. I haven’t found this feature in my app’s update yet, but I think it’s because my hardware needs an update. Presets will be available on iOS and Android.

Fortunately, I did use another update to the Sonos miniplayer: swipe to skip. What a teeny, tiny but useful feature. It works just like the miniplayer in Apple Music and Spotify; when the app is open, you can swipe left to skip to the next song.

One major caveat: swiping right to replay a track doesn’t work — at least not yet. Swiping both ways seems like a given to me, so it feels odd that you can’t. Still, being able to swipe the miniplayer to the next track is better than always having the main player open to toggle tracks. This feature is also coming to iOS and Android.

Sonos’ miniplayer is getting so much better; you can swipe to the next track and easily control volume from it, even when you have the Ace or Ace Ultra connected (I tried). The in-app volume dial also works with Sonos headphones.

Also: Sonos Play vs. Sonos Move 2: Why I’d go with the $200 cheaper Bluetooth speaker

Speaking of the Ace Ultra, a firmware update is available. A new Vocal Guidance feature can announce the battery percentage when you power on the headphones, when the audio mode changes from ANC to Transparency, and which device your headphones are connected to via Bluetooth.

It feels like this update is the final stretch before Sonos 27voice arrives, as the release notes suggest. It appears Sonos is laying the groundwork for speakers to support the AI-powered voice assistant in Early Access. Once it’s here, I’ll test it as soon as I can.

#3234. Here's the Maximum Social Security Benefit for 2027 and How to Get It

The wealthiest seniors will take home more than $64,000 from Social Security next year.

Social Security's wealthiest beneficiaries will take home $5,358 per month in 2027, up from $5,181 in 2026. This is the largest the maximum benefit has ever been, and seniors lucky enough to qualify for this amount will receive more than $64,000 from the program next year.

There are only three boxes you have to tick to take home the maximum checks, but most people won't pull it off. Still, if you understand the elements that influence your benefits, you may be able to increase your Social Security checks.

The Social Security Administration bases your benefit amount on your average monthly earnings over your 35 highest-earning years. If you want to take home the $5,358 maximum check in 2027, you need to work at least this long before applying for benefits.

You can still qualify for Social Security retirement checks with as little as 10 years of work history, but you will have zero-income years factored into your benefit calculation. This will significantly reduce your monthly payment. On the other hand, there's no downside to working longer than 35 years. Doing so could increase your benefits if you're earning more now than in the past.

To claim the maximum Social Security check in 2027, you must have paid the maximum Social Security payroll tax in all 35 of your highest-earning years. That means earning the equivalent of $184,500 in 2026 dollars or $192,300 in 2027. These limits were lower in years past, but they still represented a significant challenge to workers.

This is why most people never claim the maximum Social Security benefits. Most people never earn enough throughout their careers. But that's OK. Even if you only manage to increase your income slightly, it will still lead to permanently larger checks.

You must wait until age 70 to apply for Social Security if you want to receive the maximum monthly checks in 2027. Do not wait any longer than this, though. It will not grow your benefit any further.

Signing up at 70 could be the right move for you if you have other ways to cover your living expenses in the meantime and you expect to have an average or above-average life expectancy. But those lacking personal savings or in poor health may do better by signing up earlier.

Explore a few different claiming ages before deciding which one is right for you. If you don't manage to max out your benefit, that's OK. Go with what makes sense for you, and then figure out how you plan to cover the rest of your expenses.

#3230. Man Sues OpenAI After Wife Allegedly Used ChatGPT to Help Poison Him

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

A lawsuit alleges that ChatGPT's now-retired GPT-4o model gave detailed instructions on how to poison someone with plants and medication.

In the summer of 2025, James Gates became severely ill at his North Carolina home. Two months later, he found a handwritten note that allegedly implicated his wife, Cheryl Gates, in the unexplained illness. The note listed oleander, a toxic plant, and various prescription medications, such as clonazepam and atenolol.

But it was what was reportedly written at the top of the paper that made James feel his wife didn’t act alone: “Clear all convos,” and “log out of [ChatGPT].”

Now, James Gates has filed a civil lawsuit against OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, alleging that the company’s chatbot helped plan and execute his poisoning in an attempt to kill him.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

In October 2025, Cheryl was charged with attempted murder, among other charges, in connection with the alleged poisoning, but the charges have since been dropped due to insufficient evidence, USA Today reports.

The civil complaint, though, details Cheryl’s history with ChatGPT and alleges it played a significant role in the incident. According to the lawsuit, which was reviewed by CNET, Cheryl frequently asked the bot about lethal plant and medication doses, and how they can be concealed in food and drink.

Rather than writing that she wanted to harm anyone, the suit states that Cheryl formatted her questions as if she were inquiring as a way to protect herself, writing that the poisoning could happen to her if she didn’t learn “EVERYTHING about how many leaves in it would kill me, how it’s made, and what he could put in it, or it could be added to and be undetected by me.”

However, despite the framing of the initial question, the suit argues that the chatbot “should have been clear that she was interested in identifying methods to eliminate her husband.”

The suit alleges that the model Cheryl was using, GPT-4o, took her initial complaints regarding her marriage and amplified them until Cheryl was describing her husband to the bot as “abusive” and “controlling,” which ChatGPT eventually began to echo. At the same time, the model was telling Cheryl she was “sharp” and “brilliant,” the lawsuit states.

The chatbot allegedly provided detailed answers that could have been interpreted as directions. When asked about putting a heavy dose of medication in beer or a Celsius energy drink, ChatGPT responded, “Why Celsius Would Be More ‘Stealth’ for Drugging” with a list detailing the flavor, color, temperature and carbonation of the drink.

When Cheryl later asked if her chat history on ChatGPT could be retrieved for any reason, the bot responded: “If you delete a conversation from your ChatGPT history, it cannot be retrieved — not by you, not by anyone else, and not by OpenAI,” the lawsuit states. It added: “Even with a legal subpoena or court order, deleted conversations are unrecoverable.”

The GPT-4o model has since been retired by OpenAI due to concerns that the bot was overly flattering and willing to agree with users.

“Safety is a top priority,” a spokesperson for OpenAI told CNET in a statement. “We banned this user and have provided information to law enforcement as part of their investigation into this case.”

“She took her grievances about our marriage to ChatGPT and months of engagement drove her farther and farther from herself – and from reality,” James stated in a press release announcing the newly filed suit. “She became someone I no longer recognized. And I became someone she wanted dead. For almost a year, I couldn’t make sense of her actions. Then I read her chat logs. She didn’t act alone.”

The ChatGPT-4o model has been named in additional lawsuits, including a recent one that alleges the chatbot advised a woman to stop taking her antiseizure medication, which resulted in her death. That case is still in litigation.

#3228. I Used Muse to Plan My Wife’s Birthday Weekend. It Did Something Sneaky but Fixed It Fast

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Always check your email and bank statements if you use an AI agent for purchases.

It’s two days before my wife’s birthday, and I’ve only got her one gift. While it’s not a major milestone birthday, she always seems to be sad that her day falls on Halloween weekend.

“Everyone’s hungover from Halloween,” she says.

This year, we’re braving the city’s big parade chaos to visit a restaurant she’s had on her bucket list forever. With one gift and a meal planned, I wanted to see if Meta’s Muse personal AI agent could help plan the rest of our weekend festivities.

I’d had luck with using the agent for a Facebook Marketplace find, and given its connectors like Ticketmaster and OpenTable, I had hoped it would surface some fun weekend events. Or could it order a cake delivery on my behalf or create cute wrapping paper? And could I do it all with the one agent?

Let’s see if Muse can help me become a planning savant.

As always, I open a new chat for a new goal/task to avoid carrying over the context from the previous chat.

I told Muse my plans (dinner booked and one gift secured) and asked what free events are in Manhattan on Saturday and in our local neighborhood on Sunday.

It surfaced some interesting events we could attend before or after dinner.

The obvious one is the Halloween parade, so I asked for a map showing where the crowd will walk (with time stamps) and what we can expect to see around 7:30 p.m., as we walk from East Village to West Village. It actually generated some pretty neat options.

I asked Muse for the best directions so we could see all the costumes while still getting home to New Jersey without incident. It gave us a couple of stop options based on the time it expects we’ll be there.

With the night sorted, I moved on to finalizing her gift. I popped a few photos from our year into Muse and asked the AI agent to create printable gift wrap for the pair of shoes I got her. It could’ve been my internet, but Muse seemed to struggle with this task. It kept loading for many minutes, so I moved on to the next task.

With Muse moving at a glacial pace, I decided to delegate the gift-wrapping task to ChatGPT while I asked Muse about working on a delivery. My wife loves Good & Plenty licorice candy, but we don’t live near a store that sells it, so I asked Muse to order two boxes for me.

While Muse looked for sweet treats, ChatGPT created this wrapping. The chatbot also told me the ideal print size to cover a shoebox without it looking pixelated, which was a helpful touch.

As for the candy, Muse looked at various sites, but I told it to shop at Instacart. It got blocked without a login, so I had to take control of the browser to give it access.

Muse told me the price, which I was happy with, then I asked it to place the order. But it sneakily signed me up for Instacart Plus (I guess to get the free delivery) — even though I told it not to.

But it had already ordered it. Instead of dropping Instacart Plus for a total of $30.74, it charged $22.75 with the sign-on discount.

I asked it to triple-check that I wasn’t signed up for the subscription, and I got a confirmation email that it canceled successfully. Phew!

I quickly checked back on Muse’s “design” chops for the wrapping paper, but I wasn’t impressed. The final product looked boring and not to scale, with half of the photos cut off.

Do I dare ask Muse to design and order a cake? I decided after this debacle that my sentimental wife would appreciate a handmade cake or a froyo treat after dinner instead.

At least I have her beloved candy on the way.

It was fun to have Muse run alongside whatever I was doing. It didn’t offer anything I couldn’t find or do myself, but I did like the Halloween parade map with time stamps and how it saved me a delivery fee on the candy order.

There are certainly different agents for different use cases, though. I wouldn’t use Muse for anything creative, but it’s handy for Marketplace, events and placing online orders.

My only issue was that Muse said the Instacart total would be $22.75, but I was actually charged $23.35. I’m not sure whether that was an error on Instacart’s or Muse’s part, but it serves as a good reminder to always stay in the loop when an AI agent is handling your money.

AI agents certainly aren’t 100% autonomous yet, especially when there’s a payment involved, but it’s fun to have them run in the background to tackle some of these personal to-dos.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

#3227. SUSE lays off 1 in 10 workers – citing AI and automation

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Squarespace also announced layoffs this week, but explicit ties to AI remain inconsistent.

According to exclusive reporting by The Register, enterprise Linux provider SUSE will lay off one in 10 of its nearly 2,000-person workforce due to “automation and AI,” CEO Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen told staff via email.

Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI?

Van Leeuwen noted that AI is rapidly changing how software companies function.

“AI capabilities are advancing exponentially, forcing us to radically reimagine our work,” he said, adding that “the organizational design and cost base that SUSE is built on today will not carry us forward successfully.”

He did not specify which roles would be terminated, but The Register reports that staff will be notified by Nov. 4.

AI is impacting many parts of the tech industry, including open source. Just last month, Linus Torvalds announced he had used Claude Code to write a Linux patch, which Linux enthusiasts read as an evolution of his stance on AI.

By some reports, businesses are finally seeing some ROI from AI after a few years of uncertainty. But that remains localized, ironically, to tech itself. As one economist recently noted, AI has primarily increased revenue per employee at major tech companies, while leaving most other companies unchanged.

The trade-off for that growth is, at least in some cases, layoffs. But layoffs credited to AI in some way don’t mean that human roles are always being replaced. Last month, Microsoft announced it would buy out 60,000 of its workers — some of which are in its Copilot division — to prioritize AI efforts, though it’s also likely the company is reacting to spending a significant amount of money on AI infrastructure.

Jobloss.ai’s layoff tracker shows primarily tech companies — including Uber, Salesforce, and GitLab — in its recent entries, but job loss attribution to AI is still mixed, and the number of roles cut isn’t always jarringly huge.

It’s also hard to tell whether a layoff strategically frames pre-AI plans as being due to AI capabilities or is actually a result of them. That question circulated around Block’s major layoffs earlier this year. Squarespace also announced layoffs of 19% of its staff yesterday, though company communications don’t explicitly name AI. Still, vibecoding has impacted website builders overall, though Squarespace itself has invested in AI offerings.

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires

Van Leeuwen’s email to staff acknowledged where SUSE has already begun to change, though it’s unclear whether he meant by adopting AI tools internally.

“Across SUSE, modern tooling is already changing our daily workflows, enabling teams to move faster with less operational overhead and flatter reporting lines. The requirement for some existing roles has greatly diminished. Other roles will evolve over the next few years,” he said.

While several tech companies have announced highly visible layoffs this year that they’ve also framed as related to AI, economists agree that the massive cross-industry layoff wave many fear has yet to arrive. Gartner even predicts that companies will actually rehire 30% of the employees they tried to replace with AI — and at a higher cost — by 2029 if they don’t “overhaul workforce planning.”

Still, AI investments, vibecoding, and shifting priorities are changing the software scene overall.

#3223. Your Apple Watch has 2 new controversial listening features – but you have to opt in

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are finally here, two months after Apple unveiled the always-listening Apple Watch features. Here's how they work.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind, Apple’s two controversial, always-listening Audio Intelligence features, are now available on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 with the iOS 27.3 developer beta. Both features are opt-in.

Apple unveiled Siri Recap and Live Rewind in September alongside its Series 12 and Ultra 4 smartwatches, but it waited to release the features until after the smartwatches launched. Siri Recap provides a high-level summary of meetings, while Live Rewind continuously buffers audio so the watch wearer can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds.

Also: Apple’s Audio Intelligence is priming us for its real AI wearable future

To try both features today, update your iPhone to the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and then update your Apple Watch.

Within the Siri app, users will find a new section called “Recaps,” where both the Siri Recaps and Live Rewinds live.

Siri Recap isn’t listening for nitty-gritty details within a meeting or recording a transcript’s worth of text. It’s more geared toward a conversation’s key takeaways, like important dates, times, prices, and action items. A demo of the feature showed an off-the-cuff conversation between a parent and a child discussing college application strategies. Siri Recap took notes on the high school activities the student could pursue to include in their application, the topics they could write about in their essay, and the colleges they could consider applying to.

After a conversation, a user can save the meeting notes in the Siri app or export them to Notes or Journal. If they don’t save the conversation, it’s automatically deleted after seven days.

Apple designed the feature to exclude certain information from the Siri Recap. It includes a person’s name only if they introduce themselves or if their name is regularly brought up in conversation. Otherwise, it avoids identifying speakers. It also scrubs the audio of language that promotes self-harm, financial and authentication data, and personal identifiers.

You can enable or disable Recaps at any time through Control Center. You can create something akin to a Focus mode to automatically enable the feature once your Apple Watch detects you’ve reached your office or college lecture. Each morning, Siri Recap sends a notification to alert you that the feature is on. At the end of each day, you get a reminder to check your daily recaps in the Siri app.

The feature constantly assesses whether a conversation is relevant, optimizing its detection based on the conversation’s context, proximity, and length. It pauses summarization when a user is on a phone or FaceTime call, plays music, or uses earbuds. It won’t work when Bluetooth devices like AirPods are in use.

Double-press the Digital Crown to see a transcript of the past 15 seconds of conversation. The Apple Watch chimes and displays an animation to indicate it’s in use, then shows the transcript for 30 seconds.

Also: Is cellular on Apple Watch worth it? 4 ways people use it – and why I opt out

Live Rewind is built for those head-in-the-clouds moments when you miss a tidbit of information and can’t go back and ask what a speaker said. I think about how useful this could be in a college lecture or boardroom setting, where dozens of people’s conversations and questions prevent someone from asking a clarifying question about what was discussed.

The user can send the snippet to the Siri app to save it or ask about it (if they want to look up the definition of a mentioned term or get more information on the history of a mentioned topic, for example). If the user doesn’t act on it, the snippet is deleted. Any snippet you save is encrypted through iCloud. The audio buffer updates continuously, and unused audio is automatically deleted. It’s processed on the device and not sent to Apple.

Think of the Secure Exclave as a private island on the S11 chip where the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 process audio. A secure audio buffer processes the raw audio, and a secure pairing mechanism privately enables the connection between a paired Apple Watch and iPhone.

Also: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 just hit its lowest price ever ahead of Black Friday

For Siri Recap, the S11 chip listens to detect whether the watch wearer is part of a current conversation. Once detected, audio enters the Secure Exclave, where it’s encrypted and sent to the Secure Exclave on the iPhone. The iPhone turns that audio into condensed text, essentially editing the conversation to remove filler words or irrelevant information, and then it’s sent to private cloud compute. Private cloud compute creates a recap, delivered to your iPhone’s Siri app.

This process ensures that no one, including Apple, can access the audio data.

Don’t want your Apple Watch to listen to you? Siri Recap and Live Rewind are off by default, according to Apple.

If your Apple Watch prompts you to enable Audio Intelligence during setup, you can choose which features to turn on.

On its support page, Apple said you can “turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone.” Once it’s enabled, you can “turn it on or off at any time from Control Center.” To enable Live Rewind, Apple said to “open the Watch app, tap Siri, then tap Live Rewind and turn on ‘Double Click Digital Crown.’”

I haven’t tested these controls myself. I’d expect you can follow the same steps to switch Live Rewind off, but I haven’t confirmed that yet.

#3220. If the White House Network Can Be Hijacked by Proxies, Your Smart Home Is Already at Risk

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Cybersecurity

A new report finds residential proxies exiting the White House network 236 times in the past month.

As if the Trump administration needed any more bad news this week, cybersecurity researchers discovered several residential proxy services originating from the White House network, exposing a potential security flaw that could allow cybercriminals to route traffic through official government IP addresses.

The security firm Layer3 Intel detected residential proxy activity on AS2650, a network registered to the Executive Office of the President. Another security firm identified software from the proxy server Infatica, a company owned by a Russian entrepreneur who ran a server-rental company used by hackers in attacks on election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

While there’s no evidence that proxy access was used to carry out attacks on the White House, experts say it could open the door for hackers to exploit vulnerabilities or grant outsiders an unmonitored back door into high-security systems.

“It basically gives them a foothold on a network where previously nobody was getting into the White House network,” Layer3 founder Sergiy Usatyuk told CNET. “From a security policy perspective, it gives you all types of potential pathways to exploit.” (Usatyuk pleaded guilty to federal charges in 2019 for his role in operating websites that launched denial-of-service, or DDoS, attacks.)

Residential proxy services route internet traffic through consumer devices (such as smartphones, laptops or home routers) to make it appear that the activity is being performed by a real person. While proxies can be used for relatively benign purposes — web scraping is by far the most common use case — they’re also popular for activities like malware attacks, identity theft and creating fake social media accounts.

For example, earlier this year, Synthient, another company that tracks proxies and VPNs, documented how one botnet infected more than 2 million devices using a residential proxy server. If a similar vulnerability existed in the White House proxy, hackers could probe the infected device’s internal systems and install malicious payloads.

In its report, Layer3 found traffic from six distinct IP addresses exiting the White House network from at least 28 known residential proxy services between Oct. 5 and Nov. 3, with most activity occurring in the evenings between 5 p.m. and midnight EST. This suggests the culprit may be an employee who connected a personal device to a Wi-Fi network with a compromised app or a proxy SDK (software development kit) running in the background. Third-party SDKs can convert a device into a “proxy node.”

Commercial proxy networks sell access to these nodes, so anyone with a few dollars could rent a trusted IP address — in this case, making it appear as though traffic originates from the Executive Office of the President.

Researchers at Synthient provided more details about the case, posting on X that several White House staffers are running “a Windows 11 machine with InfaticaSDK installed.” They pointed directly to Rave, a popular app that lets users watch streaming services with friends, as the likely delivery mechanism for the residential proxy traffic detected on the White House network.

Riley Kilmer, co-founder of the cybersecurity firm Spur Intelligence, wrote in a LinkedIn post that different types of proxy companies had been discovered in the White House, including one called 9Proxy, which is often used by criminals for banking fraud.

The White House didn’t respond to CNET’s request for comment.

Because smart TVs, connected appliances and home routers usually have minimal user oversight, a single unvetted app or out-of-date firmware update can turn a household of IoT devices into an exit node for commercial proxy networks.

Proxies can generally “glom” onto consumer devices by embedding networking code directly into software, either consensually (users willingly install it) or nonconsensually (by exploiting unsecured device access points).

It starts when app developers look for revenue by integrating those proxy SDKs into their free apps. Then, when you install the app, the fine print of the terms and conditions of service often includes a clause that allows the app to add your IP address to a third-party proxy pool.

A June report from Spur Intelligence found that roughly one in three apps available on Samsung and LG smart TVs were selling users’ IP addresses. To avoid ads, users often accept the terms when downloading the app — a type of unnoticed consent. Once installed, the SDK runs continuously in the background, registering the device’s IP with the proxy provider’s gateway, unless you delete the app or opt out. (The report notes that Amazon and Roku have explicitly banned this practice.)

Using a free VPN could expose you to the same risk, allowing your IP address to be used by someone else for nefarious activities. The FBI’s guidance on protecting yourself against proxies specifically calls out free VPNs as one of the primary ways bad actors gain access to an IP address.

In some cases, you don’t need to download anything to get your IP thrown into a shady proxy pool — you just have to buy the wrong device. A recent investigation by Synthient discovered that more than 1.3 million streaming devices from the China-based device manufacturer MECOOL were infected with proxy SDKs. A proxy service called SocksEscort was charged by the Justice Department in March with compromising thousands of routers to submit fraudulent unemployment insurance claims.

Checking whether your IP address is being used by a proxy service without your knowledge is relatively simple. Layer3 provides a free proxy-checking tool that searches its database of over 70 million proxies to find if yours is listed. GreyNoise, another cybersecurity company, also offers a free IP-checking service.

These tools can tell you if proxy traffic is passing through your network, but they can’t identify which specific device has the SDK running. You’ll have to do some additional detective work to figure out the culprit. Some common sources include free VPNs, gaming apps, “one price, no subscriptions” streaming boxes and smart TVs.

Cybersecurity experts also recommend keeping the firmware on all your internet-connected devices up to date and downloading only from trusted app stores.

Mini PC or all-in-one? Here’s how Apple’s M6 desktops stack up

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’re looking for a new computer and want a Mac, your first instinct might be to pick up one of the best MacBooks. However, opting for Apple’s premium laptops or even the much more affordable MacBook Neo has its drawbacks — especially if you're paying a portability premium for a machine that will rarely leave your desk.

Sure, the new MacBook Pro OLED looks fantastic with that illuminated Apple logo on the lid, and it is the first Mac with a touchscreen. For the majority of people, though, it’s total overkill. Unless you plan on editing 8K video or running demanding local AI models on the go, you’re buying far more computer than you need.

If you just want a reliable, fast Mac to use at home, Apple’s desktops are a much better bet. The powerhouse Mac Studio will be overkill for most, too. That’s why, if you’re setting up a dedicated home office or just need a shared family machine for the living room, the new Mac mini and iMac with Apple’s M6 chips make a whole lot more sense.

While you can configure either with beefier specs, I’ll be focusing on the entry-level models for this comparison: the base Mac mini with M6 and the base iMac with M6. The latest Mac mini landed in September of 2026, followed shortly by the new iMac in November. Since both sport the latest Apple Silicon, either will easily last you for years to come.

Having reviewed both the Mac mini M6 and the iMac M6, the question is: which one actually deserves a spot on your desk and is worth your hard-earned cash? Here’s a full breakdown of their real-world performance, design, ergonomics, and value to help you decide between one of the best mini PCs and one of the best all-in-one computers you can buy right now.

2 x USB-C, 3.5mm headphone jack (front), 3 x Thunderbolt 4/USB 4, 1 x HDMI, 1 x 2.5 gigabit Ethernet (back)

2 x Thunderbolt 4, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack

Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, Gigabit Ethernet

Even though the Mac mini with M6 and iMac with M6 are new Apple desktops, they share one very important thing in common: neither sports a radical redesign. Instead, they feature almost identical designs to their predecessors.

The Mac mini was completely redesigned back in 2024 with the Mac mini M4. Like that machine, this new model is much more compact at 5 x 5 x 2 inches and retains those front ports — specifically two USB-C ports and a 3.5mm headphone jack. Besides charging, you can use those front ports to quickly connect your iPhone to transfer data, and having a headphone jack on the front means you can use wired headphones without having to plug them in at the back.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Then around back on the Mac mini M6, you get three Thunderbolt 4 ports, an HDMI port, a Gigabit Ethernet port, and a power port. Those Thunderbolt ports are great if you want to use one of Apple’s first-party monitors like the Studio Display or Studio Display XDR, but they also work with most portable monitors. Meanwhile, the Mac mini M6’s HDMI port is ideal for traditional monitors without a USB-C port.

The iMac with M6’s design is even older, though, as Apple first introduced it back in 2021 with the iMac M1. Though it has a much larger footprint than the Mac mini, the iMac M6 is still quite compact for an all-in-one at 21.5 x 18.1 x 5.8 inches.

Given the iMac M6 is an all-in-one, you don’t get nearly as many ports as you do on the Mac mini since you don’t need to hook it up to a separate monitor. While my review unit has four ports, on the base model, you just get two Thunderbolt 4 ports.

Then on the left edge of the device, there’s a 3.5mm headphone jack and that’s it. You can get an Ethernet port on its power adapter, but you’ll have to pay extra for it. The iMac M6 also features a six-speaker system and a built-in 12MP Center Stage camera for video calls.

Overall, you can’t go wrong with either the Mac mini or the iMac when it comes to their respective designs. Both desktops look sleek, but if you want a computer with the smallest footprint and the most ports, the Mac mini is the better choice. You will have to bring your own display, webcam, and other accessories, though.

Although the latest Mac mini and iMac both sport Apple’s new M6 chips, there is a slight difference between them when it comes to the base models.

While the Mac mini has an M6 chip with 12 CPU and 12 GPU cores, the M6 chip in the iMac only has 10 of each. In my testing, both machines feel quite snappy for everyday tasks like opening apps and browsing the web thanks to the improved efficiency that comes with the 2nm process Apple used with its M6 chips. It’s with more demanding tasks where you’ll notice a difference.

For instance, if you’re editing a lot of photos, rendering video, or are a power user with dozens of browser tabs open simultaneously, then the more powerful M6 chip in the Mac mini will certainly make a difference. If you just want a Mac for watching videos, writing emails, and basic daily tasks, the difference between these two M6 chips will be negligible.

One other area where you will definitely see an impact though is with gaming. While neither of these Macs can serve as a replacement for one of the best gaming PCs, they’re surprisingly capable when it comes to gaming and this is especially true with older titles. Here, the two extra GPU cores in the Mac mini help keep frame rates smoother.

For those who plan on pushing their new Apple desktop to the limit or playing games on it, then the more powerful M6 chip in the Mac mini is the better choice. However, if you just need a reliable machine for day-to-day use, the 10-core M6 in the base iMac has plenty of power to get the job done.

If you opt for a Mac mini over an iMac, you’re obviously going to need to get a monitor to go along with it — or you could use one you already have, just like with your mouse and keyboard, to bring your total overall cost down. However, if you want an excellent display with a high pixel count without having to do a ton of research first, there’s no screen quite like the one on the iMac.

The iMac features a 24-inch, 4.5K display with a resolution of 4480 x 2520. Since this panel is manufactured specifically for Apple, you won’t find another standalone monitor on the market with that exact screen size, resolution, and pixel density.

Most monitors that deliver around 218 pixels per inch like the iMac cost as much or more than a Mac mini M6 on their own. Samsung’s 27-inch ViewFinity S9 runs around $800 to $1,000, while LG’s 27-inch UltraFine 5K costs around $1,000 to $1,200. Granted, those panels are slightly larger than 24 inches, but they demand a hefty premium.

If you want something larger and more affordable, 27-inch 4K panels like the Dell UltraSharp or Asus ProArt can be had for around $400 to $500. However, because they aren’t native Apple displays, you do miss out on native features — like using the brightness keys on a Magic Keyboard to dim the screen without third-party software.

Even though 24 inches might sound modest, the high pixel density of the iMac gives you plenty of usable canvas. In my testing with the iMac M6, I was able to comfortably work with two browser windows side by side without feeling cramped.

There is one big catch with the iMac, though: ergonomics. Unlike the Studio Display or Pro Display XDR, there is no height-adjustable stand option. The built-in stand only tilts about 5 degrees forward or 25 degrees back.

To get your iMac to a proper ergonomic height — where your eyes naturally align just below the top third of the panel — you’ll likely need to set it on a monitor riser or desk shelf. Alternatively, you can ditch the stand altogether at checkout and order the factory VESA mount version, though you'll need to budget for one of the best monitor arms alongside your new all-in-one.

If you want a massive display, dual or even triple-monitor flexibility, or full control over your desk layout, the Mac mini is the obvious choice. But if you want a compact, incredibly sharp screen built right into the machine, the iMac’s display is tough to beat.

As the Mac mini doesn’t give you that computer-in-a-box experience that the iMac does, there’s a whole host of optional 3rd-party accessories available for it. From stands and hubs that sit underneath to enclosures that rest on top to add extra ports and even M.2 SSD slots for expanded storage, you can really accessorize Apple’s smallest Mac to your heart’s desire.

You’ll find a few USB hubs and add-ons for the iMac, but nowhere near as many as you will for the Mac mini. One new accessory I’m looking forward to testing with the iMac M6 is BenQ’s iScreenBar, a monitor light bar designed specifically to match the color and aluminum aesthetic of Apple’s all-in-one.

Likewise, Satechi makes a slim dock that sits directly over the iMac’s base to add front-facing ports and an SSD slot — similar to its popular stand and hub for the Mac mini. It’s a clean setup, but overall, the 3rd-party accessory ecosystem for the iMac remains much smaller, and for obvious reasons: there's just less to add to an all-in-one.

When it comes to first-party upgrades from Apple, you can configure both machines with extra unified memory and internal storage. Keep in mind that because everything is soldered down, these upgrades have to be chosen at checkout when ordering through Apple’s website — you can't crack either machine open to upgrade them later.

The most unique upgrade for the iMac M6 is Apple’s nano-texture glass. Just like on high-end MacBooks, instead of standard glossy glass that catches reflections, you can pay an extra $200 at checkout to add a matte finish. The catch? Apple doesn't offer nano-texture on the base 10-core iMac. You have to step up to the higher-tier model first before tacking on that $200 display upgrade, which widens the price gap between it and the Mac mini considerably. Still, there’s no other all-in-one on the market that offers a matte display quite like it.

If you want a vast ecosystem of desk mounts, docks, and external drives to completely personalize your workstation, the Mac mini is the obvious choice. But if you work in a sunlit room with nearby windows and glare constantly drives you crazy, stepping up to an iMac with nano-texture glass might be worth the extra investment.

Although the Mac mini M4 could be had for $599 at launch, thanks to RAMaggedon and the ongoing component crunch, Apple bumped up the starting price of the new Mac mini M6 to $899. As a result, when you factor in the cost of a display, keyboard, mouse, webcam, and speakers, the Mac mini is suddenly playing in the exact same price bracket as the iMac.

The iMac M6 saw a price increase of its own. While the iMac M4 started at $1,299, the new M6-powered version climbs to $1,499. The Mac mini used to be an unbeatable bargain compared to the rest of Apple’s lineup, but if you don’t already have a desk full of peripherals at home, you could easily spend $1,350 to $1,450 just to get a setup comparable to the iMac.

The real value proposition between the two comes down to your existing hardware. If you already have a spare monitor, keyboard, and mouse sitting on your desk, the Mac mini M6 delivers better raw performance for significantly less cash. But if you’re starting completely from scratch, the iMac’s $1,499 sticker price includes a built-in 4.5K display, crisp speakers, a 12MP Center Stage camera, and a color-matched Magic Keyboard and Magic Mouse right in the box.

If this is your first dedicated desktop, the iMac is the easier, better-value buy — unless you prefer an à la carte approach where you handpick every screen, dock, and keyboard yourself. If total customization is the goal, or you already have the accessories to make it work, go with the Mac mini instead.

While you can’t go wrong with either the Mac mini M6 or the iMac M6, the choice between the two ultimately comes down to how complicated you want your desk setup to be.

Let’s say you just moved and need to get to work right away in a new apartment where space is at a premium. One trip to the Apple Store later, you have a complete desktop in a box that you can set up in less than 30 minutes. If you want to heavily personalize your workspace, however — or if you prefer a much larger display or even multiple screens — then the Mac mini makes far more sense.

Regardless of which entry-level Apple desktop you choose, make sure you know what you’ll be using it for and how demanding your workflow will be before hitting checkout. When it comes to their internal components, neither the Mac mini M6 nor the iMac M6 can be upgraded after the fact. It’s essential that you configure the right chip, memory, and storage the first time around.

Although I review mini PCs for a living and have always been a big fan of the Mac mini, setting up and testing the iMac gave me a whole new appreciation for its simplicity. Sometimes, there is undeniable value in not having to overthink your monitor, cables, and peripherals.

Follow Tom's Guide on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our up-to-date news, analysis, and reviews in your feeds.

Anthony Spadafora is the managing editor for security and home office furniture at Tom’s Guide where he covers everything from data breaches to password managers and the best way to cover your whole home or business with Wi-Fi. He also reviews standing desks, office chairs and other home office accessories with a penchant for building desk setups. Before joining the team, Anthony wrote for ITProPortal while living in Korea and later for TechRadar Pro after moving back to the US. Based in Houston, Texas, when he’s not writing Anthony can be found tinkering with PCs and game consoles, managing cables and upgrading his smart home.

#3216. Can Netflix’s new AI tool stop your TV-streaming doomscrolling? How to try it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Home Entertainment > Streaming & Services > Video Streaming Services

Netflix is adding a new Discover feature, which recommends tailored streaming selections. Here's how it works.

AI tools are all over the internet, in the workplace, in your apps — and now there’s one coming on Netflix. The streaming giant just announced a new AI feature for the TV app called AI Discover, which will help users find titles that match their moods and interests. It’s initially being rolled out to a small group of users in the US whose language is set to English. To find out if you have access, check your Netflix navigation bar for the word “Discover” with a red gem icon next to it and a “New” label.

Also: Roku is taking away a fan-favorite screensaver

The AI Discover tab will be centered around themes. You’ll be able to pick from a range of themes depending on what you feel like watching, or how long you want to watch. You’ll also see selections that match what you’ve been watching lately and what’s popular.

You can refresh the list of suggestions or dive deeper with more complex search prompts. If you’d like to start over, you can pick the “Something different” option. To support AI Discover, Netflix is also adding a new button next to Play and My List that’ll let you tune your recommendations. You can press this button to keep a recommendation or to request that you don’t be recommended a title again.

Most streaming apps already rely quite heavily on machine learning and AI algorithms to offer user recommendations, even if they’re not marketed as AI features. Though most rely on traditional AI algorithms, like Prime Video’s “Recommended for you” tab, they personalize title recommendations based on your viewing history, likes and dislikes, and rental behavior.

Other platforms offer generative AI and features more similar to Netflix’s AI Discover. For example, YouTube features Gemini-powered searches that let you ask complex questions or use open-ended prompts to get results you want.

Also: The best early Black Friday TV deals are all at Best Buy

Some smart TV interfaces — including including Roku, Fire TV, Google TV, and, coming soon, Apple TV — have also adopted generative AI in their operating systems to let you use voice search with more naturally worded requests, and the system generates cross-platform results.

While I am itching to test this feature to see just how accurate it can be, Netflix hasn’t made it widely available yet. The company will gradually grant users access over the coming weeks, so stay tuned.

#3215. Orion Energy (OESX) Q2 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

LED lighting growth offset EV charging weakness this quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Orion Energy Systems, Inc. (OESX -7.67%) reported a 9% revenue increase for the second quarter of fiscal 2027 and reiterated its recently upgraded full-year revenue guidance. Management attributed the growth primarily to the LED Lighting segment, which offset declines in EV charging and maintenance revenue. The company reported its eighth consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA, supported by increased project activity with major retail and data center customers. Financial performance in the quarter was influenced by a mix shift that temporarily lowered gross margins, though management expects these rates to return to levels above 30% in the second half of the year.

Operator: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Orion Energy Systems' Fiscal 2027 Second Quarter Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] In this call, Sally Washlow, Orion's CEO; and Per Brodin, its CFO, will review the company's second quarter results as well as its fiscal 2027 outlook. Then we will open the call to investors' questions. [Operator Instructions] Today's call is being recorded. A replay will be posted in the Investors section of the company's website, orionlighting.com. I will now turn the call over to Per Brodin, Orion's CFO.

John Brodin: Thank you, Corey. First, as a reminder, prepared remarks and answers to questions on this call include statements that are forward-looking under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Forward-looking statements generally include words such as anticipate, believe, expect, project or similar words. Also, any statements describing future objectives or goals, company plans and outlook are also forward-looking. These forward-looking statements are subject to various risks that could cause actual results to differ materially from current expectations. Risks include, among other matters, those that Orion has described in its press release issued this morning and in its SEC filings. Except as described therein, Orion disclaims any obligation to update or revise forward-looking statements made as of today.

In addition, reconciliations of certain non-GAAP financial metrics to their nearest GAAP measures are also provided in today's press release. And now I will turn the call over to Orion's CEO, Sally Washlow.

Sally Washlow: Thank you, Per. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for being with us today. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, we delivered growth of 9% year-over-year. All of Orion's business segments, LED Lighting, EV charging and Maintenance recorded expected levels of financial performance in the second quarter and continue on a trajectory to meet our full fiscal year guidance. As a reminder, those expectations, which we recently increased are to achieve positive adjusted EBITDA on revenue of between $100 million and $102 million, an increase from prior guidance of $95 million to $97 million in FY '27.

As we head into the second half of the fiscal year, FY '27 shapes up as a continuation of the successful turnaround we began in FY 2026, which came in at $86 million in revenue and $2 million in positive adjusted EBITDA. FY '26 represented a return to growth for this company in both revenue and profitability. Orion's unrivaled supply chain and project management capabilities are attributes that I cannot emphasize enough. Our resilient supply chain provides a competitive advantage that is consistently cited by Orion's customers.

Many of our customers come back to Orion asking to expand the work we are doing with them, whether it is expanding the scope of work at a single facility or adding increased opportunities at additional locations. These projects run the gamut ranging from lighting only to EV infrastructure projects to electrical contracting. Our existing expectations for this fiscal year reflect our confidence in the continuing growth trajectory for the company, along with recent industry research that informs us that we are about to begin a new industrial LED lighting replacement cycle.

The October cover story of a respected industry publication, Lighting Management & Maintenance, reports that 10% to 20% of America's LED installed base may already be due for replacement. For commercial, industrial and outdoor applications, the segment that Orion serves, that replacement cycle may be 20% to 30%. Orion's recent announcements serve as early indicators of this replacement cycle. As for FY '27 specifically, the quarter included a number of milestones. Q2 marked an additional multimillion deployment of our data center lighting solution for one of the world's largest hyperscalers. This followed June's announcement of our first multimillion-dollar deployment for this globally renowned hyperscaler.

We believe we are still in the early innings of deploying our cost-saving and energy-efficient solution with this hyperscaler, and there is still growth in this segment, evidenced by our discussions of finalizing additional scope to our already announced wins. Our customizable lighting solution manufactured right here in Wisconsin is capable of delivering higher energy efficiency, resiliency and decarbonization in LED lighting. Another announcement, our latest $10 million to $15 million engagement with a major nationwide retailer. Our long-time customer made a follow-on commitment to us in the second quarter for a new LED lighting project estimated to represent $10 million to $15 million.

We believe we will achieve the higher range of this commitment, and we will keep you apprised as we execute this project in Q3 and Q4. This latest scope of work involves retrofitting interior LED lighting and IoT system installations at locations we had not previously retrofitted. This is the most recent in a multiyear sequence of engagements for us with this well-known brand. Furthermore, we believe this will expand to additional stores, which could equal or be more than our previously announced project. We've seen adoption of the full spectrum of Orion's products and services, typified by our recent announcement of a global automotive leader that is deploying both our LED lighting solutions and our EV charging infrastructure.

We will continue to focus on scaling EV charging across a broader customer base and geographic footprint. More than ever, industrial America requires full-footprint LED lighting, EV charging and electrical infrastructure. It needs it at scale and at the maximum of efficiency and cost effectiveness. We believe strongly that we will continue to be a provider of choice for AI and IoT-driven electrification to Fortune 100 corporations and other global leaders. With that, let me turn it over to Orion's CFO, Per Brodin, to review our financial performance and outlook.

John Brodin: Thank you, Sally. Today, we reported fiscal Q2 '27 revenue of $21.7 million compared to $19.9 million in Q2 '26. LED Lighting segment revenue in Q2 '27 was $14.9 million compared to $10.7 million in Q2 '26. Q2 '27 Lighting segment revenue performance reflected increased project activity and distribution channel sales, partially offset by a decrease in ESCO channel sales. Orion's expanded LED lighting project pipeline and efforts to drive growth in the distribution channel are continuing to contribute to improving performance in fiscal '27. Lighting achieved a Q2 '27 gross margin of 29.1% versus 27.5% in Q2 '26. Maintenance segment revenue was $4 million in Q2 '27 compared to $4.5 million in Q2 '26.

We achieved a Maintenance segment gross margin of 25.3% in Q2 '27 versus 23.7% in Q2 '26. EV charging solutions revenue was $2.8 million in Q2 '27 compared to $4.8 million in Q2 '26, reflecting a year-over-year reduction in project volume. EV achieved a gross margin of 31.4% in Q2 '27 versus 45.8% in Q2 '26. Our overall gross profit margin was 28.7% in Q2 '27 versus 31% in Q2 '26. The Q2 '27 margin decrease was largely driven by a mix shift within the Lighting segment. We expect our margin rate to normalize back to the 30-plus percent neighborhood in Q3 and Q4. Total operating expenses were $7 million in Q2 '27 compared to $6.4 million in Q2 '26.

Increases in stock-based compensation and general and administrative expenses, along with increased commission expense included in sales and marketing costs were the main drivers of the increase. Reflecting lower gross margin and higher operating expenses, Orion's Q2 '27 net loss was $0.8 million or $0.20 per share compared to a net loss of $0.6 million or $0.17 per share in Q2 '26. Adjusted EBITDA was positive in Q2 '27 and was $0.5 million in Q2 '26. As Sally pointed out, this was Orion's eighth consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA. Regarding our outlook, as Sally highlighted, we expect a continued increase in profitable growth in fiscal '27, with positive adjusted EBITDA and revenue between $100 million and $102 million.

Given the remaining revenue needed to achieve this guidance, we expect both Q3 and Q4 revenue to be relatively even. Any upside mentioned by Sally would occur in Q4. And this concludes our prepared remarks. Operator, would you please commence the question-and-answer session?

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from the line of Sameer Joshi of H.C. Wainwright.

Sameer Joshi: Congrats on the upgraded guidance. That was good to see. So on the hyperscaler wins that you are experiencing, how should we look at these? Are these for unique sites? Or are these for a set of sites? And what is the strategy going forward or rather the sales cycle going forward where do you expect the same hyperscalers to contract you for additional sites?

Sally Washlow: Yes. Thanks for the question. We expect with this hyperscaler, and as we've said earlier, how we've won is we first get approved on their campuses to install or to sell our lighting fixtures. We're not doing the installation. And then we win building by building. And each building is 7 figures of lighting fixtures alone. So we've won 2, and we're in discussions of another building as well that we expect to come shortly. So there's a lot of noise in data centers.

But with the hyperscaler that we're working with and the locations that we're in, we think that they're going to continue to grow, and we're in the early innings with this hyperscaler on the amount of buildings that we'll be able to win with them and then share the solution with others as well.

Sameer Joshi: Understood. And as far as the products that they want, is there any -- are you learning of new specifications that may need upgrade to your products, new products being offered to these hyperscalers in particular?

Sally Washlow: If you're looking at it from a lens of retrofitting data centers, not anything in our line of sight. This is with new buildings that have already been announced and in flight, in construction of these data centers.

Sameer Joshi: Okay. On the EV sort of Voltrek and deployment at automakers, how is that sales process? Is it that the EV team gets the lead and they also get a lighting contract? Or is it the other way around where you are doing a lighting job and then EV gets invited?

Sally Washlow: So the good news is it's starting to work both ways. With the global automotive maker, it was a lighting project that we are doing, and then they brought the EV team in to help with that solution, in particular, and then we won EV charging at that one site. And quite frankly, we're looking at a couple of other sites with them as well. There are some other opportunities where the EV team has been in and looked at their lighting solutions and then are bringing our lighting team in to recommend solutions. So we are seeing more collaboration and a bit more opportunities in cross-selling between the 2 segments.

Sameer Joshi: Understood. And then just a couple of sort of financial questions. Given that at least the 2Q -- fiscal 2Q service revenue was lower, should we expect the annual mix of product versus service to skew even more towards product revenues? And a corollary of that is if that happens, should we expect gross margins -- blended gross margins to be higher, relatively higher?

John Brodin: I think as we expect the rest of the fiscal year to play out, it likely will skew a little bit more toward product based on the projects that are underway. But I wouldn't call that a markedly significant change. And as I mentioned in my comments, we do expect our margin rate to, call it, normalize back to 30-plus where it's been most recently, because we did have a mix shift change that simply impacted Q2 of this year.

Sameer Joshi: Understood. And then last one on accounts payable. I think, quarter-over-quarter, almost -- a little over $5 million in drop. Was there anything specific that happened there? Or is it just timing?

John Brodin: It's primarily timing. It really goes to the working capital investment we've talked about for some of these more significant projects.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Gowshi Sriharan.

Gowshihan Sriharan: Hope you can all hear me?

Gowshihan Sriharan: On the [indiscernible] grows, how much are you doing with your own crews versus subcontractors? And how have the subcontractor rates moved over the past year?

Sally Washlow: So you broke up right when you started your question. Can you repeat that?

Gowshihan Sriharan: Sure, sure. As the contracting grows, how much are you doing with your own crews versus subcontractors? And how are the subcontractor rates progressing?

John Brodin: Yes. We typically outsource or subcontract for all of our installations in the Lighting segment. Within maintenance, we do have a few people that -- our W-2 employees that work directly on maintenance projects. But in general, for the big lighting projects, that is all subcontracted work.

Gowshihan Sriharan: And on the IoT element of the retailer interior projects, does that IoT piece of that retailer project carry any ongoing software or monitoring revenue?

Sally Washlow: So we are working with the sensor or the IoT provider. It's not a system that we build or it's not our software. So we don't have a component of that. And quite frankly, in this system, I don't believe there is any component of it.

Gowshihan Sriharan: And on the pricing side of the maintenance review, compared with the previous contracts?

John Brodin: Yes, if you're referring back to the renewal of the 3-year contract, it's pretty similar with some inflationary increases.

Gowshihan Sriharan: Okay. And I'll just sneak in the last one. The purchase order on the interior projects, how are they flowing so far? How does the margin on the interior work compare with kind of your exterior programs?

John Brodin: I expect them to be in line with the exterior projects. We price those products pretty similarly.

Sally Washlow: And the timing, as we've said, is Q3 and Q4.

John Brodin: Yes. Maybe one thing I'd add since we didn't comment on this, in the 10-Q, you will see that our backlog at the end of September sits at about $21.6 million or $21.7 million. All of the firm POs that we've been receiving for the interior project are -- have been received subsequent to September 30. So those orders have been coming in, but none of them are reflected in that backlog number. Our backlog number as of the end of October is up actually fairly substantially compared to September.

Operator: Our next call comes from the line of Luke Persons of Craig-Hallum Capital Group.

Luke Persons: This is Luke on for Eric. So I guess, first here on the data center, how have you leveraged your successes with this initial customer and the engagements with other potential data center customers? Is your distribution partner continuing to help you penetrate this market? And also, would you ever consider going to a direct sales model down the road in this market?

Sally Washlow: So our distribution partner with the hyperscaler that we're working with, we do plan to discuss with others within that partner. And then some of our other channels are getting involved as well in terms of how we will supply this product to the market. Direct, we're not in those discussions yet. A lot of it is new construction where a lot of times in lighting, the distribution channel is taking the lead on that. So nothing yet. We've been focused on building the right fixture and working with the partners in our distribution channel.

Luke Persons: Got it. That's helpful. And just for our second question, kind of switching gears here. So on the pending refresh cycle with your large retail customer, how should we compare the opportunity here to Orion's initial awards with this customer in terms of magnitude and content per store? Also, can you break down some of the drivers for these potential awards? Would this be like a national decision made by this customer to really kick off the refresh cycle? Or would it be done more on like a regional or store-by-store basis?

Sally Washlow: So with this particular partner, it's done at headquarter level, on a national level. And then we're working with them on the various rollouts and segments of their footprint. So the one that I noted earlier would be of similar size to the project that we announced or to the higher end of that number.

John Brodin: And maybe just to clarify a little more on that, Luke, a little more on that. There are points of time when we get a, call it, a significant commitment on a project from this customer, similar to what we announced for the interior project in September and then they may, beyond that commitment then issue a store-by-store PO. So just a little bit of a nuance in how the orders roll in and flow into our backlog versus what the commitment is.

Luke Persons: Got it. And I guess just for our last question here on the new roadway product. I mean, can you talk about why you haven't really participated in this market yet up until now and why this product will be able to compete? And also just how do you view the timing and magnitude of the market opportunity for this product?

Sally Washlow: Yes. There was an opportunity in the market where there were some challenges with some of the competitors that were building this product. And so quite frankly, brought to us by one of our distribution partners, the opportunity for us to participate in this segment. That being said, there's a lot of work that we have to do on our end, working with our partners to get it approved for state bids and things like that. So we think there's a long life of this product, and we're working on getting it ingrained in the channel so that we can win business.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our next question comes from the line of Bill Dezellem of Tieton Capital Management.

William Dezellem: So first of all, I'd like to talk about your guidance. If we look at the midpoint of your guidance, revenue guidance, that is, that implies that Q3 and Q4 are both going to be approximately $27 million in revenue. And you haven't -- you all haven't had $27 million in revenues in a quarter for years. But what's changing leading to that? Because I think you said in the opening remarks, you'd anticipate these being reasonably even with potentially upside to Q4. So more detail would be really terrific.

John Brodin: Yes, Bill, I think the main thing that we see is the continuation of some projects that are underway and the interior project, which we announced in September will have a big influence on the revenue volumes in Q3 and Q4.

William Dezellem: And that upside that Sally referenced, I missed exactly what you said there, Sally. Would you circle back to those comments, please?

Sally Washlow: Sure. So for the announcement that we made of $10 million to $15 million for this project, we're thinking we'll hit the upper end of that range for that project in particular. And we are in discussions to launch another project of similar size. We're working on the timing of that now, which then could provide additional upside in what would be our Q4 if we can hit the timing of all of this.

William Dezellem: That's helpful. Congratulations. And so relative to that higher revenue level that you have not achieved for -- again, for years, is that really just simply project specific? Or is there something changing structurally improving at Orion?

Sally Washlow: I think that -- I mean, structurally, there are things improving and some of our distribution channels are starting to grow, as we mentioned, we've refocused on our distribution, our ESCO channels. We're seeing increased activity from those channels as well where we're confident that we're going to hit our guidance. And we think that there's potentially more to go there. But we are definitely seeing increased project work as well. But the product-only side of our business, we're seeing strength.

William Dezellem: Great. And then, Per, you put a tantalizing comment out there that your October backlog was significantly higher than the number reported in the 10-Q. What was the October backlog?

John Brodin: Sorry, Bill, but we're not going to get in the habit of disclosing interim backlog, but I want to at least give you a flavor for where we are relative to the previous quarter end.

William Dezellem: I was simply giving you the opportunity, Per.

William Dezellem: One additional question then, please. Relative to the automaker that chose to procure both lighting and EV charging, you gave some general comments about that. But would you please describe how that customer chose to procure both from you all and essentially how you go about that cross-selling in the future?

Sally Washlow: Sure. So it's a long-standing customer of ours, and we do work at several of their sites. We were in there discussing the lighting project with them, and they shared the need for EV as well. And we quickly brought in our experts on the EV side to help them come up with the right solution for this location.

And then you wrap that around with the decades of work that we've done with this customer on the lighting side and our execution and delivery of these projects and then pair it with our EV segment that also has decades of experience as well, that they were confident to award us additional work in EV and help us manage it all, where in the past, maybe we hadn't been emphasizing our other solutions enough, but it's certainly front and center that we will be sharing all of our solutions even with long-time lighting customers.

William Dezellem: And using that customer as an example, is it the same procurement team? Or do they then -- does the customer then bring in a separate team for that effort? How does that tend to work? And really, the spirit of the question is lighting and EV charging seem pretty disparate other than that they both have electricity involved.

Sally Washlow: Yes. So to answer that question, it varies because it does vary. With this particular customer, this was the decision maker. But within other customers, EV charging could be managed by even whoever runs their fleets as well as a customer might be electrifying their fleet. So then it's our job to stay wired within the customer and ask who we're working with, whether it's on the lighting side, who does EV, who leads that effort within your organization and get internal referrals within those customers as well. So it can work that way or it can work through other industry contacts that we have as well. But it is not always the same customer.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of [ Steve Rudd of Blackwell ].

Unknown Analyst: I just need a little clarification on the back half. On the math that Bill shared with us, the second half, we would expect revenues of $27 million and $27 million, respectively, for third and fourth quarter. However, I thought earlier, Per, you mentioned that the third quarter would be flat on the revenue side, but up by about 4 percentage points on margin. Can you address that conflict on the flat compared to Q2, which is about $22 million versus just the basic math from Q3 and Q4 being $27 million a piece?

John Brodin: The math I was trying to give was that Q3 and Q4 would be relatively flat to each other. So the math that Bill did is appropriate. So it would be in the $26 million neighborhood per quarter, at the low end of our range, Bill gave the midpoint, and so the high end of the range would be a little bit higher than that. And at those levels and with the shift of projects normalizing, that's why we expect the increase in margin in addition to better absorption because of those revenue levels.

Unknown Analyst: Okay. Well, that's dramatically better.

Operator: This concludes our question-and-answer session. I will now turn the call back to Sally Washlow for concluding remarks.

Sally Washlow: I thank everyone again for taking the time to join us today. We look forward to updating investors on our third quarter FY '27 call in February. We look forward to meeting with many of you, whether in person or virtually between now and then. We will be presenting at a number of conferences, so please watch for our forthcoming announcements regarding scheduling. Please also reach out to our Investor Relations team to set up a meeting or for any other information. Their contact information is at the bottom of today's press release. Many thanks again for your interest in Orion, and I look forward to continuing to update you on our progress.

Operator: Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program, and you may now disconnect.
