#3194. Bluetooth 7 Speeds Are Set to Quadruple in 2027, Especially for Audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The Bluetooth Group has announced a new standard. Here's how it works and when you can expect to benefit from it.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Wireless tech is about to get a whole lot snappier. On Thursday, the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, the trade association that oversees Bluetooth, officially unveiled Bluetooth High Data Throughput, a flagship upgrade set to arrive as part of the Bluetooth Core 7.0 standard. The revision supercharges Bluetooth Low Energy by pushing maximum bit rates to 7.5Mbps, effectively quadrupling the throughput of the existing LE 2M technology. Compatible devices are slated to hit store shelves starting in 2027.

That’s good news for phone users, tablet havers, laptop groupies, smart speaker stans and more. Bluetooth is still the most popular medium-to-short-range wireless standard for connecting devices. But this is a big rollout, and the changes will start with premium wireless, such as earbuds, with other applications following.

Those other applications could include spatial computing, exchanging AI-related info with local devices, connecting to health wearables and a host of smart home applications, like playing Spotify through an Amazon Echo Studio or dimming a smart bulb.

“In practical terms, a smartwatch could sync hours of sensor-rich training data to a phone in seconds. A smart home product could complete a firmware update with little visible downtime,” Damon Barnes, Director of Technical Marketing at the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, told CNET. “Smart glasses and other AI-enabled devices could exchange more data with a companion device or the cloud. And in audio, the additional capacity can support richer experiences, including high-resolution, lossless, surround, and spatial audio.”

A representative from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group didn’t respond to a request for comment.

The biggest change in this update is a new physical layer for Bluetooth. Layers are like different sections of the Bluetooth protocol, and the physical layer is the bedrock of the standard, the foundational layer involved in transmitting and receiving data signals.

Improvements in the physical layer can have very significant effects on all Bluetooth communications. In this case, new modulation schemes let the physical layer handle data more efficiently and transmit more data at once, which is why the speed increases are so significant.

These improvements also make the new standard more efficient, saving battery life in many applications. So your smart lock may last longer before you need to exchange the AA batteries, earbuds won’t need to go back in the case as fast, and so on.

We know the first flagship devices are expected to appear with the technology in early 2027, but don’t have an exact date.

Barnes also told use that since the update is starting with wireless audio, the first devices to see it will be headphones, earbuds and speakers.

With protocol changes like this, it can take some time for new products to reach the market, and manufacturers may take a long time, even years, to adopt it.

#3193. 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Bluetooth Core 7.0 could make your smart home devices easier to set up, for one. Here's what we know about the new core specification.

Bluetooth Core 7.0 is here, and each new specification from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG) offers a glimpse of what we can expect from our devices in the future. The major feature incorporated into the new core standard is High Data Throughput (HDT), which can enable lossless wireless audio and improved multi-channel spatial audio on more Bluetooth devices.

Also: Apple has a Bluetooth problem, and Android is taking advantage

Bluetooth Core 7.0’s standout feature is that it can achieve wireless lossless audio. However, the improvements to the Bluetooth stack architecture — particularly, expanding the Bluetooth spectrum — allow for faster data transfer, improved energy efficiency, more resilient connections, and create more room for devices and their data-intensive applications.

HDT means good news for audiophiles, smart home enthusiasts, VR/XR fans, wellness wearable aficionados, AI companion devotees, and much more. I explained applications of HDT in a wireless audio context earlier this year. Now that it’s officially adopted, here’s what you can expect.

A major milestone in Bluetooth Core 7.0 is the ability to stream lossless audio over a wireless connection. Bluetooth is lossy, requiring data compression that diminishes audio quality. HDT’s faster data transfer and greater wireless data capacity enable it to handle the massive volume of data required to achieve lossless quality.

Also: Your Bose headphones are getting a major Bluetooth upgrade – what to expect

Audiophiles typically avoid wireless headphones for intensive listening due to the necessary data compression, opting for wired headphones that can accommodate larger lossless files. Bluetooth’s innovation here is widely regarded as a major leap in wireless technology.

HDT also promises to standardize spatial audio, with expanded data transfers allowing for multi-channel audio setups. Standardizing this form of audio transmission could mean consumers can expect more affordable brands and products to adopt this premium feature.

Every consumer-friendly feature possible within Bluetooth Core 7.0 can be traced back to its ability to accommodate more devices and their ever-expanding data needs. According to a Bluetooth blog post, Bluetooth HDT delivers nearly four times the previous maximum Bluetooth throughput.

Data throughput is the amount of data received, transmitted, and processed over the Bluetooth network. With nearly four times the processing power, HDT can move more data, faster. HDT increases Bluetooth’s maximum supported bitrate to 7.5 Mbps, up from the current 2 Mbps.

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

The result is shorter download times for a device’s firmware update, faster device location when Find My Device is activated, or faster transfer of a large photo album via Android’s QuickShare or Apple’s AirDrop.

In the same blog post, Øyvind Strøm, executive vice president of the short-range business unit at Nordic Semiconductor, gives examples of a smartwatch syncing hours’ worth of workout data to your phone in seconds, or a pair of headphones, a smart speaker, or a security camera that can download a firmware update with nearly zero interruption to the user experience.

In a smart home context, Bluetooth Low Energy (LE) is the wireless technology that works in the background, connecting your devices. Bluetooth LE is the baseline technology for quick device discovery and connection. The most recent example of this is Apple’s HomeView, which uses Bluetooth LE to discover a nearby, trusted iPhone to unlock that user’s personalized home hub display.

The less you feel its presence through lags, wait times, and dropouts, the better it’s working. HDT’s goal is to make Bluetooth connectivity frictionless, which is especially valuable when your smart lights, shades, speakers, TVs, refrigerators, and more rely on the technology.

Also: Forget Wi-Fi: Apple is betting on Bluetooth with its new home devices

For example, HDT’s improved data throughput could allow doorbells, cameras, and robot vacuums to quickly offload large amounts of data to your smart home hub. It could also enable near-instantaneous setup of a new device onto your smart home network and firmware updates.

Finally, HDT also addressed network stability and reliability, especially in high-traffic areas such as apartment complexes and dense cities, where a busy network can cause delays and backups. Alongside improvements to Wi-Fi and Thread, a truly seamless smart home is on the horizon.

Bluetooth’s Human Interface Device (HID) profile refers to the wireless communication used by peripheral devices, such as mice, keyboards, and game controllers, when connecting to a host device. Smart glasses and controllers connected to XR/VR headsets also use this profile, and their data-intensive computing will benefit greatly from HDT.

Devices using the HID profile can expect HDT to lay the foundation for making cloud gaming more reliable, spatial computing more responsive, and offloading audio/visual data from smart glasses less power-intensive.

Also: Frustrated with your Bluetooth? How multipoint works – and why it sometimes won’t

Additionally, gaming keyboards and mice can expect HDT’s expanded data processing to deliver shorter device communication intervals, reducing latency and lag.

In 2026, we’re starting to see more Bluetooth Core 6.0-equipped devices, with Samsung’s recently announced Galaxy Buds On featuring Bluetooth 6.2. Though Bluetooth’s blog post states that the first application of HDT will be for premium wireless audio, many audio manufacturers are behind, still releasing products with Bluetooth 5.4.

Smartphones, smartwatches, and smart home products tend to move a little faster, with the majority of current Bluetooth Core 6.0 products falling into these categories.

The Bluetooth SIG announced Auracast in 2022, and audio manufacturers are now beginning to adopt this technology more widely. Channel Sounding was released with Bluetooth Core 6.0 in 2024, with some early adopters releasing compatible products this year, including Google’s Pixel Tag and Motorola’s Moto Tag 2; more are expected next year and into 2028. With these adoption cycles in mind, we may be well into the next decade before HDT becomes standard.

After all those unseasonably warm weekends (thanks global warming), it's finally starting to feel like fall, and I'm ready to cozy up on the couch and catch up on my watchlist. That ain't exactly a walk in the park, though, with the best streaming services adding so many great new movies this month — including a whopping 51 new flicks on Netflix alone!

To cut through the noise quickly, I make a beeline for the Netflix Top 10. Granted, not every movie that makes the cut is guaranteed to be a winner, and this weekend's crop is weaker than it's been in months. To save you from getting caught endlessly scrolling, I'm here every weekend to separate the wheat from the chaff and call out which Netflix Top 10 picks are actually worth watching.

This weekend, that includes a heist movie that'll leave you guessing a la "Reservoir Dogs," Guy Ritchie's historical epic that critics got wrong, and a true crime drama that's every parent's worst nightmare.

None of these picks fit the vibe? No worries: Our guide to everything new on Netflix this month has plenty more recommendations on what to watch. So without further ado, here are the three must-watch movies in Netflix’s top 10 this weekend. Enjoy!

This article is based on Netflix's top 10 movies list in the U.S. as of 10:30 a.m. ET on Saturday, November 7, 2026.

There's something about settling in for a heist movie that just makes a lazy weekend afternoon fly by. Netflix's latest, "Collision Course," is proving to be a crowdpleaser (if you don't mind subtitles). Set in 2013, against the backdrop of Spain's economic crisis, it follows four people looking to turn their fortunes around with a daring bank heist in Madrid.

With help from a man on the inside, they break into the bank and raid a safety deposit box said to contain highly valuable loot, only to find it empty. Their botched heist takes an even worse turn when their getaway ends in a spectacular automobile collision that sends the plot careening into "Reservoir Dogs" territory. With suspicions mounting, before long, the question isn't whether they'll get away with the heist, but whether you can trust anyone to be telling the truth.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

My husband has a rolodex of "boy" movies (at least, that's what I call them) that he revisits from time to time, and "King Arthur: Legend of the Sword" is one of the hear-me-outs he convinced me to watch that I actually enjoyed. You're likely already familiar with the story of King Arthur, but Charlie Hunnam's performance as the fabled ruler of Britain breathes new life into the legend while there's plenty of Guy Ritchie's signature pulse-pounding action sequences to keep your attention.

Robbed of his birthright by his tyrannical uncle Vortigern (Jude Law) and with no idea of his lineage, Arthur grows up in exile, scrapping by as best he can in the back alleys of London. When Vortigern uncovers the legendary Excalibur stuck in a stone, he rounds up everyone last man to try to remove it. Naturally, Arthur is the only one who can, and he assembles the scrappiest fighters in the land, who later become the first knights of his Round Table, to overthrow Vortigern and avenge his father's legacy.

Watch "King Arthur: Legend of the Sword" on Netflix now

For all the true crime girlies looking for a stranger-then-fiction story to lose themselves in this weekend, look no further than "Kidnapped in Her Own Home: The Martha Carelli Story." It's based on a terrifying true story: Convicted felon Michael Anderson (played by Tyler Perez a.k.a. Mr. C's much cooler brother in "Abbott Elementary") escapes from prison and secretly begins living in a suburban home while the family is none the wiser.

When he finally reveals himself, he holds matriarch Martha (Stana Katic) at gunpoint, ties her up, and demands money and a getaway car. His plans take a turn when her pre-teen son Bennet (Gavin Keoni Spinner) arrives home with a friend, followed by her husband John (Dove Meir). Now holding the entire family hostage, Anderson forces Martha to drive him out of town, setting off a tense psychological game of cat and mouse as she desperately tries to outsmart her captor.

Watch "Kidnapped in Her Own Home: The Martha Carelli Story" on Netflix now

StandardAero, Inc. (SARO +9.21%) reported third-quarter results marked by a leadership transition and a significant increase in full-year financial guidance. Management reported that the company's diversified portfolio provided resilience across commercial, business, and military end markets. The company initiated a $350 million accelerated share repurchase program and increased its total buyback authorization to $1.0 billion. Management reported that core growth in the commercial aftermarket offset the headwind from the intentional elimination of low-margin pass-through material revenue. Operational focus centered on scaling the LEAP engine program and expanding component repair capabilities through internal development and strategic acquisitions.

Operator: Good afternoon, and welcome to StandardAero's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. A definition and reconciliation of these measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures can be found in our earnings release and in the appendix to the earnings slide presentation on our website at ir.standardaero.com. Non-GAAP financial measures should be considered in addition to and not as a substitute for GAAP measures. And with that out of the way, I would now like to turn the call over to Russ. Russ?

Russell Ford: Thank you, Rama, and thank you to everyone for joining our call today. As you know, this is my final earnings call following my tenure as StandardAero's CEO, and I'm especially pleased to be joined today by Paul McElhinney, who assumed the role of CEO in October. Paul will be sharing his perspectives on the business and our strategic priorities later in today's call. Let me begin on Slide 3 with an overview of our third quarter performance.

StandardAero delivered another strong quarter with continued revenue growth across all 3 major end markets, 30% year-over-year adjusted EPS growth, 15% adjusted EBITDA growth and 130 basis points adjusted EBITDA margin expansion to 14.4%, underscoring the resilience of our diversified portfolio and the progress of our operational initiatives. We intentionally built StandardAero with the breadth and resilience to sustain double-digit earnings growth over time, even when individual end markets or engine platforms experience periods of slower growth. This balanced portfolio allows us to navigate different market cycles while capturing growth opportunities across the enterprise. Looking at our end markets. Commercial aerospace revenue grew at a high single-digit rate year-over-year, excluding the impact of lower pass-through materials revenue.

Demand across commercial aerospace engine aftermarket remains robust with visibility into our customer demand and revenue forecast now extending into 2028. Aircraft utilization remains strong. Industry MRO capacity continues to be constrained and the growing maintenance requirements of the global fleet are supporting sustained demand for our services. Our growing backlog and sustained bookings momentum provide meaningful visibility and reinforce our confidence in the long-term outlook. Business Aviation grew 7.4% year-over-year, supported by demand across the midsize and super midsized engine platforms we serve. We continue to benefit from the strategic investments we've made to expand our capabilities and capacity, particularly on the HTF7000 platform.

Military & Helicopter revenue increased 7.2% year-over-year, supported by continued demand across our military engine portfolio and the ongoing ramp of previously awarded programs. As we've discussed in prior quarters, increasing defense spending, higher operational tempo and the growing focus on aircraft readiness and sustainment are creating attractive long-term opportunities for StandardAero. While the timing of certain military engine and component inputs have created near-term challenges, particularly within our Component Repair Services segment, we remain confident in the attractive long-term growth opportunity in this end market. Stepping back from the quarter, I'm particularly pleased with the progress we've made on the strategic investments that we've discussed with you over the past several years.

Our LEAP and CFM56 DFW programs reached profitability earlier this year, and we continue to move down the learning curve as these programs scale. Our CF34 and business aviation investments are supporting growth and margin expansion, and our Component Repair Services business continues to expand its repair capabilities across the broader enterprise. These strategic investments were made with a long-term view, and we're beginning to see the benefits in our operating performance. I believe we are still in the early stages of realizing their full potential. As I reflect on my time leading StandardAero, what I am most proud of is not just what we have accomplished, but the people and the culture that have made it possible.

We built a company with a process-oriented culture where we hold ourselves accountable, honor our commitments and take tremendous pride in serving our customers. That culture has been the foundation of our success, enabling us to consistently execute our strategy of building leading positions on attractive engine platforms, investing ahead of demand, continuously improving our operations, deploying capital with discipline and creating long-term shareholder value. I firmly believe that our people and culture are among StandardAero's greatest competitive advantages and will remain central to our success for many years to come. I've worked closely with Paul for more than 7 years, and I have tremendous confidence in his ability to lead StandardAero through its next phase of growth.

He brings deep engine MRO experience, an exceptional understanding of our business and industry and a shared commitment to the values, disciplined execution and customer relationships that have defined the 115-year history of StandardAero. Paul also brings a fresh perspective and new ideas on how we can build upon the strong foundation already in place. I believe the opportunities ahead of StandardAero are significant. Our markets remain attractive. Our investments are delivering results, and our strategy continues to provide a clear path to sustained double-digit earnings growth and long-term shareholder value creation. I cannot think of a better leader than Paul to guide StandardAero through this next chapter.

I want to express my sincere gratitude to our employees around the world for their dedication and commitment, to our customers for the trust they place in us and to our shareholders for their continued support. It's been an extraordinary privilege to lead this company, and I cannot be more proud of what our team has accomplished together. With that, it's my great pleasure to turn the call over to Paul McElhinney, our new Chief Executive Officer, who will walk you through our strategic priorities and outlook. Paul?

Paul McElhinney: Thank you, Russ, for those kind words and more importantly, for your extraordinary leadership and everything you have done for StandardAero. Having worked closely with Russ and the team, I've had the opportunity to see firsthand the culture, customer relationships and operating capabilities that make this company so special. I've spent more than 30 years in the aerospace and industrial aftermarket, about half of that time in the aviation finance and leasing space and half on the industrial side, including leading GE Aerospace's global aftermarket business and also leading GE Vernova's global aftermarket business. That experience gives me strong conviction in StandardAero's differentiated position, a purposefully diversified portfolio combined with compelling long-term opportunities across all of its major end markets.

Having served on the Board for more than 7 years, I have been closely involved in the company's strategic direction. In many ways, I believe we are only beginning to capture the earnings potential of those investments and decisions. I believe strongly in the strategy that Russ and the team have established. My focus is on building upon that foundation, accelerating execution and converting the significant opportunities ahead of us into sustained earnings growth, cash generation and long-term shareholder value. Turning to Slide 4. Our first strategic priority is LEAP, which is a major program that I have personally been involved with for well over a decade as part of my earlier GE career.

I believe LEAP represents one of the most compelling long-term growth opportunities in the aerospace aftermarket. LEAP and the opportunity it represents for StandardAero were among the key reasons I was excited to take on the CEO role. StandardAero's premier MRO authorization, its investments in capacity and technical capabilities and its strong customer relationships have established what I believe is a highly attractive competitive position in the LEAP aftermarket. Importantly, we believe this growth opportunity is still in its early stages. As Russ alluded to, we reached profitability on the program earlier this year, and our focus now is on continuing to improve productivity, expand our component repair capabilities and increase margins as volumes scale.

We remain on track towards our objective of exceeding $1 billion in annual LEAP revenue by the end of this decade with an opportunity to grow to several billion dollars as the aftermarket matures into the 2030s. Our next priority is productivity and operational execution. Over the past several years, StandardAero has made significant investments in its facilities, capabilities and workforce to support the next phase of growth. As those investments mature, we see a substantial opportunity to drive higher throughput, improve turnaround times and realize greater operating leverage across the business. The completion of our Winnipeg facility expansion marks another important milestone in supporting the continued growth of our CF34 business.

Equally important is our continued emphasis on operational excellence and continuous improvement across our facilities. We have leading positions on attractive engine platforms. Our focus now is on leveraging those positions and investments to drive sustained productivity gains, margin expansion and stronger cash flow. Our next priority is Component Repair Services, where I see significant opportunity to expand our capabilities, increase repair content and drive attractive long-term growth. CRS is a strategically important business for StandardAero, not only because of its attractive economics, but also because of the value it brings to our customers and our broader engine services operations.

By developing new repair capabilities and increasing internal repair capture, we can lower material costs, improve turnaround times and deliver more cost-effective solutions to our customers. We will continue investing in new repair development across both the engine platforms we service and the broader aerospace market. The acquisition of Unified Turbines is a good example of this strategy in action, adding differentiated technical capabilities with meaningful opportunities for both revenue and cost synergies over time. I have strong conviction in the long-term growth and margin opportunity in our repair business because of the tangible value it delivers to customers and the broader StandardAero network.

Our final priority is disciplined capital deployment, which will be an important area of focus for me as the CEO. StandardAero has a strong track record of generating attractive returns through organic investments, strategic acquisitions and expanding our capabilities on the engine platforms we serve. We see meaningful opportunities to continue to deploy capital in these areas, particularly through strategic M&A that strengthens our competitive position and enhances our long-term earnings power. At the same time, we believe share repurchases represent an attractive use of capital when our stock is trading at a meaningful discount to our assessment of intrinsic value. Today, we are announcing an increase to our share repurchase authorization, taking it to over $1 billion.

In conjunction, we are also announcing a $350 million accelerated share repurchase. We have already repurchased $160 million year-to-date. After completing our ASR, we will have $500 million remaining on the authorization. This decision reflects our confidence in StandardAero's long-term outlook, the cash-generating ability of our business and our belief that repurchasing shares at current levels represents a compelling opportunity to create value for shareholders. Our approach is not to favor one form of capital deployment over another. It is to allocate capital where we believe we can generate the greatest long-term return for shareholders while maintaining appropriate balance sheet and financial flexibility.

Based on our current assumptions, we expect to end the year at net leverage below 2.7x after these actions, thus preserving meaningful flexibility to pursue additional attractive opportunities. Ultimately, our objective is straightforward: to translate StandardAero's attractive growth opportunities and increasing cash generation into sustained long-term per share value creation. Finally, turning to our outlook. I'm pleased that we are once again raising our full year 2026 guidance. We now expect revenue growth of approximately 9% year-over-year versus our previous guide of 6%. Adjusted EBITDA growth of 13% versus 11% and adjusted EPS growth of 26% versus our previous guide of 23%. We are reiterating our adjusted free cash flow guidance, which represents a 36% growth year-over-year.

Our improved outlook reflects the strength of underlying aftermarket demand, the progress we are making on our growth programs and continued productivity improvements across the business. Stepping back, I want to reinforce that StandardAero's long-term investment thesis remains firmly intact. We operate in attractive, structurally growing markets. We have leading positions on critical engine platforms, differentiated repair capabilities and a diversified portfolio that provides resilience across market cycles. Our opportunity is to continue converting those advantages into sustained double-digit earnings growth, improving free cash flow generation and delivering attractive returns on invested capital. The strategy is proven. The opportunities ahead are significant, and my focus is on execution and delivering consistent long-term value creation for our shareholders.

With that, I'll turn the call over to Dan to walk you through our financial results and guidance in greater detail. Dan?

Daniel Satterfield: Thank you, Paul. I'll begin on Slide 5 with a brief overview of our third quarter financial results, focusing on the key drivers of performance across our segments, cash flow and balance sheet. For the third quarter, StandardAero generated revenue of $1.56 billion, an increase of 4% year-over-year with continued growth across both operating segments. Adjusted EBITDA increased 15% to $225 million, with margins expanding 130 basis points year-over-year to 14.4%. Our continued earnings growth reflects improving productivity across the business, particularly in Engine Services, increased availability and utilization of Used Serviceable Material or USM and continued progress down the learning curve on our LEAP and CFM56 DFW growth programs.

In addition, the elimination of low to no-margin pass-through revenue continues to benefit our reported margin profile, yet creates a temporary reduction in top line growth as anticipated. Net income increased 36% to $93 million, while adjusted diluted EPS grew 30% to $0.39, reflecting stronger operating earnings and the benefit of share repurchases. Turning to Engine Services on Slide 6. The segment delivered another strong quarter with revenue increasing 3.5% year-over-year and segment adjusted EBITDA increasing a robust 24% to $205 million. Margins expanded 250 basis points year-over-year to 15%, reflecting several factors. First, continued productivity improvements across our engine programs and across all 3 end markets.

Second, LEAP and CFM56 DFW, both of which reached profitability earlier this year and continue to progress down the learning curve. Third, increased availability and utilization of USM across several commercial platforms, which has supported better material economics and operating performance. Fourth, the continued elimination of low to no-margin pass-through material revenue from restructured customer contracts. Taken together, these factors are driving meaningful improvements in the underlying profitability of Engine Services, and we remain encouraged by the progress we are making. Moving to Component Repair Services on Slide 7.

Revenue increased 7.3% year-over-year to $189 million, supported by continued strength in commercial aerospace repairs, particularly on the CFM56, GTF, V2500 and CF34 platforms as well as growth in our aeroderivative business. Segment adjusted EBITDA was approximately $49 million with margins of 25.8%, reflecting unfavorable mix and the timing of certain military programs. In particular, we continue to experience delays in material inputs and repair activity on select military platforms, especially training-related programs. We also experienced some residual costs associated with the ramp of new labor capacity that dragged over from the last quarter. Despite these timing-related headwinds, our commercial Component Repair business continues to grow, supported by strong demand and an expanding portfolio of repair capabilities.

We remain confident in the long-term growth and earnings potential of CRS, although the timing of a recovery in military-related activity remains a factor we are closely monitoring. Turning to free cash flow on Slide 8. We generated approximately $100 million of adjusted free cash flow in the third quarter compared with $50 million in the second quarter. This improvement was supported by higher earnings and continued progress on working capital management, including the benefits of our company-wide supply chain initiatives and improved material planning. Net working capital represented a use of approximately $37 million during the quarter, while capital expenditures were approximately $30 million.

We continue to focus on improving working capital efficiency as our growth programs scale, particularly by reducing turnaround times, optimizing inventory levels and improving the timing of material purchases. We remain on track to deliver our full year adjusted free cash flow guidance of $270 million to $300 million, supported by improving operating earnings and our continued working capital initiatives even as supply chain constraints persist. Turning to our balance sheet on Slide 9. We ended the third quarter with net debt to adjusted EBITDA of 2.66x compared to 2.9x in the third quarter last year.

As Paul discussed, the Board has increased the share repurchase authorization to $1.01 billion, of which year-to-date, we have purchased $160 million of shares, including $50 million in the third quarter. This leaves $850 million under the authorization. In addition to the authorization increase, we are entering a $350 million ASR. We will have $500 million left on the authorization after completing the ASR. Based on our guidance, we expect to end the year well within our long-term target range of 2 to 3x, which leaves us with substantial flexibility to fund organic growth investments and M&A while practicing disciplined capital deployment. Finally, turning to Slide 10.

We are raising full year revenue guidance by $148 million at the midpoint to a range of $6.525 billion to $6.645 billion, with this increase reflected in our updated revenue guidance for the Engine Services segment. This implies an 8.6% year-over-year growth at the midpoint. We are also raising our adjusted EBITDA guidance to a range of $905 million to $920 million or 13% year-over-year growth at the midpoint. As a result, we are raising our adjusted EPS guidance to a range of $1.57 to $1.62. This increase, which implies 26% year-over-year growth is supported by higher earnings and a lower tax rate and share count.

We are reiterating our adjusted free cash flow guidance of $270 million to $300 million. From an end market perspective, we continue to expect commercial aerospace growth in the low double-digit to mid-teens range once the pass-through material revenue that was eliminated is normalized. We expect Business Aviation growth in the high single-digit to low double-digit range and Military & Helicopters growth in the low double-digit range. This quarter is another strong demonstration of the resilience and earnings power of the StandardAero business model. We have deliberately built a diversified portfolio across engine platforms, end markets and customers, each with distinct growth drivers and complementary operating cycles.

Ultimately, what sets StandardAero apart is our ability to consistently compound earnings and free cash flow over the long-term. We believe that sustained enterprise-wide performance rather than short-term fluctuations in any single platform or end market is the true measure of our earnings power and long-term shareholder value creation. With that, I'll turn it back over to Paul.

Paul McElhinney: Thank you, Dan. Before we open the call for questions, I want to leave you with a few final thoughts. As I mentioned earlier, I'm incredibly excited about the opportunity ahead for StandardAero. We have an exceptional portfolio of engine platforms, strong customer relationships and the team with the technical expertise and operational capabilities to capitalize on the long-term growth in the aftermarket. I also want to express my sincere appreciation to our talented team of more than 8,000 employees around the world, whose dedication, expertise and unwavering commitment to our customers are the foundation of our success. We've made significant investments over the past several years, and we are now beginning to realize their benefits.

My focus will be on continuing to execute against our strategy, accelerating growth where we see the greatest opportunities and translating those investments into sustained earnings growth, strong cash generation and attractive returns for our shareholders. I also want to take one final opportunity to recognize Russ. On behalf of our employees, our leadership team and our Board, thank you for your extraordinary leadership, your friendship and everything you have done for this company. I am personally grateful for your trust and support, and I look forward to continuing to work closely with you.

Finally, to our shareholders and the broader investment community, I look forward to meeting many of you personally over the coming months, hearing your perspectives and sharing more about our vision for StandardAero's future. Thank you all again for joining us today. And with that, operator, we will now open it up for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from the line of Ken Herbert with RBC Capital Markets.

Kenneth Herbert: Let me congratulate Russ and Paul on the transition. And congratulations, Russ, and good luck on retirement. First, maybe if I could, just to -- just obviously, you're not talking about 2027 in detail yet. But how do we think about visibility in Engine Services, in particular, just with the increasing concern around what could be slower demand for engine maintenance activity as a result of lower capacity growth or higher fuel prices. Just can you talk at all about what you're seeing in terms of backlogs across the MRO shops and if you've seen any signals yet that we could see any softening of demand in the next year?

Daniel Satterfield: Kenneth, it's Dan. Yes. So listen, as we've said last quarter, we've seen zero impact from the macro on our business. No meaningful changes observed in bookings. As a matter of fact, backlog has increased since the conflict began. It's true in the comments we made on the call, we've got clear visibility all the way through early 2028 and revenue is spoken for in large part for 2027. Why is that? There's scheduled engine maintenance. We've got customer deposits on hand. We have, as you know, often, the flight cycle hour reporting on these engines, we know when they're coming in. Again, our long-term arrangements stretch out many years. That's providing the visibility.

We would not call a macro event impact on the business at this time.

Paul McElhinney: Ken, I'll just add a couple of comments. First of all, thanks for the welcome. I've spent a lot of time -- even in the first 4 weeks, I've spent a lot of time talking to customers and our OEM partners. Really, nobody is seeing any impact on demand, just like Dan has said. So our visibility is actually quite good through to 2028. So, no change in customer behavior, no impact on inductions and planned induction. So nothing that we are seeing or hearing that would change anything.

Kenneth Herbert: Okay. That's great. And if I could, just on supply chain and the material availability has been a major headwind as you think about the revenue growth and turnaround times. What are you seeing on material availability or material flow as it relates to the LEAP or the CFM56? And are you seeing improvements there that might also be sort of a tailwind as we think about confidence into next year?

Russell Ford: Yes, Ken, thanks. Listen, first of all, LEAP had a great quarter. A lot of our profitability growth has come from both LEAP and CFM56 and Dallas having fantastic quarters, just as we called it, right? Last quarter, they hit profitability. Now they're ramping up. So we're really proud of that. Material availability for LEAP and any of -- all of our programs continues to be constrained. If I have to call it, probably LEAP might be in a little bit better shape than the other programs. Now of course, there's no USM available on LEAP where CFM56 can take advantage of that, although those are constrained as well.

The supply chain environment, we're saying, listen, it's kind of the way it's been all year. But LEAP is probably benefiting from a little bit of better availability than other programs.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Myles Walton with Wolfe Research.

Myles Walton: Best wishes, Russ, and welcome, Paul. You raised the Engine Services rev guide by about $170 million and about $50 million of that, I guess, is the low-margin pass-through. What was the bigger source of the uplift aside from the pass-through? And then just looking at it sequentially, it does look like a pretty steep ramp sequentially. Is there a lot that has to happen in terms of USM availability remaining really high or other aspects?

Daniel Satterfield: Myles, it's Dan. Thanks for the call out. I think you're referring to the earnings growth, you said rev. Earnings growth, fantastic, right, 15%, sorry, 250 basis points -- sorry, 24% on Engine Services, 250 basis points. So that came kind of equally LEAP and CFM56, like I said earlier to Ken's comments. That, together with the pass-through impact is about a little bit less than half of the total 250 basis point improvement. Those 2 programs coming down the learning curve and achieving on their milestones. The rest of it is kind of split equally between the USM opportunity and general productivity. Now on USM is the following. I wouldn't say that USM is generally better, more available market-wise.

We had some great opportunities in Q3 that we took advantage of. We have a dedicated team out there sourcing USM. At some of our better platforms, they did a really great job on USM. Those were really great lifts for the company. We'll continue to take advantage of USM as it's opportunistically available, and we'll continue to see the LEAP and CFM Dallas programs become more profitable.

Myles Walton: Dan, I was actually asking about revenue. So I think in the full year guidance of revenue, you did raise ES revenue by $170 million, and I think the pass-through was lower by about $50 million. So there's $120 million of business revenue raised there. Could you just tell us what was that higher outlook coming from?

Daniel Satterfield: Yes. The ES, on the commercial side, we're seeing fantastic growth, primarily on LEAP and CFM56, CF34 is having a fantastic year as well and the turboprop programs. All of those are leading to that. The material pass-through number, we're taking down just a little bit, but that really is not impacting the revenue guide. The revenue guide is coming up and it's coming up with incremental margins.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of David Strauss with Wells Fargo.

David Strauss: Congrats to you both. Dan, I just wanted to ask about the -- some of the moving pieces on working capital year-to-date and what to expect in the fourth quarter, specifically looking at the big increase in receivables year-to-date. And then I think inventory has been a source, but contract assets have been a drag. If you could just walk through those and what to expect in the fourth quarter?

Daniel Satterfield: No, great question. Thank you. First of all, we're really proud of the $99 million -- $100 million of free cash flow in the quarter, up from $50 million in Q2. Within the working capital build of only $37 million, inventory has come down, right? It came down big in Q1. We kind of held it flat in Q2. In Q3, it's a nice decrease. That is a direct result of the effort we're putting into material ordering practices. Contract assets did increase.

But this is becoming clear that this is our cycle, a big increase before the big shipment unwind in Q4, just like we've achieved last quarter -- sorry, last Q4, where Q1 is a build, Q2 is kind of a decline. Q3 is a big build right prior to the Q4 big shipment period. This is a sort of expected increase in contract assets, along with billed accounts receivable. Those are up as well, also following kind of a similar pattern where Q1 goes up, Q2 is a big collections quarter, Q3 climbs and then Q4 is a big collections quarter, all on the way to the cash flow guide that we've given you, midpoint, $285 million.

Nothing really unusual here, except we're reaping the benefits of our sales and operation planning discipline and material ordering practices.

David Strauss: Okay. And on the license agreement, you've talked about the EBITDA contribution over the next couple of years. What can we expect from a revenue standpoint? How much that's going to add in revenue?

Daniel Satterfield: Yes, we haven't called that. What we have called on the license expansion. By the way, we're super excited about that. Those are new variants of engines that we already serve. It's about $25 million next year, it's going to be going to a total of about $30 million of earnings kind of on normal ES margins, so you can reverse engineer the revenue figure.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Sheila Kahyaoglu with Jefferies.

Sheila Kahyaoglu: Congrats again, Russ, and congratulations, Paul, as well. Maybe just a follow up on just the Q4 margins implied for Engine Services. I guess how do we think about the implied margins of about 14% versus the 15% in Q3 despite sales accelerating to low teens. Can you walk us through some of the puts and takes on the relatively high sales growth versus the margin disconnect there and what you're assuming for the material pass-through?

Daniel Satterfield: Sheila, good question. It's primarily the USM opportunity that we took advantage of here in Q3. I'd like to say that USM is going to be sort of an increasing entitlement that we have on a very consistent basis. Unfortunately, as you know, it's not like that. We had a great opportunity on USM in Q3 that I'm not going to call for Q4 being like that. Then we are also having an increase of the ramp programs, right? So LEAP and DFW, CFM56 DFW, as you know, are dilutive. There'll be higher revenues of those in Q4 as those programs ramp. So that will provide some dilution as well.

Sheila Kahyaoglu: Okay. Got it. That's super helpful. And then maybe if you could just talk about what's going on with military. I feel like this is the second quarter in a row where military is coming a little bit lighter. I guess how do we think about what's driving some of that slowness within the military training platforms and how you're thinking about the pickup in Q4 and into '27?

Daniel Satterfield: Yes. The military, in particular, on the Component Repair side, the inputs have fallen significantly. We are seeing that this is an impact of the Middle Eastern conflict. We're calling it really not a shift in funding, but a shift in outlays, right? As engines remain in theater for longer and for operational readiness of the conflict, maintenance, in particular, on some of the training platforms that make up a large part of component repair military platforms are suffering. Not forever, as you know, the engine maintenance is not discretionary. It will come back, although I don't think this is going to be something, and I'm not going to call how long the conflict is going to last.

But as long as it does, we're going to see some shift between outlays between programs. Now you're not seeing that as much on the total military end market, and that has to do with the Q2 announced new business that we're receiving on NATO platforms unrelated to the component repair business.

Operator: Our next question comes from the line of Seth Seifman with JPMorgan.

Seth Seifman: Russ, congrats and it's been a pleasure. Paul, congrats as well. I wanted to ask just starting off on the sales from Component Repair into Engine Services. As Engine Services has grown, we haven't really seen growth in the internal sales. When would you expect that to pick up? And what does the trajectory of that look like in the coming years?

Daniel Satterfield: Yes. Thanks. That's the in-sourcing effort that we've talked about. That continues, right? As you know, when we launched this in-sourcing activity, the lower-hanging fruits, we've taken advantage of. Now there's additional work to do. There was a business -- a discrete business piece that we lost that is going to impact that in-sourcing impact. But we're continuing to proceed on it. In Q3, it was up 1% versus the prior year.

Russell Ford: Seth, we talked about it last quarter, it was the "Conair" contract. We're still getting the parts for the part repair side of it, but we no longer run that contract on the ES side. That's parts that are now reported as external sales. That affects the in-sourcing number.

Seth Seifman: Okay. Okay. Excellent. And then maybe as a follow-up, Paul, when you talk about making it a priority to be the leader in LEAP MRO over the next few decades, what does it take to be that leader? Is there -- do you have kind of the capacity for that? Is that something that will require more capacity over time? Is there something about the customers that you've gathered thus far or see potential to gather in the future? What's going to sort of differentiate StandardAero and allow you to have that leadership position?

Paul McElhinney: Thanks, Seth. Yes. So interestingly, as I said in the comments earlier, I've spent probably 15 years in my career on the other side of the table in LEAP. So LEAP was one of the big program launches that we had when I was running the aftermarket. I was heavily involved in designing the aftermarket strategy for LEAP from a GE perspective and a Safran perspective. Honestly, it's one of the real reasons I thought about taking the job as CEO. In my opinion, this will become the most successful commercial engine in history. It's already proving that in orders. We've made significant investments to prepare for LEAP volume.

We're well on our way and tracking closely to what we've told you and others for some time, which is we turned profitable this year. We see a very clear sight to $1 billion of revenue by 2030. The pipeline is quite strong. A lot of demand, constrained supply, constrained capacity. I'm very confident, firstly, about the overall LEAP volumes that are coming for the industry. Then inside that, Seth, I would say I'm particularly confident about the positioning of StandardAero and what we can do as a partner to CFM and what we can do for our customers, and that's proving itself every day as we win additional contracts.

And for the full year, if you could ballpark commercial end market growth accounting for those eliminations, that would be helpful, too.

Daniel Satterfield: That's right. Yes. Commercial was, what, 1.3% growth. Excluding that, it's high single digits, you'll see that on the page. And then the -- for the full year commercial growth, we're calling high teens, ex material takeout.

Andrew Steinhardt: Could you quantify what's the takeout?

Daniel Satterfield: It's right. We think -- we called the material takeout for the full year, we were saying $350 million to $400 million. It's now going to be closer to $300 million. As you recall, in Q1, it was a minimal impact. Then Q2, it was significant and Q3 and Q4 are going to be right in line with expectations. We kind of lost the quarter, and we're saying the full material takeout impact instead of $350 million to $400 million would be closer to $300 million for the full year.

Andrew Steinhardt: Got you. Okay. And just on CRS margins, can you talk about how the work migration efforts have progressed since last quarter?

Daniel Satterfield: Yes. There's a great opportunity there that between -- that we launched between our -- some of our back shops and the Cincinnati site, where capability and on that repair was already in place. That continues to occur. There are even more opportunities out in the future that we're going to take advantage of across our -- we have 50 sites in total at StandardAero. Most of the MRO sites have what are called back shops that do component repair for the engines in the shop, right, for a quick turnaround. When these back shops have additional capability and capacity, that's an opportunity for the overloaded CRS sites to offload, and we're taking full advantage of that.

Paul McElhinney: Andrew, this is Paul. Just a couple of comments. Firstly, CRS is a very strategic part of the business. I've spent a lot of my career running repair businesses in the aftermarket. Quite apart from the fact that they're financially very attractive for the company, their impact on customers is very important and very impactful to their turnaround times, lowering the cost of maintenance. It's a key part of our offering to our customers. In the first 3 weeks here, I've spent time with our repair teams in both Dallas and Cincinnati, which are 2 of our larger repair locations. Demand is not an issue here. Commercial demand, very robust, I would say.

The entire focus of the team is on internal execution, increasing and improving throughput. You can expect me to be spending quite a bit of time with that team, and I look forward to sharing some of the results of the work we're doing here, improving that as we go forward.

Paul McElhinney: Thanks for the question, Kristine. The investments we did, the company has positioned itself extraordinarily well for LEAP. You're right, LEAP is near and dear to my heart as an engine product. It's exciting for me to now sit on this side of the table and be able to talk to customers about how we support them and their needs. Kristine Liwag: Great. Super helpful. And if I could add a second question. On the 4Q CRS margins, the implied for the quarter will be 27.5%, so a sequential increase versus this quarter. So how do you -- how much visibility do you have into that recovery? And is that sequential margin expansion dependent on the return of the military programs you guys have previously discussed?

Daniel Satterfield: Yes. Thanks, Kristine. The decline in margins that we called out had to do with some -- 2 things, really the residual effects from the labor ramp. Don't forget, the commercial business of CRS is booming. A lot of strong volumes there. Their volumes are being somewhat depressed because of the military issues that we mentioned before due to the outlay change as a result of the Middle Eastern conflict. What that has an impact on the margin rates is that military business is a pretty good business. Losing that has a negative mix impact. Then we have some residual effects from the labor ramp on the commercial business, which is quite strong.

That we're working through that we have a better line of sight to recovery than on the military side, which is dependent on the macro.

Gavin Parsons: Russ and Paul, congrats to you guys both. Paul, I guess sort of echoing Seth's question a little bit on CRS, which you brought up as a priority. I've talked about. So I've been a little surprised that one has grown slower than ES for a couple of years now. So just any insights you can shed on that and how you might quantify the growth opportunity there over the medium term would be helpful.

Paul McElhinney: Thanks for the question, Gavin. CRS is very strategic for me, a very important part of our customer tool set and the offerings that we can give them. I would say, right now, I see a lot of demand. I intend to spend a fair amount of time with the team helping them get to where we need to be with the offerings.

Gavin Parsons: And then on the military side, I think you guys do have a lot of exposure to deployed assets, something like C-130, V-22. I mean any way to help us frame your exposure to those versus, say, the training platforms where the drag is today, rough order of magnitude?

Daniel Satterfield: Yes. So we're really -- those are our fixed wing transport aircraft that we support, and they're in good shape. When we talk about the military issues, it is primarily related in large part to these training programs that are -- the demand is not going away, it will definitely come back. These are programs that the U.S. Air Force needs more pilots on. As far as the C-130 or the AE2100 and the Osprey or the 1107 programs, those are looking good. That's why we're having still a strong military guide, low double digits for the full year.

Edward Morgan: This is Ned Morgan on for Andre. Russ, congrats on a great tenure as CEO. And Paul, we look forward to working with you. #3189. Claude’s new Personal Finance tool aims to help analyze your spending – read-only, of course

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Anthropic has released what appears to be its answer to ChatGPT Finances.

You can now share your financial information with Claude and ask the chatbot for insights on your spending.

Also: Researchers asked people to use AI chatbots for election info

Personal Finance in Claude, which Anthropic announced Thursday, reviews your connected accounts through read-only access via Plaid. That security measure follows OpenAI’s equivalent feature, ChatGPT Finances, which launched in May. Here’s what to know.

Functionally, this feature appears similar to ChatGPT Finances: It lets you link as many bank and credit card accounts as you’d like to Claude via Plaid with read-only access. You can then ask Claude where you spent your money this month or whether you can afford to take a vacation in six months, for example.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Also: Stop sharing your passwords with AI agents

According to Anthropic, the feature is a response to existing use patterns: the company’s April usage report found that financial advice was one of the main topics users ask Claude for help with.

“For the accounts you choose to connect (and only those), Claude sees the bank’s name, each account’s name, type, and last four digits, balances and credit limits, and up to two years of transactions. When you chat with Claude in the Personal Finance hub, those conversations aren’t used to train our models.”

The idea behind the feature is that you can ask follow-up questions and request more insights about spending habits, trends over time, and future goals based on what Claude finds, similar to any other Claude conversation. The tool will also generate tables and charts to visualize your financial information.

“You can ask for a weekly spending chart, a calendar of what’s due, or a dashboard of the numbers you choose, and Claude builds it as an artifact you can keep adjusting and coming back to,” an Anthropic representative told ZDNET via email.

Also: I connected ChatGPT to my bank, and it’s my go-to finance app now

You can also expect an ad-free experience in the feature.

“Like the rest of Claude, Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it doesn’t offer credit cards, loans, or savings accounts of its own, so your money questions get a straight answer,” the company said in the announcement.

The company added that because Claude is using actual transaction data and not memory, the feature shouldn’t hallucinate.

“It can list the exact transactions behind any number so you can check its math,” Anthropic said via email. “Like any AI, it can make mistakes, so for anything important, we recommend confirming with your bank.”

Still, the difference — and for many, the appeal — here is the natural language interface. Other finance apps don’t necessarily have an easy, accessible chat function where users can shoot off quick questions like they would to a human financial planner. These assistants also present historical budget analysis in plain English, rather than requiring users to interpret dashboards themselves, which users may see as a perk.

Also: 5 ways to use AI when your budget is tight

On Reddit, many users find ChatGPT Finances to be accurate and reliable. One Reddit user said ChatGPT Finance seemed to have Mint or Monarch potential, but noted it was still “weaker” than those apps in some areas, such as historical syncing, high-quality dashboards, and generating full statement PDFs.

“ChatGPT has genuinely helped me make better financial decisions,” she wrote.

Anthropic noted that users shouldn’t look to Personal Finance for Claude as a total authority. “Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust,” the company said in the announcement.

“We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it” — indicating a more integrated financial planning system within Claude may be on the way.

#3187. OpenAI and Anthropic Drop New AI Tools for Cybersecurity, Images and Finance

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Here are three AI product drops you might've missed this week.

Every week is a busy week in the artificial intelligence industry, and this week is no exception. As voters expressed serious concerns about AI and data centers at the ballot box, OpenAI and Anthropic — makers of ChatGPT and Claude, respectively — each dropped new updates to make their chatbots a little more capable.

All these changes come amid rapidly changing government and financial environments. The midterm elections, in which Democrats handily beat Republican candidates across the country, showed that anti-AI and anti-Big Tech campaigns resonated with voters. Tech critics told CNET this week that there is a clear desire for government officials at every level to change how they interact with technology companies — to keep their campaign promises. The election results are also shaking up Wall Street, as investors’ fears about AI’s long-term financial viability grow.

Smaller updates like these are helpful for everyday AI users, and there’s a benefit for AI companies, too. They can prove they’re competitive in a market that is losing confidence in AI. Here are the three biggest AI updates to ChatGPT and Claude.

Gone are the days when every new AI tool got an immediate general release — and that’s probably for the best. Now, when a major AI lab has a new frontier AI model, it slow-rolls its access, and it starts with cybersecurity defenders. That’s exactly what OpenAI did with its newest model variant, GPT-6 Cyber.

Introducing GPT‑6 Cyber: a major advance in security research that pairs stronger capabilities with better model alignment.The model powered the Linux kernel research we announced yesterday, and security teams at companies like Mozilla, Palo Alto Networks, Calif, and… pic.twitter.com/34uAeNnhwP

GPT-6 Cyber is a version of OpenAI’s newest flagship model that’s specifically made for security research and work. OpenAI says it’s best at finding vulnerabilities and staying in its secure container. Those two things matter a lot. Earlier this fall, an OpenAI model was partially responsible for helping researchers identify a major vulnerability in PHP, a programming language that’s used in the majority of websites. And any improvements to keep AI secure are necessary. We saw many instances this summer of AI agents breaking out of their testing environments and making cybersecurity experts fear future autonomous hacks.

You won’t be able to use GPT-6 Cyber unless you’re a cybersecurity expert who’s part of OpenAI’s Daybreak program. Cisco and Mozilla teams are already using the model, according to OpenAI.

OpenAI also added a minor model update to its AI image model, called ChatGPT Images 2.6. The biggest improvement is its speed; OpenAI says the new model is 50% faster than before. That matters for AI enthusiasts who are generating multiple variations of a prompt. The new model also lets you animate your AI images into short GIFs. It’s available globally now for all ChatGPT users.

This isn’t the return of the long-dead Sora AI video model, but it is a sign that OpenAI isn’t giving up on the creative AI space entirely. Anthropic, by comparison, has never had a traditional AI image or video generator and opted for a design tool that’s better suited for mocking up websites and apps.

Anthropic is teaming up with fintech platform Plaid to help you bring your financial information into its Claude chatbot.

Both companies say they have strong security measures in place to keep your information safe. But CNET always recommends a cautious approach when it comes to sharing your financial information (or any sensitive information) with an AI product.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

#3186. 6 default Pixel 11 settings I changed that made a big difference – and why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

If you’re a new Pixel 11 user, here are six things I recommend changing right away to get the most from your phone.

I’ve been a dedicated Pixel user since the beginning, so I was naturally excited to get my hands on Google’s latest iteration, the Pixel 11 Pro XL. I’ve been impressed with it overall, but I noticed that, as Google has done before, the device isn’t set up perfectly out of the box.

Also: Pixel 11 is $200 off in this early Black Friday deal

After spending a few weeks with the device, I found that several features are either turned off by default or need optimizing to work in the best way possible.

If you’re a new Pixel 11 user, here are six things I recommend changing right away to get the most from your phone.

The camera was the biggest reason I first joined team Pixel back in 2016, so it’s one of the first places I looked on the Pixel 11 Pro XL. New this year is Camera Looks, a setting that changes how images will be processed before you take them. You can change a number of settings, including contrast, shadows, tint, sharpness, and warmth.

Also: A week with the Pixel 11 changed my mind about Gemini

I’ve always loved the camera on any Pixel I’ve had, but I’ll admit that images can look a little over-processed at times. If picture quality is important to you at all, it’s vital to set this feature right out of the box because it applies to every image you take from that point on. You can find Camera Look by opening the camera app, tapping the settings icon in the bottom-right corner, and making your changes.

Pixel’s “At a Glance” lock screen widgets are one of the most sneakily useful features, and you’re missing out if you’re not using them. These widgets are off by default, but when you enable them, you can see real-time information without unlocking your phone. You can see weather info, sports updates, flight information, rideshare and food delivery updates, fitness information, and more.

Also: These tech gifts topped our experts’ 2026 holiday wish lists

To use these widgets, long-press on an open space on your home screen. To customize your widgets, go to Settings > Wallpaper & style > More lock screen settings > Widgets on lock screen. To access your widgets, you just swipe left from your lock screen.

Out of the box, your Pixel 11’s display isn’t set to utilize its full capability. The Pixel 11 series comes with a fantastic low-temperature polycrystalline oxide (LTPO) display, but it’s slightly throttled in the name of battery life. You’ll notice the increased resolution most on text and in fine details. It won’t make a huge difference to your streaming or large display elements, though. If you read consistently, either articles or e-books, you’ll want to make the change.

To change this, head to Settings > Display > Screen Resolution. Bump the setting from “High resolution,” which is 1080 x 2404, to “Max resolution,” which is 1344 x 2992.

If you’re anything like me, your phone usually needs a quick charge some evenings. The Pixel 11 series introduced Extreme Charging Mode, which accelerates charging by pausing background activity and non-essential apps. Google says the mode should charge the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro to over 50% in 30 minutes, and the Pixel 11 Pro XL to 75% in 30 minutes. From my testing, that estimate was pretty accurate.

Also: After testing the Pixel 11, I feel fine about skipping the Pro models

There are a few caveats: this feature is only available when your phone is at or below 50% battery, and you do need to turn it on every time you use it. But after the first time you do it, it’s available in your quick settings. Head to Settings > Battery & charging > Extreme Charging to turn it on the first time.

If you have the newest Pixel, you might as well take advantage of one of its biggest selling points. I felt like this feature was gimmicky at first (and I’m still a little grumpy it replaced my beloved thermometer), but the more I use it, the more I like it. The multicolor LED on the phone’s rear camera bump can indicate who’s calling, serve as a status indicator for Gemini, and more — and it’s almost certain that more usability will arrive over time.

Where I found the most use was when I had my phone on silent. After assigning specific colors to contacts (you can do this from the contact information screen), I could easily see whether a call was worth picking up without reaching for my phone.

To make sure you’re getting the most out of your new device, head in and change your contact HiLight colors right away. It only takes a few seconds and makes deciding whether to answer a call a lot easier.

We’ve all accidentally swiped away an important notification or missed a notification in a sea of updates. The Pixel 11 offers two notification features to help you stay on top of things.

Notification History is a feature that logs every alert from the last 24 hours, including those you swipe away. This is off by default, meaning when you dismiss a notification, it’s gone forever. With this on, you get a searchable, chronological backup.

Also: Google’s big flagship is more Pro than ever

AI Notification Summaries, as the name implies, takes long multi-notification threads and stacked notifications and turns them into bullet points. This feature is powered by on-device Gemini Intelligence, and you can choose which apps to summarize.

You can find both of these under Settings > Notifications > Notification history & Notification Summaries.

#3185. Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge

A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.

Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields for Nvidia-backed CoreWeave continued to reach new heights. (An article in The Financial Times that the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showing CoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield. Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%. Nebius Group and Iren, popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.

Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

#3184. Nvidia Stock Has More Than 60% Upside According to Analysts' Average Price Target. Should You Buy While the AI Trade Wobbles?

Nvidia stock looks cheaper, and its growth prospects are well intact.

Investors are skeptical of many AI stocks right now, questioning the long-term return on investment for tech companies spending so much on data center infrastructure. And as a leading semiconductor company for AI infrastructure, Nvidia (NVDA +2.77%) has felt the pain from the sell-off, with its share price falling 13% over the past month.

That's put Nvidia's share price at around $202, far below analysts' average price target for Nvidia stock of $327. If it reaches that target, investors stand to gain around 62%. So, is now the right time to buy Nvidia stock, despite the concerns about AI spending?

I think so, especially given that recent tech earnings reports indicate tech companies are likely to continue investing in infrastructure over the next few years.

Let's start with SK Hynix's (SKHY +2.78%) recently reported third-quarter results. The company is the leading high-bandwidth (HBM) memory company with 50% market share and the second-largest DRAM and NAND flash memory company with 24% and 19% market share, respectively.

The company has benefited immensely from a ramp-up in AI spending, sending its sales 328% higher in the quarter and its operating profit up 632%. Even more impressive is that the company's management said in a press release that 50% of its available memory supply for 2027-2028 is already sold out -- and that it expects its supply to remain constrained through 2030.

What does this have to do with Nvidia? Well, SK Hynix is the leading supplier of HBM memory for many of Nvidia's data center components. If SK Hynix is experiencing exponential demand for its memory processors, part of that is due to Nvidia placing substantial orders. And if Nvidia is placing large orders for memory, it's because AI spending continues to rise.

This leads me to Alphabet's and Microsoft's recent cloud sales. These two companies hold a combined 35% of the cloud market, and they're both experiencing impressive sales gains from their AI spending. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled in the third quarter to $30.7 billion and Microsoft's Azure sales rose 48% to $33.2 billion.

Alphabet says it will spend up to $205 billion this year in capital expenditures (capex), mostly for AI. Microsoft says it will spend $170 billion in fiscal 2027. That's an acceleration of spending for both companies and it's a result of Microsoft and Alphabet realizing that their cloud investments are paying off.

And they're not the only ones. Bank of America said recently that AI data center spending is estimated to more than double to $2.1 trillion by 2028. While investors are rightly concerned that some AI spending is too high and won't be worth the investment, Alphabet and Microsoft are already benefiting from their spending and are doubling down.

Again, that's great news for Nvidia because these two companies are critical customers for Nvidia, and it's a good indicator that AI infrastructure investments aren't slowing down yet.

Nvidia's shares have a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of around 26 right now, which makes them slightly cheaper than the tech sector P/E average of 28.5. Investors don't have to back the truck up and go all-in on Nvidia stock right now. But the recent pullback does present a buying opportunity for some investors to start a small position or add to an existing one.

The chipmaker will report its fiscal 2027's third quarter results on Nov. 17 and Wall Street's consensus estimates are for earnings per share of $2.47 and nearly $109 billion in sales. Considering Nvidia has beaten analysts' earnings estimates in seven of the past eight quarters, shareholders could be pleasantly surprised again soon.

More importantly, with Nvidia's customers already experiencing significant growth and continuing to invest in AI, Nvidia's long-term growth prospects remain intact.
